sources.citation: James McClure Glasgow missionary journal (https://revjamesmcclureglasgow.blogspot.com/), first-person journal repeatedly identifying Adam as James’s brother and tracing his movements from Belfast to New Zealand (accessed 17 July 2026).

History of Knox Church, Dunedin (https://archive.org/details/historyofgreatam02myer), account identifying Adam Dickey Glasgow as born at Ballymena, Ulster, in 1815 and stating that he joined his brother Dr. Glasgow in India (accessed 17 July 2026).

Emigration to New Zealand
Adam emigrated from Ireland to New Zealand about 1861.

His burial record states that he had lived in New Zealand for two years at the time of his death. His last address was Dunedin, and his occupation was recorded as minister.
Death and burial
Adam died at Dunedin, Otago, New Zealand, on 18 March 1863, aged 48.

His death was registered in New Zealand in 1863 under the name Adam Dickie Glasgow. New Zealand Births, Deaths and Marriages, death registration 1863/2037, Adam Dickie Glasgow, aged 48.

sources.citation: William Macafee, Names of Householders Listed in the 1831 Census Returns for the County of Londonderry (https://www.billmacafee.com/1831census/1831derrycensusnames.pdf), p. 231, record 28190: Adam Glasco, house 91, Inishrush, Tamlaght O'Crilly; one family containing three males and five females, all Presbyterian (accessed 16 July 2026).

On 3 October 1831 Adam gave notice that he intended to register at the Magherafelt General Sessions on 2 January 1832 as the holder of a £10 freehold comprising “Houses and Lands” in Inishrush, barony of Loughinsholin. The notice is direct evidence that Adam claimed a legally qualifying interest in the Inishrush property, but it does not prove that his registration was accepted or identify his landlord, predecessor, relatives or lease lives. Londonderry Sentinel, 8 October 1831, p. 3, article 44, row 97 (https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0001480/18311008/044/0003), notice dated 3 October 1831 for registration at Magherafelt General Sessions on 2 January 1832: Adam Glasgow, Innisrush, £10 freehold, “Houses and Lands” in Innisrush, barony of Loughinsholin (inspected 10 August 2026).

Public Record Office of Northern Ireland, Tithe Applotment Book for Tamlaght O'Crilly parish, 5 November 1833, PRONI FIN/5/A/254B, image 20, manuscript folio 16, Inishrush no. 1; duplicate full-page scan PRONI FIN/5/A/254A, images 42–44 (inspected 10 August 2026). The National Archives of Ireland's source guide (https://www.nationalarchives.ie/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/Family_History_Sources_NAI.pdf) explains that tithe acreages are normally in Irish or Plantation measure, equivalent to 1.62 statute acres.
Public Record Office of Northern Ireland, Valuation Revision Book, PRONI VAL/12/B/34/10A, Inishrush plot 29, James Glasgow, 1860–1863.

"Tamlaght O'Crilly Lower Graveyard" (https://www.oneirishrover.com/tamlaght-graveyard/), transcription and photograph of the Glasgow gravestone recording Rose Glasgow, wife of Adam, who died 31 July 1833 aged 66; Adam Glasgow, who died 30 June 1844 aged 86; their children Eliza and James; and grandson William Glasgow (accessed 16 July 2026).

* Eliza Glasgow, who died aged 26. The gravestone identifies her as their daughter, but the surviving inscription does not preserve a clear death date. 

A further documented daughter of Adam was:

* Nancy Glasgow, who married John Kyle of Tyanee on 14 January 1842. The marriage notice described her as Adam's sixth daughter. The notice does not name Nancy's mother, although Rose is the likely mother. "Marriage Notices 1840–42" (https://cotyrone.com/~inthenews/marriages-notices-1840-42/), notice published 29 January 1842: John Kyle of Tyanee married Nancy, sixth daughter of Adam Glasgow of Inishrush, on 14 January 1842 (accessed 16 July 2026).

William's civil death registration describes him as a bachelor farmer of Inishrush and names Lindsey Glasgow as his brother and the person present at his death. The registration confirms an additional member of the later family but still does not identify their parents. IrishGenealogy.ie (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/en/), civil death registrations for James Glasgow of Inishrush, December 1878, and William Glasgow of Inishrush, 21 November 1882.

He was buried or commemorated with Rose in Tamlaght O'Crilly Lower Churchyard, also known as St Nossonus's Churchyard, near Inishrush, County Londonderry.

The gravestone does not state Adam's place of death. Inishrush is probable because he was recorded there in 1831 and was still described as being “of Inishrush” in Nancy's 1842 marriage notice. 
Research Notes
Birth
Adam's approximate birth year is calculated from the gravestone statement that he was aged 86 when he died in June 1844.

No baptism or other contemporary record has been found stating his birth date or place. His birth should therefore be recorded as about 1758 and marked uncertain.

The available evidence does not prove that Adam was born in Ireland, County Londonderry, Tamlaght O'Crilly or Inishrush.
Possible 1799 reference
A County Londonderry declaration supporting the Act of Union includes an Adam Glasco among the subscribers in September 1799.

The original newspaper image gives no address or ditto mark after Adam's name. The apparent association with a nearby place in a derivative HTML abstract resulted from separate newspaper columns being flattened together.

The signatory may be Adam Glasgow of Inishrush, but the county-level entry does not prove his identity or residence and should not be used as evidence that he lived at Inishrush in 1799. Belfast News-Letter, 27 September 1799, original newspaper image reviewed during research; compare derivative name and place abstract (https://www.kinsleuth.com/belnews/1790-1800.htm) (abstract accessed 17 July 2026; original image rechecked 10 August 2026).

William Macafee, 1740 Protestant Householders' Return (https://www.billmacafee.com/1740returns/1740religiousreturnsulstername.pdf); collector-order transcription for Tamlaght O'Crilly (https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/books/Kilrea/Kilrea07.html), surviving typescript PRONI T/808/15258 (accessed 17 July 2026).
Belfast News-Letter extracts for the Kilrea area (https://arborealis.ca/records/newspapers/kilrea-news/1770-1779/), notice dated 14 April 1772 (accessed 17 July 2026).

Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, Will Book 3, no. 252, pp. 492–493, will-book image (https://www.ancestry.com/imageviewer/collections/8802/images/005537856_00276?pid=1733435); corresponding loose probate packet, FamilySearch DGS 5538049, images 239–243, packet cover (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QS7-L991-GV6H?cc=1999196&wc=9PMK-MNG%3A268499101%2C281697201) (accessed 17 July 2026).
Registry of Deeds memorials 74015 (https://www.irishdeedsindex.net/mem.php?memorial=74015) and 76724 (https://www.irishdeedsindex.net/mem.php?memorial=76724) (accessed 17 July 2026).

Dublin Gazette, 13–15 December 1785, no. 4695 (https://virtualtreasury.ie/item/DGZ-1785-4695); Johnston, Roll of Commissioned Officers in the Medical Service of the British Army, 1917 (https://archive.org/details/rollofcommission00ande/page/61/mode/1up), p. 61 (accessed 17 July 2026).

Richard John Torrens, "Kilrea First Presbyterian Church Records: Baptisms in 1827" (https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/KilreaP1/Baptisms/1827.html), entry 146: Robert, son of Daniel Glasgow and Margaret Irwin of Kilrea, born 1 September and baptised 30 September 1827 (accessed 16 July 2026).
PRONI Will Calendars (https://apps.proni.gov.uk/willscalendar_ie/willssearch.aspx), registered will of Daniel Glasgow of Kilrea, 1871.

Genes Reunited descendant account (https://www.genesreunited.co.uk/boards/board/general_topics/thread/465937), naming Alexander Glasgow and Rosanna Shaw as Thomas Glasgow's parents; considered with Daniel Glasgow's 1871 will naming Thomas as his late brother (reviewed 10 August 2026).

Tamlaght O'Crilly 1831 census transcription (https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/Tamlaght/1831census_3.html), entry 1019: John Glasco, Inishrush house 2, four males and four females, all Presbyterian (reviewed 10 August 2026).
John Glasgow family page and Bible images (https://hiltner.com/mckeown/getperson.php?personID=I368&tree=tree1), Bible printed in 1797 (accessed 17 July 2026).

John Glasgow to Jane Glasgow Gray, 20 March 1847 (https://www.hiltner.com/mckeown/documents/John%20Glasgow%20letter%20to%20Jane%20Glasgow%20Gray%203-20-1847.pdf), scan and transcript (accessed 17 July 2026).

The strongest current working hypothesis is that John was Adam's brother; cousin remains a live alternative. No accessible record explicitly calls them brothers or names a shared parent, so John should not be attached to Adam as a proved sibling.

John's sons were Adam, James, John and Arthur, and his second daughter was Maria. If John and Adam were brothers, this order is consistent with traditional naming patterns and makes an older Adam and Maria the leading candidate names for their shared parents. This is indirect naming evidence only and does not identify real people who can yet be attached. Scotland's People, “Forenames” (https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/help-and-support/guides/forenames), discussion of traditional Scottish naming patterns; considered with John's family Bible (reviewed 10 August 2026).

Marriage registration image, 17 March 1851: James Glasgow, aged 38, farmer of Inishrush, son of Adam Glasgow, and Rosanna Barkley, daughter of Henry Barkley; reviewed during research on 10 August 2026.

First Kilrea Presbyterian marriage register (https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/KilreaP1/Marriages/1825.html), 6 October 1825: Mary Patton of Tyanee, daughter of John Patton and Margaret Glasgow, married Wilson Gordon (reviewed 10 August 2026).

Glasgow Y-DNA project (https://www.familytreedna.com/public/Glasgow?iframe=ydna-results-overview); FamilyTreeDNA, “Understanding Y-DNA Genetic Distance” (https://help.familytreedna.com/hc/en-us/articles/6019925167631-Understanding-Y-DNA-Genetic-Distance); Legacy Tree Genealogists, public Glasgow Y-DNA report, 2016 (https://www.legacytree.com/wp-content/uploads/T1508095.CLIENTGlasgow1508.report.public.pdf) (accessed 17 July 2026).
County Londonderry church-record inventory (https://www.billmacafee.com/churchrecords/churchrecordsderry.pdf), Drumbolg or Drimbolg entry, PRONI MIC1C/15 (accessed 17 July 2026).

Findmypast, “Ireland, 1766 Religious Census” (https://www.findmypast.co.uk/discover/census-land-and-surveys/census/ireland-1766-religious-census); Roots Ireland, County Derry census-substitute coverage (https://www.rootsireland.ie/derry-genealogy/derry-census-substitutes/); Findmypast, “Ireland, 1775 Dissenters' Petitions” (https://www.findmypast.ie/discover/census-land-and-surveys/census/ireland-1775-dissenters-petitions) (accessed 17 July 2026).

PRONI D1201/53, an 1853 Encumbered Estates rental concerning the Hercules and Eliza Ellis estate at Inishrush, Shilling Hill and Drumane, contains no Glasgow in its indexed Inishrush entries. The material appears to concern a different portion of the intermixed townland and should not be used as evidence that Adam or his successors lacked an Inishrush holding. PRONI D1201/53, Encumbered Estates rental for the Hercules and Eliza Ellis estate at Inishrush, Shilling Hill and Drumane, 14 April 1853; collection index and rental reviewed 10 August 2026.
PRONI T1762, item-level catalogue hierarchy, Glasgow-family item concerning William Glasgow of Oritor, County Tyrone (reviewed 10 August 2026).
Presbyterian Historical Society of Ireland, G61 Glasgow envelope, catalogue description reviewed 10 August 2026.
*Londonderry Sentinel*, 8 October 1831, p. 3, article 44, row 97 (https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0001480/18311008/044/0003).
Loughinshollen list heading (https://ulsterlees.azurewebsites.net/records/census/).
1831 census householder transcription (https://www.billmacafee.com/1831census/1831derrycensusnames.pdf).

* James Glasgow, christened 8 September 1707. Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950, database, FamilySearch (VQ4K-6MS (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQ4K-6MS)), James Glasgou, christening 8 September 1707, Kirknewton and East Calder, Midlothian, Scotland; father Alexander Glasgou.

Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950, database, FamilySearch (VQ4K-H54 (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQ4K-H54)), Marion Glasgou, christening 18 May 1711, Kirknewton and East Calder, Midlothian, Scotland; father Alexander Glasgou.

James Glasgow and Marion Glasgow were christened after Alexander's 1705 marriage to Janet Graham. Their christening records name Alexander as father but do not name a mother. Janet is therefore a plausible mother of both children, but the relationship should not be treated as proven solely from these records.

No source for Alexander Glasgow as a child has yet been included in this profile.
Research Notes
This profile incorporates information previously represented by two profiles for an Alexander Glasgow.

One profile gave Alexander's birth year as 1685. However, the indexed parish record identifies an Alexander Glasgow born on 7 July 1673 and christened on 20 July 1673 at Kirknewton and East Calder, with father Alexander Glasgow. The 1673 date is therefore used here. The origin of the 1685 date remains unclear.

The family chronology is:

* 7 July 1673 — birth of Alexander Glasgow. 
* 7 November 1701 — marriage to Margaret Aikman. 
* 21 November 1703 — christening of their son Andrew Glasgow, with both parents named. 
* 16 November 1705 — marriage of Alexander Glasgow to Janet Graham. 
* 8 September 1707 — christening of James Glasgow, father Alexander named but no mother recorded. 
* 18 May 1711 — christening of Marion Glasgow, father Alexander named but no mother recorded. 

This sequence is consistent with one Alexander Glasgow marrying Margaret Aikman in 1701 and Janet Graham in 1705. It also explains why Andrew can be assigned to Margaret while the maternity of James and Marion remains uncertain.
Current research
FamilySearch VQ4K-X9V supports Alexander's 1673 Kirknewton event and names his father Alexander. His 7 November 1701 marriage to Margaret Aikman and their children are separately indexed.

Glasgow-3119 may duplicate him, but that profile supplies no birth source. Its structured 1673 date and same-father attachment conflict with its biography's 1685 estimate. Its 1705 marriage to Janet Graham could be a second marriage or could identify another Alexander.

This assessment draws on the cited records and public source material. www.familysearch.org (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQ4K-X9V).

The reported 1829 occurrence: an age and identity test
The original newspaper alert of 12 September 2025 was inspected directly on 13 September 2026. Its MyHeritage result, 12021-100828509 MyHeritage result, 12021-100828509 (https://www.myheritage.com/research/record-12021-100828509-/alexander-glasgow-in-united-kingdom-names-stories-in-newspapers-from-oldnewscom).

independently locates the Lisnagaver entry in page 4, article 015. Its OCR mangles Glasgow, explaining why a surname search missed the article while a townland search found it. These are two derivative extracts of one newspaper occurrence, not two independent historical records.

The archive’s damaged heading excerpt appears to concern persons applying to register, with special sessions at Ballymoney, under County of Antrim. That makes a registration notice the specific working context, but the full image and governing columns remain unread: MyHeritage now presents a subscription paywall and the archive viewer requires sign-in. The extract cannot yet establish an adult qualification, successful registration or the man’s identity. The earlier claim that even the alert was uninspected is superseded; the historical interpretation remains open.

The important distinction is between an older birth date for the same man and a second, older man. Even if the notice proves adult status, it would not automatically make the subject Alexander's father. Conversely, identifying the subject from the 1888 age and then using him to validate that same death identification would be circular. No birth estimate or parent ranking changes on the extract alone.

If the subject is Alexander-951, the occurrence would support a premarital Lisnagaver association before the couple's Gortereagh baptisms of 1837–38 and their documented Lisnagaver residence by 1843. That would make a temporary residence near Mary's possible family a more focused hypothesis; it would not prove a move, tenancy or inheritance.

The supplied extract also lists Robert Elder of Gortaragh, Arthur O'Neil of Tehorney, Henry and James Wallace of Culmore, James Tomb of Ballymaconly and James Elder of Drumcon. Their combined names and literal place spellings are useful for locating the correct column despite imperfect OCR. They must not yet be treated as neighbours, fellow freeholders or relatives. The 1829 Robert Elder cannot comfortably be the later son-in-law whose 1871 marriage gives age forty and father Nathaniel; the corresponding 1894 death 1894 death (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/deaths_returns/deaths_1894/05952/4691448.pdf).

Research Notes
Testing the 1888 death identification
The death at Gortahar on 16 May 1888 remains the best-supported located match for Alexander Glasgow of Lisnagaver (Glasgow-951), but its identification is probable rather than uniquely proved. The case rests on a connected family and landholding sequence. The register supplies an exact death date; uncertainty concerns the deceased’s identity, not the precision of that date.
The record and its limits
Original death entry 348 supplies the following details. Nancy’s age and marital status are not recorded; no wife, parent, birthplace or former Lisnagaver address identifies the deceased more narrowly.

The identity chain, in dependency order
# The 1851 Lisnagaver house-35 return establishes Alexander and wife Mary, both reported aged 40, with children Robert, James and Ann. This is the starting household; its identity does not depend on either Gortahar death.
# Mary Glasgow’s 14 June 1871 marriage identifies a 28-year-old Lisnagaver spinster, daughter of Alexander Glasgow, farmer, marrying Robert Elder, 40, farmer of Gortereghy. It directly establishes the bride’s father. Linking that father to the established Lisnagaver household uses name, residence and occupation; the marriage does not name her mother.
# PRONI valuation revisions , VAL/12/B/4/16C–D, follow Alexander’s removal from Lisnagaver lot 25 and Robert Elder’s subsequent occupation. Succession to the particular holding strengthens the identification of Robert with the daughter’s husband. The book neither declares an inheritance nor records Alexander’s destination or exact death. It supplies a separate administrative connection, not another explicit statement of kinship.
# The 16 September 1878 birth of Jane Matilda Elder 16 September 1878 birth of Jane Matilda Elder (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/birth_returns/births_1878/02945/2078820.pdf).

, entry 234, records a widow aged 89 at Gortahar, with daughter Mary Elder present. That named relationship supplies the strongest connection between the elderly Glasgow woman and the Elder family. With the preceding marriage and household evidence, it supports the high-confidence identification of the widow as Mary McCaughan (McCaughan-222). It does not name her deceased husband.
# The 1888 death of a married Alexander Glasgow in the same townland fits the husband of that widow. This last step remains inferential: neither death expressly identifies the other deceased as spouse, and Nancy has not yet been connected independently to the Lisnagaver family.

The 1901 and 1911 Elder households strengthen the family continuation. They are not independent sightings of Alexander. Likewise, the two civil deaths cannot first be assumed to concern a married couple and then cited as independent proof of that assumption. Their combined value depends on the independently established Elder connection.
Ages and occupation: compatibility with genuine conflicts

|-
! style="background:#dce8d5;" | Person !! 1851 reported age !! Later death age !! Approximate discrepancy
|-
| Alexander || 40, implying c.1811 || 84 in 1888, implying c.1804 || Seven years older than expected
|-
| Mary || 40, implying c.1811 || 89 in 1892, implying c.1803 || Eight years older than expected
|}

The two death ages describe near-contemporary people, as does the census, and both imply births several years earlier. This parallel is compatible with one elderly couple whose ages were reported differently across records. It does not prove shared identity: the informants may have had incomplete knowledge, the census ages may be inaccurate, or a namesake could be involved. Neither age should silently replace the maintained approximate birth estimate. The paired pattern becomes relevant only after the family connection has been established.

Alexander’s change from farmer to labourer is less problematic. Ann Glasgow’s 13 October 1876 marriage to Robert McCracken already calls her father Alexander a labourer. Thus the 1888 occupation is compatible with the known father twelve years earlier; it does not require a different man. Conversely, labourer is too common an occupation to identify him by itself.
Nancy and the competing Alexander
Nancy’s possible identification with Ann (Glasgow-438) remains open. Ann had married in 1876 and would ordinarily appear as McCracken. No inspected record calls her Nancy or places her at Gortahar in 1888. Use of Glasgow does not establish that Nancy was unmarried, but it is a real obstacle to equating the two. Another daughter, absent in 1851 or born later, remains possible; no such birth or relationship should be invented.

Alexander of Glenleslie (Glasgow-2385) is a genuine competing labourer. His 1847 marriage to Mary Anne Martin 1847 marriage to Mary Anne Martin (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1847/09322/5375567.pdf).

Nancy's will independently calls Margaret (Dysart) Kennedy her niece and Robert Anderson her nephew, and the Rasharkin Presbyterian register records both as children of Glasgow mothers — Jane Glascaw at Granagh and Betty Glascaw at Drumack. Together these records support a probable network of deceased sibling branches: John, Alexander, Robert, Jane, Elizabeth, Ann and Mary. Elizabeth is identified through the baptism and household records, not named as a parent in the notice. The list's completeness and each person's exact relationship remain to be checked in the underlying petition.

The Alexander of this citation is probably Alexander of Lisnagaver. His daughters' marriages of 1871 and 1876 each name Alexander Glasgow of Lisnagaver as father, his son James was baptised at Lisnagaver in 1843, and he died in May 1888 — "formerly of Rasharkin" in the citation's language. Nancy, born about 1820–21, was roughly ten years his junior: probable sisterhood fits these ages; daughterhood does not. He spent his last years at Gortahar, where the citation places his sister Elizabeth's Anderson sons in 1892. His son Robert is not named. The proposed Scottish continuity and alleged survival to 1902 need original-record verification; this potential omission prevents treating completeness as already demonstrated.

The John of the citation is probably John Glasgow of Lisnagaver; Lizzie and the Ballydonnelly residence remain identity checks. His documented children were Ann (born 1848; married Bellingham in 1875, naming father John) and James Garvin Glasgow — the "James G." of the notice; the "Lizzie" of the notice is an otherwise unrecorded daughter (the Elizabeth Ann on the family memorial, died 1933, was James Garvin's widow). A John Glasgow of Lisnagaver died on 24 June 1885 with son James as informant, which agrees with "late of". General Register Office of Ireland, civil death return, Ballymoney superintendent registrar's district, Dirraw district, entry 2: John Glasgow, Lisnagaver, 24 June 1885; register image (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/deaths_returns/deaths_1885/06280/4799372.pdf).

If Alexander and John shared a father, that father would be John Glasgow, farmer. Probable siblinghood alone does not distinguish a shared father from a shared mother or more complex half relationships.

The same document tells against the alternatives. Thomas Glasgow of Lisnagaver, whom earlier research treated as Alexander's possible brother, died in 1870 leaving children who were adults at Lisnagaver in the 1880s; had he been Nancy's brother they would have been her next of kin, yet none is cited while nieces in New Zealand are. This omission weighs against a simple reconstruction only if expected inclusion and completeness are established. It does not exclude Thomas or his proved brother Daniel as Alexander's brothers or collateral relatives: Alexander could also share a parent with Thomas without Thomas being Nancy's sibling. The tradition naming an older Alexander and Rosanna concerns Thomas; its extension to Alexander of Lisnagaver remains unproved. Likewise no member of the Glenleslie family of Robert Glasgow and Catherine, previously attached as Alexander's parents, appears among Nancy's next of kin; Robert of Doonbought's daughters were Catherine, Margaret, Maria, Netta and Jane, not the Mary Jane and Ann of the citation. The Robert of the citation is more likely the second Lisnagaver tithe occupier of 1834 — 35 acres entered immediately after Alexander's 29 — and perhaps the Robert Glasgow of Gortereghy in Griffith's Valuation who died in Ballymoney district in 1868 aged 71; his daughters have not yet been found. Griffith's Valuation, Rasharkin parish (https://www.failteromhat.com/griffiths/antrim/rasharkin.htm), Glasgow occupiers at Lisnagaver (Alexander, John, Thomas), Gortereghy (Daniel, Robert) and Dromore (James).

The reconstructed family of John Glasgow, farmer, runs from Samuel (about 1790, County Londonderry) through Robert (about 1797), John (about 1801, County Antrim), Jane (about 1804), Alexander (about 1811), Elizabeth (by about 1816), Ann and Mary, to Nancy (about 1820–21) — a span that warrants checking estimated ages, identities and possible multiple unions; it does not establish two marriages of a particular parent. If these identities and a shared household are correct, their different birth counties suggest a possible movement from County Londonderry to Rasharkin parish; the John Glasgow recorded as a Desertoghill flax grower in 1796 (Glasgow-4090) is a plausible but unproved identity for the father, and John of Lisnagaver later married a Desertoghill woman at Garvagh. No record yet names Alexander's father in his own right, and the citation cannot distinguish full from half siblings. The decisive record is Nancy's underlying Clinton County probate petition, which should state each cited person's relationship to her.

What the original Canadian deeds change
The 1861 deed now establishes the Canadian connection for Thomas and Daniel: their documented siblings include Robert and Samuel of Prescott, John the watchmaker, Mary Glasgow Black and brother James. Mary Black’s deed identifies six children, including John and Rose Ann of Drumoolish. Their family records now provide a specific local route to the siblings’ parents, independently of the repeated Alexander-and-Rosanna tradition.

The 1868 father statement belongs to Alexander Glasco of Rochester, express agent, son of James the Prescott carpenter. It cannot be transferred to Alexander-951 without a wife, age, birthplace or migration bridge. The carpenter’s identity with Robert’s brother also remains to be established because the daughters’ property shares do not fit a simple division of the will’s sixth. James is a named family hypothesis to test; the deed has not selected him as Alexander-951’s father. The full family and property analysis distinguishes the established relationships from these identity steps.

Mary/Molly’s parents remain unknown, and James and William McCaheran occur locally. Naming could reflect either side of the family; the surviving child sequence cannot establish a fixed naming rule.

For parentage, the first record priority is the family-group material in PRONI CR5/32/1/1/1–2, alongside the actual source behind the Thomas parent tradition. Extract named households and dated admissions/removals across Alexander’s childhood, rather than another surname-only list. The existing enquiry remains pending. Rosanna’s maternity must be assessed separately from older Alexander’s paternity: even paternal half-brotherhood with Thomas would not transfer Thomas’s mother. Mary/Molly’s McCaughan connections concern Alexander’s wife, not his own mother.
How the evidence supports this account
The account separates the recorded event, the identification of its people, and the conclusion drawn from it. A baptism can directly name a child’s parents while leaving the child’s later identity unknown. A death can have an exact date while remaining a probable match to Alexander. These are different questions and should carry different qualifications.

An index, a transcription and a tree quoting the same original do not provide three independent confirmations. The surname-project report, STR reconstruction and later discussion can likewise reuse the same genetic observations. Independent civil, church and land records are valuable because they offer different routes through the identity problem; even then, their logical dependencies must remain visible.
What an unsuccessful search means
Missing evidence is useful only when we know what should have been recorded and what survives. The unnamed 1838 child’s absence from all relevant parts of the household return has more bearing on a survival hypothesis than an unrestricted web search finding nothing. It still cannot establish a death date by itself. A gap in the baptism transcription, a register starting after the marriage, and an archive image requiring onsite access are three different limitations.

The research history records completed searches and the wider register of inaccessible originals and unresolved identities; the focused next tests appear below. The next work is prioritised by the proposition it could resolve, not by the number of databases left to search. No numerical parent score is treated as a probability or allowed to replace these source-based arguments.
The next records that could change the conclusions
The first task could distinguish the early Alexander identities directly. The American and Larne tests still address the wider family reconstruction. The Canadian deeds now establish the Irish sibling connection and identify the Rochester and Black families. Their earlier family records and unresolved title fractions form the next collateral tests.

Research NotesDeath
No death or burial record has been found. The before-1917 death date is only an upper bound based on the estimated 1816 birth and is not a recorded date.
Father
Alexander's marriage proves that his father was John Glasgow, a labourer. The record-only profile for the older John is attached as Alexander's confident father. No inspected record gives John's age, wife or residence.

John Glasgow of Lisnagaver was formerly attached, but his family gravestone places his birth about 1816 or 1817, while the conflicting 1851 return places it about 1801. Neither date permits him to be Alexander's father, and he was a farmer rather than the labourer named in the marriage. sources.citation:
National Records of Scotland,
Edinburgh Commissary Court, CC8/8/32, images 123–124, testament testamentar and
inventory of Andro Glasgw, made 6 February 1597/8, death stated as 7 February,
confirmed 10 July 1598; working transcription of the original register images.
See also Scottish Record Society, Commissariot of Edinburgh: Register of
Testaments, 1514–1600, p. 108 (https://archive.org/details/scottishrecordso01scotuoft/page/n117/mode/1up).

Family and executors
Andrew's wife was Elizat Stevinsoun (Elizabeth Stevenson). The testament
expressly calls Robert Glasgow their son:

 “Robart Glasgw his sone begottin be him vpoun the said Elizat his
wyff” 

It also names Andrew's daughters Marion, Janet and Isobel. The dispositive
clause refers to “his said sone and his said [dochter… struck through] Marione,
Jonet, Isobell.” 

{| class="wikitable sortable" style="padding: 5px; width:100%;"
|+ Household named in Andrew Glasgow's testament
|-
! style="background-color:#E1F0B4;" | Person
! style="background-color:#E1F0B4;" | Relationship
! style="background-color:#E1F0B4;" | What the record proves
|-
| Elizat Stevinsoun || Wife || Appointed with Robert to administer the movable estate; explicitly called Andrew's spouse and wife.
|-
| Robert Glasgow || Son || Explicitly Andrew's son by Elizat; he had not yet reached the age fixed for taking the land.
|-
| Marion Glasgow || Daughter || Named in the operative inheritance clause as one of Andrew's daughters.
|-
| Janet Glasgow || Daughter || Named in the same inheritance clause.
|-
| Isobel Glasgow || Daughter || Named in the same inheritance clause.
|-
| Unnamed possible child || Conditional only || Provided for only if Elizat was pregnant; the will does not prove a later birth.
|}

Andrew appointed Elizat and Robert to take charge of his goods, movable
property and debts receivable, and to pay his debts. He also named advisers
whose counsel they were to use. One readable adviser was James
Stevisoun. The shared surname makes him a useful lead for Elizat's family,
but the will does not call him her father, brother or other relative. 
Estate and financial network
The inventory describes a working rural household. It appears to include
three cows with calves, although the number is uncertain; two yearling cattle;
two horses valued at £10 each, £20 altogether; nine sheep; eight bolls of oats
in the barn and barnyard; four firlots of barley; household utensils and
furnishings; and Andrew's clothing. Several quantities, individual valuations
and the inventory total remain unresolved and should not be supplied from the
usual form of other testaments. 

Private family details withheld.

Andrew provided that Elizat was to “bruik his [word unclear] land quhill his
said Robart cum to aige”: she was to possess or enjoy the land until Robert
reached legal age. The unclear word before land is not supplied here. This
is direct evidence of intended succession within Andrew's household, but the
record does not say from whom Andrew obtained the land or whether his interest
was heritable or tenanted. 

The will also allowed for the possibility that Elizat was pregnant: “incais his
said spous be with bairne to him.” That conditional wording does not establish
that another child was born. Andrew further directed that, if “Elizat his spous
do not hir pairt to his said bairnis,” she was to be removed from the
administration, protecting the children's interests. 

The closing clause records execution by a notary at Andrew's direction because
he could not write. The subsequent confirmation again names Elizat Stevinsoun
and Robert Glasgow. A further man, Johne Sandelandis, appears in the confirmation,
but the surviving reading does not establish a relationship to the family. 
Research Notes
Calendar and locality
The manuscript year is 1597 in the Scottish record, while the confirmation was
in July 1598. Andrew's death should therefore be recorded as 7 February
1597/8, not 10 July 1598. The readings “Corsoun” and “Calder Clair/Cleir”
remain qualified until the handwriting is independently resolved.

The place has been rendered both Corsoun and Corstoun in derivative work. It
has not been safely equated with a modern settlement. The profile's structured
death place should reflect only the documented household locality, marked
uncertain, rather than the unsupported Kirknewton value.
Corrected family reading
An earlier transcription identified a Jonet Anderson as Andrew's wife and Marion, James, Andrew and William as four children. Re-reading
images 123–124 does not support that reconstruction. The secure relationships
are Elizat Stevinsoun as wife; Robert as Andrew and Elizat's son; and Marion,
Janet and Isobel as Andrew's daughters. Profiles Glasgow-4006 and
Glasgow-4007 represent supposed sons Andrew and William from that reading;
neither man is named as Andrew's child in the corrected testament. Their
profiles should preserve the history of the mistake without treating it as
evidence that either person existed.

The current spouse should not be detached merely to leave an empty field before
an evidenced Elizabeth profile is available, but the relationship is
contradicted and must not be presented as proved. Robert, Marion, Janet and
Isobel each require a new documentary profile. Glasgow-1156,
Glasgow-3062, Glasgow-3917, Glasgow-3183 and Glasgow-3336 were
compared but do not have a direct Corsoun, Stevenson, sibling, property or
succession bridge. They must not be substituted merely from name, chronology
or regional compatibility.

The currently attached James Glasgow, John
Glasgow and David Glasgow are not named as sons in this
testament. They should remain uncertain unless another record independently
connects them to Andrew. The attached spouse is now the record-defined Elizat Stevinsoun (Elizabeth Stevenson). The earlier Jonet Anderson identification is retired.

The earlier model reading of the 1577 testament's second child as Androw
has been superseded by the accepted Marjory (m[ar]iory) reading, so no
comparison with this Andrew profile arises from that record. The 1577 household
is associated with the place provisionally indexed as Hirmenschelis, while this
testament places Andrew at Corsoun; no record bridges the two households, and
this profile is not the present match for any child of John Glasgow.
Parentage and next evidence
No parent is named. John Glasgow remains an uncertain working
father only; Andrew's evidence is in the rural Calder setting, whereas John's
proved family is concentrated in Glasgow burgh records. The highest-value next
search is the National Records of Scotland's Morton estate material:
GD150/696–757 (Barony of Caldercleir), GD150/2027–2060 (Midlothian rentals), and
GD150/320–493. An occupier succession naming Robert after Andrew could identify
The proved son and clarify the nature of the landholding. National Records
of Scotland, GD150, Papers of the Earls of Morton (https://catalogue.nrscotland.gov.uk/nrsonlinecatalogue/details.aspx?reference=GD150), especially GD150/696–757,
GD150/2027–2060 and GD150/320–493.

sources.citation: National Records of Scotland, Edinburgh Commissary Court, CC8/8/8, images 355–356, testament dative and inventory of Margaret Glasgow; Commissariot of Edinburgh: Register of Testaments, 1514–1600, p. 108 (https://archive.org/details/scottishrecordso01scotuoft/page/n117/mode/1up).

Research Notes
The manuscript gives both Kaddell and Keddell, not Edstoun. Keddell is used as the principal surname and Kaddell should be preserved as another-surname form. This profile represents the same executor already attached to Margaret, so its surname should be corrected rather than a duplicate created.

John Edstoun was Margaret's husband and is a natural candidate for Cuthbert's father, but the testament never calls Cuthbert his son. The existing father attachment should remain uncertain pending direct evidence.

The derivative index dates Margaret's entry 8 November 1580 and calls her sometime spouse to John Edstoun in Croftmalloch. Daniel Neely Glasgow married Mary Jane Boyd at Boveedy First Presbyterian Church on 28 June 1888. He was described as a farmer of Lisnagaver and named his father as Thomas Glasgow, farmer. IrishGenealogy.ie (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/en/), civil marriage registration of Daniel Neely Glasgow and Mary Jane Boyd, 28 June 1888, Boveedy First Presbyterian Church; groom's father recorded as Thomas Glasgow, farmer (accessed 17 July 2026).

IrishGenealogy.ie (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/view/?record_id=cidenc-772683), civil death index entry for Thomas Glasgow, aged 55, Ballymoney registration district, second quarter of 1870 (accessed 19 July 2026).

His recorded age gives an estimated birth in about 1795 or 1796. It does not provide an exact birth date.

A derivative index was previously read as naming Peter Glasgow at Daniel's death. The original civil image instead clearly names Kate Glasgow, present at death, Kilrea. It states no relationship, so Kate should not be attached as a daughter or other relative without further evidence. 

Daniel's will was proved at Londonderry by Samuel Neely of Kilrea, assistant land agent and sole executor. His effects were valued at under £300. 

The original will named:

* David Glasgow of the City of London, his son;
* Thomas Glasgow, his late brother; and
* Daniel Neely Glasgow, his nephew. 

The will does not name Adam Glasgow, Rose Glasgow, James Glasgow of Inishrush or any property at Inishrush. This omission does not prove that Daniel had no connection with that family, but the will provides no support for attaching him as a son of Adam Glasgow of Inishrush.

Daniel's burial place has not been identified.

The original death image identifies Kate Glasgow as the informant. 

The only Kate active in Ireland at this time was Catherine Glasgow
Brother Thomas and the Prescott siblings
Daniel's will calls Thomas Glasgow his late brother and Daniel Neely Glasgow his nephew. sources.citation: British Museum, "David Glasgow" (https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/term/BIOG70412), biographical authority record identifying David as an Irish watchmaker born at Coleraine, with life dates 1824–7 December 1911, address at 20 Myddleton Square, London, and service as vice-president of the British Horological Institute (accessed 16 July 2026).

"English Watch Work: BHI Exhibition, 1873" (https://theoldwatchword.blogspot.com/2015/12/english-watch-work-bhi-exhibition-1873.html), The Old Watchword, biographical discussion of David Glasgow's training, London businesses and work for the Spanish market (accessed 16 July 2026).

Public Record Office of Northern Ireland, Will Calendars (https://apps.proni.gov.uk/willscalendar_ie/willssearch.aspx), registered will of Daniel Glasgow of Kilrea, proved 1871; original will naming David Glasgow of the City of London as his son. The portal does not provide a stable item-level URL (accessed 16 July 2026).

Richard John Torrens, "Kilrea First Presbyterian Church Records: Baptisms in 1827" (https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/KilreaP1/Baptisms/1827.html), entry 146, transcribed by Barbara Braswell: Robert, son of Daniel Glasgow and Margaret Irwin of Kilrea, born 1 September and baptised 30 September 1827 (accessed 16 July 2026).

Len Swindley, "Glasgow Genealogy Notes, Counties Tyrone & Londonderry, Northern Ireland 1840–69" (https://www.cotyroneireland.com/surnames/glasgow.html), transcription of a Londonderry Sentinel notice dated 18 February 1853, describing James Glasgow as the third son of Daniel Glasgow of Kilrea (accessed 16 July 2026).

By the 1870s he was trading from 20 Myddleton Square, London. A surviving watch movement in the British Museum is signed:

:D. Glasgow, 20 Myddleton Square, London, No. 1516. British Museum, half-hunter watch movement (https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/H_1958-1201-1008), made by David Glasgow at 20 Myddleton Square, London, about 1875 (accessed 16 July 2026).

Publication
In 1885 David published Watch and Clock Making, a technical manual covering the construction, repair and manufacture of watches and clocks. David Glasgow, Watch and Clock Making (https://archive.org/details/watchandclockma00glasgoog) (London: Cassell & Company, 1885), Internet Archive digitisation (accessed 16 July 2026).

Official England and Wales probate search (https://probatesearch.service.gov.uk/), National Probate Calendar, 1912, entry for David Glasgow, recording his death at 20 Myddleton Square, Clerkenwell, on 7 December 1911 and the grant of probate on 2 February 1912 to Cecilia Glasgow and Madeline Glasgow, spinsters. The calendar does not state their relationship to David (accessed 16 July 2026).

Jane Stewart estate connection, 1823
An assignment of mortgage dated 8 November 1823 names Elizabeth Glasgow of Larne, widow, administratrix of Jane Stewart late of Curran, County Antrim, deceased. She assigned the mortgage interest to Roger Brown Curry, a Royal Navy lieutenant. The premises were a tenement and garden on the south side of New Town, Larne, 21 feet in front and 189 feet deep, bounded east by the lane to Larne Quay and west by James Mitchell's tenement. William Walsh McNeill, attorney, and James Glasgow, writing clerk, both of Larne, witnessed the assignment. Registry of Deeds, memorial 548257, p. 522, assignment of mortgage dated 8 November 1823, registered 17 May 1826; FamilySearch image 359 (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJ7-9935-Y). sources.citation:
Research Notes
Current research
This is a genuine two-family conflation. FamilySearch X1Y9-V87 indexes Euphame in 1634 with father Johnne Glasgow . The same event is claimed in Glasgow-1030's biography as a child of John Glasgow and Jonet Mathie, while Euphame is structurally attached to Rev. John Glassford and Jonet Morriel within an otherwise coherent Edinburgh Glassford sibling sequence.

The event's Edinburgh placement favours the Glassford household over the Glasgow High Kirk family, but the index surname favours Glasgow. The original parish image is required. It must not be attached to both families meanwhile.

The 1850-52 Euphemia Glasgow occurrence in the biography is more than two centuries later and unrelated.

This assessment draws on the cited records and public source material. familysearch.org (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XTP4-XLG).

The funeral was to Kildress parish churchyard. Presumably this means Clare Churchyard.

Geillis's estate owed money to a James Glasgow in Stevenston. 
Research Notes
Current evidence assessment
The testament does not identify Geillis's parents or state James Glasgow's
relationship to her. James Glasgow younger of Corsankell
remains an uncertain father candidate only.

The debts also name the lord of Eglinton and servants Robert Boyd and a Bessie
whose surname is unresolved; Robert and Bessie were owed wages. The servant
Bessie is not thereby identified with Bessie Wilson in the executor clause. 

Katherine Glasgow also died in January 1603 in neighbouring
Stevenston parish. The common date, adjoining parishes and Stevenston creditor
justify researching them as a kin network; they do not prove sisterhood.

sources.citation: William Melanchthon Glasgow, History of the Glasgow Family, digital copy (https://www.wikitree.com/photo.php/0/0a/Glasgow-590.pdf), p. 2.

Bill Macafee, compiler, Protestant Householders’ Returns (1740) for County Londonderry, entries for Hugh Glasgow in Tamlaght O’Crilly Parish; PDF (https://adamsfamilydna.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/02/1740-Protestant-Returns-Londonderry-County-Ireland.pdf).

William Murphy, transcriber, “Census (Partial) of Protestant Householders in Tamlaght O’Crilly Parish in 1740,” Ireland Genealogy Projects Archives, online transcription (https://www.igp-web.com/IGPArchives/ire/derry/census/cens-prot-tamlaght-1740.html).

They had seven children:

* John Glasgow
* Clatworthy Glasgow, called “Tatty”
* Hugh Glasgow
* Nancy Glasgow, twin of Hugh
* Alexander Glasgow
* Mary Glasgow
* Robert Glasgow

The family history states that Hugh and Nancy were twins, lived to the age of 88, and died in the same year. 

Hugh’s will names John, Hugh, Alexander, Nancy and Robert, together with his granddaughter Sarah, daughter of Alexander. Allegheny County Will Book 3, no. 252, pp. 492–493 (https://www.ancestry.com/imageviewer/collections/8802/images/005537856_00276?pid=1733435), will of Hugh Glasgo of Deer Township, signed 29 March 1827 and proved 25 April 1831.

They lived for about five years near Little York in York County, Pennsylvania. In 1802 they moved briefly to Washington County, then settled in Deer Creek Township, Allegheny County. 
Will and death
By 1827 Hugh was living in Deer Township, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania.

He signed his will on 29 March 1827. It named:

* sons John, Hugh, Alexander and Robert
* daughter Nancy
* granddaughter Sarah, daughter of Alexander
* an unnamed wife

John and Robert were appointed executors. Robert received Hugh’s land and the residue of the estate, with responsibility for supporting his mother. 

The will was proved on 25 April 1831. A matching loose probate packet also survives. FamilySearch DGS 5538049, Allegheny County probate packet no. 252: cover (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QS7-L991-GV6H?cc=1999196&wc=9PMK-MNG%3A268499101%2C281697201), will, p. 1 (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QS7-L991-GVS6?cc=1999196&wc=9PMK-MNG%3A268499101%2C281697201), will, p. 2 (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QSQ-G991-GV3K?cc=1999196&wc=9PMK-MNG%3A268499101%2C281697201), and probate (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QS7-L991-GVD7?cc=1999196&wc=9PMK-MNG%3A268499101%2C281697201).

His will proves he was alive on 29 March 1827. The earlier source list gave 26 March, but the recorded will and probate packet show the correct date was 29 March.

His death occurred before probate on 25 April 1831.
Earlier Hugh Glasgow records
Two men named Hugh Glasgow appear in the 1740 Protestant Householders’ Returns for Tamlaght O’Crilly Parish. 

Neither can be this Hugh, who was born about 1739. One is likely to have been his father, Hugh Glasgow.

A Hugh Glasgow also appears in a 1772 Belfast News-Letter notice concerning inhabitants of Tamlaght O’Crilly Parish who surrendered arms. Belfast News-Letter, 14 April 1772 (https://arborealis.ca/records/newspapers/kilrea-news/1770-1779/), notice dated 6 April 1772 naming Hugh Glasgow among inhabitants of Tamlaght O’Crilly Parish.

Twin Sister
The family history identifies Hugh’s twin sister as Nancy and states that both twins lived to be eighty-eight and died in the same year. 

Hugh’s obituary instead identifies his twin sister as Margaret Cunningham. It states that her farm adjoined Hugh’s and that she died on 14 January 1874, both twins then being in their eighty-eighth year. 

The obituary is unusually specific, supplying Margaret’s married surname, death date and neighbouring residence. It is therefore strong evidence that the twin was known as Margaret Cunningham.

Nancy was historically used as a form of Ann or Anne. It was not ordinarily a form of Margaret, whose common forms included Maggie, Meg, Peg and Peggy. Hallie Borstel Kirchner, “An Introduction to Nicknames,” Vita Brevis, American Ancestors, 12 April 2021; https://vitabrevis.americanancestors.org/2021/04/introduction-to-nicknames.

The cemetery transcription independently records the same death date and states that he was in the eighty-eighth year of his age. 

Hugh was buried at the cemetery now identified as Depreciation Lands Museum Cemetery in Hampton Township, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania. His Find a Grave memorial also associates him with this burial place.

* The family history states that his brother John was born on the family farm in County Londonderry near Portglenone, but does not explicitly say that Hugh was born there. 
* Both sources place the family’s emigration in 1796.

County Down should not be replaced with County Londonderry solely from the birthplace reported for John.

Possible explanations include:

* the family lived in County Down in 1786 and later moved to the Portglenone-area farm;
* Hugh’s mother was temporarily staying with relatives or other acquaintances in County Down when the twins were born;
* the obituary’s contributor misunderstood the family’s Irish geography; or
* the later family history incorrectly assumed that all siblings were born on the same farm.

A baptismal entry, contemporary family Bible or other Irish record naming Hugh and his twin would be needed to resolve the issue.
Hospital-Birth Theory
No evidence has been found that Hugh and his twin were born in a hospital.

Belfast’s Poor House Infirmary opened in 1774, but it was a general charitable infirmary rather than a specialist maternity hospital. Belfast’s first dedicated lying-in hospital did not open until 1794, eight years after Hugh’s birth. “The NHS at 70: Belfast before Universal Healthcare,” Clifton House, 6 July 2018; https://cliftonbelfast.com/news/the-nhs-at-70-belfast-before-universal-healthcare/.

Registry of Deeds, Dublin, memorial 63221, lease dated 10 March 1736; registered 10 April 1738. FamilySearch image 542 (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSN1-FXR2), image group 008088380, volumes 87–88; original image inspected 21 September 2026.

The annual rent was £1 16 shillings sterling, with receiver's fees of two pence per pound. The term began on the preceding 1 November and was measured by the lives of George II, Frederick Prince of Wales and Prince William Augustus Duke of Cumberland, with provision for replacement lives. The named lives were royal family members, not Glasgow children. 

The lease witnesses were James Stenhouse of Larne and William Harrison, clerk to Alexander Stewart of Ballylough. Stenhouse and Robert Wilson of Larne, merchant, witnessed the memorial. Stenhouse proved execution at Carrickfergus on 28 March 1738, stating that Alexander Stewart had executed the lease in the Earl's name and that William and Hugh had executed the lease and memorial. 

The memorial names no parent, spouse or child of either lessee and states no relationship between them. The later renewal endorsements remain separate research targets.
Joint lessors named in a 1757 assignment
A deed poll dated 4 June 1757, Matthew Stewart of Carncastle, farmer, to Robert Rainey of Larne, weaver, concerned a conditional assignment for £20 of Stewart's interest in a lease granted by William Glasgow and Hugh Glasgow of Larne. The original memorial does not date their head lease or describe the holding sufficiently to identify it with the 1736 Newtown tenements. Registry of Deeds, memorial 159181, manuscript pp. 473–474, deed dated 4 June 1757, registered 26 May 1761; FamilySearch image 257, opening (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJM-MJX4) and image 258, continuation (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJM-MJP6), original images inspected 21 September 2026.
PRONI D2977/3A/4/81/72A, 1736 William and Hugh Glasgow lease with 1751 and 1767 endorsements; PRONI eCatalogue (https://apps.proni.gov.uk/eCatNI_IE/SearchPage.aspx), catalogue description only.

“Congregational Memoirs—Larne and Kilwaughter,” (https://archive.org/stream/christianunitari0003unse/christianunitari0003unse_djvu.txt) The Christian Unitarian, vol. 3 (1864), p. 197. The account quotes the Larne Session Book entry: “Hugh Glasgow … dead July 8, 1767.”

Research NotesPossible son John of Larne
John Glasgow, who married Rose Allan at Larne in 1769, is a possible son, with low confidence. His estimated birth about 1747 fits Hugh's age and Larne household, but the marriage chronology does not name John's father. Donna Jean Glasgow, Kilwaughter and Larne Glasgow chronology (https://web.archive.org/web/20101124184247id_/http://lifesweaving.com/Glasgow/Kilwaughter/Timeline.html), entry for John Glasgow and Rose Allan's 1769 marriage. A Hugh Glascoe was baptised in Dublin in 1704, the son of William Glascoe and Jone. FamilySearch record for Hugh Glascoe (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:FR3H-8L7).

Tamlaght O'Crilly
The 1740 Protestant Householders' Returns for County Londonderry contain two entries for men named Hugh Glasgow in Tamlaght O'Crilly Parish, Barony of Loughinsholin. Bill Macafee, compiler, Protestant Householders' Returns (1740) for County Londonderry, records 1195 and 1272, Hugh Glasgow, Loughinsholin Barony, Tamlaght O'Crilly Parish; PDF (https://adamsfamilydna.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/02/1740-Protestant-Returns-Londonderry-County-Ireland.pdf).

William Murphy, transcriber, “Census (Partial) of Protestant Householders in Tamlaght O'Crilly Parish in 1740,” Ireland Genealogy Projects Archives, online transcription (https://www.igp-web.com/IGPArchives/ire/derry/census/cens-prot-tamlaght-1740.html).

Belfast News-Letter, 14 April 1772, notice dated at Inishrush on 6 April 1772, naming Hugh Glasgow among inhabitants of Tamlaght O'Crilly Parish; transcript in “1770–1779: News transcripts for Kilrea & environs,” Arborealis (https://arborealis.ca/records/newspapers/kilrea-news/1770-1779/).

Later account
A later online genealogical account preserves a similar version of the family tradition:

My great-great-grandfather: Hugh,1 GLASGOW, b. 1724, was a native of the County of Tyrone, Ireland. When a young man he fell out with a neighbor, engaged in a personal combat in which he was the victor, but because of prosecution and the severe penalty, he fled to County of Derry. Being a weaver by trade, he found employment with one McCullough. He soon, however, fell in love with his host's charming daughter, [Wm. M. never mentions her given Name?] and they were happily married. To them was born three sons:

#1.1. John,1 GLASGOW

#1.2. Robert,1 GLASGOW, and

#1.3. Hugh,2 GLASGOW, b. 1753 m. Sarah BLAIR, 5Ch.

 Undated Glasgow family genealogy formerly hosted by RootsWeb, archived copy at the Internet Archive (https://web.archive.org/web/20201003134102/https://sites.rootsweb.com/~iapage/families/glasgow/GLASGOW1.HTM).

# Miranda (Glasko) Overbaugh (abt.1820-abt.1894)

Isaac, widowed, died (age 85) on 2 September 1861 in Guilford, New Haven, Connecticut, United States.

Memorial page for Isaac C Glasko (unknown-2 Sep 1861), citing Old Kinne Burying Ground, Griswold, New London County, Connecticut, USA; Maintained by John Beckstein (contributor 46939506).

By 1800 he and his wife had relocated to North Uxbridge, Massachusetts in the Blackstone Valley. His father Jacob and brother George followed him and also moved to the Blackstone Valley. 

In 1806 Isaac, his father and brother moved to Griswold Connecticut. Isaac purchased from Alexander Stewart (also a member of the Kinne family) three-quarters of an acre of land and a house, along with the rights to water-power access from the dam where Stewart had a grist-mill. That same year, Jacob Glasko (still of Massachusetts) purchased fifty acres of land and a house along the Pachaug River and by the edge of a pond (now Glasgo Pond) for $1,250, a third of which holdings he sold to each of his sons in 1807. 

Issac established a business as a blacksmith and grew it into a commercial forge employing as many as 10 blacksmiths manufacturer producing farming implements as well as harpoons for the whaling industry, among other things. His blacksmith shop was constructed near the what is now the intersection of Route 165 and Route 201. He harnessed waterpower to a large mechanical trip hammer that sped the manufacturing process and enabled him to make large tools. 

The Glaskos were active in buying and selling land in the area. Isaac owned 54 acres. By 1841, he owned at least 54 acres of land with four dwelling houses, a sawmill, a gristmill, two barns, a coal house, and a number of other small outbuildings. 

Isaac Glasko and his friend Pero Moody (1750-1830) filed a petition in 1823 to teh Connecticut General Assembly requesting exemption from taxation on the grounds that they could not vote. In part, the petition states that they were "descendants of African Citizens brought to this County against their will" and that "in the midst of most mortifying discouragement have acquired some property" Rejected Bills, Connecticut State Legislature, Records Group 002, Box 2, Folder 3).
Connecticut History Blacksmith Isaac Glasko Challenges the State Constitution (https://connecticuthistory.org/blacksmith-isaac-glasko-challenges-the-state-constitution/)

His house still stands, although it has been considerably altered. Isaac Glasko final resting place with his wife are in a quiet burying ground near the center of the village that now bears his name now known as Glasgo.

General Register Office of Ireland, civil marriage register (https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/images/marriage_returns/marriages_1886/10840/5957283.pdf), James Garvin Glasgow and Eliza Ann Aiken, 1 July 1886, Clough, entry 62.

James married Eliza Ann Aiken on 1 July 1886 at Clough. He was a
full-age bachelor farmer of Lisnagaver; she was a full-age spinster and daughter
of William Aiken, farmer. Robert Aiken and Matilda Bell witnessed the
marriage. 

The family gravestone records their infant son John Garvin, identified as John Garvin Glasgow; his civil birth return gives the birth at Lisnagaver on 3 October 1887. General Register Office of Ireland, civil birth register, Ballymoney superintendent registrar's district, Dirraw registrar's district, entry 352: John Garvin Glasgow, born 3 October 1887, Lisnagaver. register image (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/birth_returns/births_1887/02541/1940589.pdf).

James and Eliza Ann were again recorded at Lisnagaver in the 1911 census. 1911 Census of Ireland (http://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/pages/1911/Antrim/Killoquin/Lisnagaver/130063/), Lisnagaver house 22, Killoquin, County Antrim.

General Register Office of Ireland, civil death register (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/deaths_returns/deaths_1918/05197/4435754.pdf), James Garvin Glasgow, 14 February 1918, Dervock registrar's district, entry 165.
PRONI Will Calendars, 1918: letters of administration of James Garvin Glasgow, Lisnagaver, farmer, died 14 February 1918, granted to Eliza Ann Glasgow, widow.

Her probate (as Eliza Ann Glasgow, of Tullynahinion, widow) was granted at Belfast on 17 July 1933 to Robert Andrew Aicken, farmer, and William Shaw, solicitor. PRONI Will Calendars, 1933: Glasgow, Eliza Ann, of Tullynahinion, widow, died 16 June 1933, probate to Robert Andrew Aicken and William Shaw.

sources.citation: Donna Jean Glasgow, "GLASGOWS from Kilwaughter Parish and Larne, County Antrim, Northern Ireland to Newberry, South Carolina, 1669–1850," Their Story, archived at https://web.archive.org/web/20101124183914/http:/lifesweaving.com/Glasgow/Kilwaughter/TheirStory.html and continuation at https://web.archive.org/web/20101124184109/http://lifesweaving.com/Glasgow/Kilwaughter/TheirStory2.html.
Donna Jean Glasgow, "Chronology of the GLASGOW Family," archived at https://web.archive.org/web/20101124184247/http://lifesweaving.com/Glasgow/Kilwaughter/Timeline.html.

Washington District, South Carolina, Court of Equity proceedings concerning the estate of Archibald Wilson, 1817–1819; complaint transcription archived at https://web.archive.org/web/20101124220018id_/http://lifesweaving.com/Glasgow/Paper_Complaint.html.

Registry of Deeds, memorial 159661, lease dated 20 December 1764, registered 18 April 1766, pp. 415–416; FamilySearch image 542 (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSH3-33Q6-L) and image 543 (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSH3-33QZ-Y), original manuscript images inspected 21 September 2026.
Registry of Deeds, Ireland, memorial 74015, dated 13 February 1738, volume 105, page 301; transcription consulted. Original memorial not yet inspected.

The 1764 lease now provides the explicit father–son statement previously missing. The original baptism remains necessary to verify the reported exact birth date.
Marriage
James married Mary, identified in later family research as Mary Crosier or Crozier.

The 1817 equity complaint establishes that James and Mary were first cousins. It identifies James's mother Rachel as one of the six sisters of Archibald Wilson and then states that Mary, James's widow, was the daughter of another of Archibald's sisters. 

Thus James and Mary were children of two Wilson sisters.

The equity complaint itself does not state Mary's maiden surname. The identification of her as Crosier/Crozier requires evidence independent of that complaint and should not be treated as proved by the Wilson inheritance case alone.
Ireland
James remained associated with the Kilwaughter and Larne area into adulthood.

Donna Jean Glasgow's reconstruction identifies a James Glasgow with Robert Glasgow and Hugh Shannon among signatories from Kilwaughter Parish to a 1772 petition concerning the disturbances associated with the "Hearts of Steel." She interpreted the three adjacent names as James, his probable father Robert, and his brother-in-law Hugh Shannon. 

If those identifications are correct, James was still in County Antrim in 1772.
Migration to South Carolina
James and Mary emigrated from County Antrim to South Carolina sometime after the 1772 Kilwaughter petition and before November 1774.

Donna Jean Glasgow reported that the earliest record she had found placing James in South Carolina was dated 16 November 1774, when James "Glassgow" witnessed a land transaction involving James Finlay in Craven County. 

On that evidence, migration in 1772 or 1773 is plausible, but no passenger record has been found and the exact year or ship has not been established.

James settled at Gilder's Creek in Craven County, in the area that later became Newberry County, South Carolina. "Will of James Glasgow," transcription from the papers of Robert Glasgow, archived at https://web.archive.org/web/20101124215937id_/http://lifesweaving.com/Glasgow/Paper_JGlasgowWill.html; Will Book "A", p. 194; Vol. 1, Wills, p. 89.

He named his wife Mary and six children:

* Robert Glasgow
* John Glasgow
* Archibald Glasgow
* Wilson Glasgow
* Margaret Glasgow
* Rachel Glasgow 

James gave Mary one-third of his goods, chattels, and movable property. He also gave her, during her widowhood, the house and fifty acres formerly possessed by James Cannon, with authority eventually to give that property to whichever of their children she considered most deserving. 

His son Robert received one hundred acres together with the house in which James then lived, while John received fifty acres. 

The remainder of James's personal property was to be divided equally among all six named children. James also directed Mary, Robert, and John to use the profits of the lands in raising his younger children. 

James appointed his wife Mary as his chief executor. The witnesses named in the transcription were James Finley, Ann Finley, and Thomas Dugan. 

The will was proved on 13 July 1793. 
Death
James probably died in late 1775, although the exact date has not been established.

His will was made on 17 October 1775 while he described himself as very sick and weak in body. More significantly, the later equity complaint concerning Archibald Wilson's estate expressly states that James "died in America in the Year of our Lord one thousand seven hundred and seventy five." 

The fact that his will was not proved until 13 July 1793 does not by itself establish that he died in 1793. 

The presently available evidence therefore supports a death sometime after 17 October 1775 and before the end of 1775, subject to confirmation from the original probate and equity records.
Research NotesBirth: 1731 versus 1734
Some family material gives James's birth year as 1734. Donna Jean Glasgow's reconstruction instead gives 24 May 1731, and her chronology records the baptism of James, son of Robert Glasgow and Rachel Willson, in 1731. 

The 1731 date fits the known chronology and is preferable to the unsupported 1734 statement, but the original Presbyterian register should be obtained before treating 24 May 1731 as independently verified.
Father
The evidence should be stated carefully:

* the equity case directly identifies Rachel Glasgow as James's mother; 
* memorial 74015 directly identifies Rachel Wilson as Robert Glasgow's wife in 1738; 
* the same memorial names a Jas Glasgow Junr among the lives in Robert's lease; and
* later Kilwaughter family research identifies the 1731 James as a son of Robert and Rachel. 

The image-checked 1764 lease now explicitly names James as Robert’s son. The lease proves that immediate relationship; it does not identify Robert’s own father or independently prove James’s later migration.
Mary and the Crosier/Crozier surname
The equity case proves that Mary, wife of James, was James's first cousin because Mary's mother and James's mother Rachel were sisters of Archibald Wilson. 

It does not identify Mary's maiden surname. "Crosier" or "Crozier" should therefore be supported by another record before being described as proved by the equity case.
Date of death
A previous profile conclusion treated 13 July 1793, the date the will was proved, as evidence that James died shortly before that date. This conflicts with the equity complaint, which directly states that James died in 1775. 

The 1775 statement is also consistent with James making his will while seriously ill on 17 October 1775. 

Donna Jean Glasgow suggested that disruption associated with the American Revolution may explain why the will was not proved until 1793. That explanation is plausible but speculative and is not necessary to establish the earlier death date.
Distinct Larne ropemaker
A Registry of Deeds memorial dated 28 March 1768 concerns a different James Glasgow of the Old Town of Larne. The original image calls that man a ropemaker, not a soapmaker, and shows him assigning the same ropewalk lease granted in 1760. The occupational and property sequence continues in Larne and should not be attached to the South Carolina settler. sources.citation: "Armorial Sculptured Stones of the County Antrim," Ulster Journal of Archaeology, second series 6 (1900), p. 47 (https://archive.org/details/ulsterjournalofa06ulstiala/page/47/mode/1up), Glasgow monument inscription.

James married Jane, whose maiden name is not given in the monument inscription. Jane was born about 1741, based on her recorded age at death. 

James and Jane had at least one known child:

* Ann Glasgow, born about 1768; died 25 May 1832, aged 64. 

James died on 14 April 1812, aged 64. His stated age places his birth approximately between 15 April 1747 and 14 April 1748.

His wife Jane survived him. She died on 21 July 1820, aged 79. 
Tanner at Larne
James is probably the Larne tanner documented between 1768 and 1790. A 1768 assignment by a different James Glasgow, a ropemaker, was witnessed by James Glasgow, tanner. The tanner later swore to the deed's execution at Larne. Registry of Deeds transcript, assignment dated 28 March 1768, FamilySearch image (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJW-DDXW).
Registry of Deeds transcript, mortgage dated 22 June 1778, FamilySearch image (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJW-64YW).

Registry of Deeds, memorial 278037, lease 14 January 1784, sworn 17 August and registered 23 August 1790, FamilySearch image 437 (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJ4-4SJF), original inspected 21 September 2026. The online collection label 1734–1736 does not describe this image’s date.

The same monument also commemorates eleven children of Hugh and Ann, naming a daughter Jane as "the first" and a son Hugh as "the last". James is recorded separately and explicitly described as "their Son". 
Research Notes
James's exact date and place of birth have not yet been established. His birth year of about 1748 is derived from his stated age of 64 at his death on 14 April 1812.

The wording concerning the eleven children of Hugh and Ann should not be interpreted as proving that the younger Hugh was their youngest child. The monument appears to refer to a particular group of children buried or commemorated there, while James is subsequently identified separately as their son.

Jane's maiden surname is currently unknown. The inscription calls her "his wife Jane Glasgow", which records her married surname rather than establishing Glasgow as her birth surname.
Newtown title succession: identities unresolved
An 1874 deed recites a lease to James Glasgow dated 2 October 1779 and its renewal to Anne Glasgow and Jane Glasgow on 25 February 1832. The north-side Newtown property, formerly John English’s, adjoined a tenement formerly Hugh Glasgow’s. This documents succession to a lease, but does not call the women James’s daughters or identify which James held it. The monument wife Jane died in 1820 and cannot automatically be the 1832 Jane. Ann Glasgow, whose monument gives a May 1832 death, is only a candidate for Anne; the original renewal is needed. Registry of Deeds, Antrim to John Mulvenna, indenture 25 March 1874, registered 24 August 1874, FamilySearch image 475 (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CS54-77Q4-H), recital inspected in the original; continuation image 476 (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CS54-77QC-T).

The two sources concern the same death; the original civil-register date is used for the structured field and the one-day conflict is retained here.

Adam Glasgow's 1833 tithe entry gives a gross area of eleven Irish or Plantation acres, approximately 17.82 statute acres under the National Archives of Ireland's published conversion guidance. First Kilrea Presbyterian marriage transcription (https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/KilreaP1/Marriages/1828.html), Peter Aikin and Jane Barklie, 1828; Tamlaght O'Crilly 1831 census transcription (https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/Tamlaght/1831census_3.html), Henry Barkley at Tyanee; and William Macafee, Names of Householders Listed in the 1831 Census Returns for the County of Londonderry (https://www.billmacafee.com/1831census/1831derrycensusnames.pdf).
William Macafee, Church Records for County Londonderry (https://www.billmacafee.com/churchrecords/churchrecordsderry.pdf), register and session-book coverage.
“Tamlaght O’Crilly Lower Graveyard,” One Irish Rover, Glasgow family gravestone (https://www.oneirishrover.com/tamlaght-graveyard/).

“Civil Records,” database with images, Irish Genealogy, death of James Glasgow, 12 December 1878, Group Registration ID 5928386, Magherafelt registration district, indexed record (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/view/?record_id=cide-5928386) and original civil return (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/deaths_returns/deaths_1878/020497/7192875.pdf).

The family gravestone instead records 11 December 1878. 

Both sources agree that James died in December 1878 aged 84. The profile uses the date recorded in the civil return while preserving the one-day discrepancy.
Henry Glasgow
Henry Glasgow is attached as an uncertain son of James.

The 1878 civil death registration places Henry at Inishrush and records him as the person present at James's death. It does not describe Henry as James's son or state any other family relationship. 

Their shared surname, residence and Henry's presence at the death are consistent with a close family relationship, but the death return alone does not prove parentage.
Farm continuity
Adam Glasgow's 1833 tithe holding measured 11 Irish or Plantation acres, approximately 17.82 statute acres. James's later valuation plot 29 measured 19 acres 2 roods 10 perches, or 19.5625 statute acres.

The difference is only 1.7425 statute acres, approximately 9.8 per cent. Together with the proved father-son relationship and continued residence at Inishrush, this strongly supports James having succeeded to substantially the same family farm.

It does not establish exact parcel identity. The tithe entry has no map reference linking it directly to valuation plot 29, and the tithe and valuation surveys were made several decades apart for different purposes.
Younger James Glasgow, Rosanna Barkley and plot 29
Later Inishrush records involve another James Glasgow, treated in the current family reconstruction as this James's nephew.

A letter written by John Glasgow on 20 March 1847 reported news from Ireland that a James Glasgow had fathered an illegitimate child by a daughter of Henry Barkly. John Glasgow, letter to Jane Glasgow Gray, 20 March 1847, digital image (https://www.hiltner.com/mckeown/documents/John%20Glasgow%20letter%20to%20Jane%20Glasgow%20Gray%203-20-1847.pdf).

This is a transcription; the original register is PRONI MIC.1P/292.

National Archives of Ireland, Census of Ireland, 1851, Lisnagaver, Rasharkin, County Antrim, household 35, Alexander Glasgow household; household return (http://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/pages/1851/Antrim/Kilconway/Rasharkin/Lisnagaver/35/). See also FamilySearch record QV9Y-WKKX (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QV9Y-WKKX) and the public comma-delimited transcription (https://durrushistory.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/10/1851irishcensusreturnscommadelimitedtextfilejul24_071.pdf), p. 182.

Possible later life in Michigan
A James Glasgow who lived at Tecumseh, Lenawee County, Michigan, is a strong but unproved later-life candidate. The evidence has not yet supplied his parents, exact birthday or townland, so the Michigan wife, children, death date and migration should not be attached to this profile as facts.

| The conflict with the daughter's certificate cautions against treating all reported parental birthplaces as exact.
