| A James Glasgow died on 30 July 1896 and was born in Ireland.
| The index supplies no age, parents or county and does not itself prove that this was the Tecumseh man or the Lisnagaver child.
|-
| Michigan Messenger, 1 August 1896, p. 1 (https://lenawee.migenweb.org/MichMessengerVol3_1896-1897.pdf) (compilation p. 98)
| The contemporary report says the long-serving Lake Shore depot baggage master disappeared on Wednesday and was found in the Raisin River near Blood's bridge on Thursday, 30 July. It describes him as about five feet eight inches tall, with a scar across his previously broken nose and one or two missing fingers on his right hand.
| The report gives no parents or Irish locality. Its age estimate of about 55 points to about 1841 and is less exact than the cemetery and 1884 census evidence. Its claims concerning suicide and alcohol misuse are newspaper reporting rather than an inspected coroner's finding.
|}

The existing Find a Grave memorial 127743880 (https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/127743880/james-glasgow) proposes death on 29 August 1896. Both the Michigan historical index and the contemporary newspaper report establish 30 July 1896 for the Tecumseh candidate, so the memorial date should not be used.

The current FamilySearch tree profile MQ57-BVR (https://www.familysearch.org/tree/person/details/MQ57-BVR) attaches the Lisnagaver 1851 census to these Michigan records. An earlier FamilySearch identifier, MDBX-Y1G (https://www.familysearch.org/tree/person/details/MDBX-Y1G) was also recorded as a lead. FamilySearch tree links are derivative conclusions, not independent evidence that the child and adult were the same man. Several of the current profile's 20 source attachments are duplicate extractions of the same underlying event.
Dromore identification
A James Glasgow did occupy a house and small garden at plot 18b in Dromore, Rasharkin parish. The original PRONI valuation-revision books carry that name on the same holding from `VAL/12/B/3/13A` (1863-79) through `VAL/12/B/3/13C` (1891-1901). This continuing local valuation identity is unlikely to be the Tecumseh man, who was documented in Michigan by 1869 and reported residence there from about 1866. Revision-book names can lag an occupier's departure, however, and the Dromore man's identity has not been proved. The earlier Rasharkin valuation transcription (https://www.failteromhat.com/griffiths/antrim/rasharkin.htm) did not expose this entry; the original PRONI revision books supersede that negative search while the transcription remains a useful finding aid.
The unnamed 1838 sibling
The unnamed child baptised in 1838 should not be renamed Samuel or identified with Samuel Glasgow of Franklin and Blissfield, Michigan. Alexander's 1851 return lists no such child as resident, absent or dead since 1841, and no American record inspected names Samuel's parents or County Antrim.
Dromore occupier candidate
A James Glasgow occupied property at Dromore in the Rasharkin valuation revisions between 1863 and 1879. The locality and age make this James a plausible candidate, but the valuation gives no parentage and the identification remains unproved. Underlying record source: james glasgow unidentified dromore occupier (https://apps.proni.gov.uk/Val12B/Search.aspx).

sources.citation:
Presbyterian
Church in Ireland, Records of the General Synod of Ulster, from 1691 to
1820, vol. 1 (Belfast, 1890), Synod records for 1698, 1703 and 1705;
Internet Archive scan (https://archive.org/details/recordsofgeneral01pres)
and searchable OCR text (https://archive.org/stream/recordsofgeneral01pres/recordsofgeneral01pres_djvu.txt).

William Taylor was
minister of the Presbyterian congregation associated with Randalstown and
Drummaul. Randalstown was not written as a residence beside James's name; the
association is derived from the known charge of the minister whom he
accompanied.

The repeated pairing establishes an enduring connection with Taylor's
congregation rather than a single incidental appearance. As a ruling elder,
James held a lay office in Presbyterian church government and represented his
congregation in the courts of the church.

{| class="wikitable" style="background:#e6ffe6;"
! Year !! Minister !! Ruling elder !! What the entry establishes
|-
| 1698 || William Taylor || James Glasgow || James represented Taylor's congregation.
|-
| 1703 || William Taylor || James Glasgow || The earlier minister-and-elder pairing was repeated.
|-
| 1705 || James Scott || James Glasgow || Probably the same elder, now representing beside the minister of Duneane.
|-
| 1705 || William Taylor || Robert King || Taylor had a different elder representative at the same Synod.
|}
Association with Duneane in 1705
In 1705 James Glasgow appeared beside James Scott, minister of Duneane, while
William Taylor appeared with Robert King. This change was
once interpreted as evidence that James had transferred from Randalstown or
Drummaul to Duneane. A move, a congregational boundary change or a formal
transfer could explain the pattern, but none is stated in the record.

Taylor also appeared with different elders in later Synods. Rotation or
substitution of congregational representatives is therefore a sufficient
explanation for the changed pairing. The evidence supports a probable
Duneane congregational association in 1705, but it does not prove that
James changed residence or permanently transferred congregations.

It remains possible that the Duneane elder was a second contemporary James
Glasgow. No independent record of another western County Antrim ruling elder
of that name has been found, and the identical name, office, neighbouring
congregational setting and two-year interval make one man the more economical
working identification.
Birth
James's date and place of birth are unknown. He was already serving as a
ruling elder in 1698 and must have been an adult by then. A conservative
working estimate is:

:born before 1678

That estimate allows him to have been at least about twenty in 1698; it is not
derived from a recorded age, and he may have been born considerably earlier.
Randalstown, Drummaul and Duneane are documented or inferred congregational
associations and do not establish his birthplace.
Family
No inspected Synod, land, probate or congregational record names James's
parents, wife or children. His occupation outside the church, exact residence
and place of origin are also unknown.

James Glasgow of Kilwaughter is presently attached as an
uncertain father. No record identifies him as this James's father, so the
attachment remains a research hypothesis. The resulting links to
Robert Glasgow and Hugh Glasgow are likewise
uncertain rather than documented sibling relationships.

No descendant line from James has yet been proved. Uncertain attachments can
be retained as working links when clearly marked, but the surviving records do
not presently establish a wife or child.
Death
No death record has been identified. James was living in 1705, so the only
date supported by the evidence is:

:died after 1705

His place of death is unknown.
Distinction from James Glasgow of Kilwaughter
The ruling elder is distinct from James Glasgow of
Kilwaughter. The Kilwaughter man was recorded as James Glascho in the
1669 Hearth Money Roll and was active in the Larne and Kilwaughter
Presbyterian congregation by 1700. He became an overseer in that congregation
and was recorded as deceased in 1726. W. MacAfee,
transcription of the 1669 County Antrim Hearth Money Roll (https://www.billmacafee.com/1660shearthmoneyrolls/1669hearthmoneyrollsantrim.pdf), Drummaul and
Kilwaughter entries, including records 5347–5348.

Classon Porter, "Congregational Memoirs: Larne and
Kilwaughter," The Christian Unitarian, vol. 3 (1864),
Internet Archive (https://archive.org/details/christianunitari0003unse).

At about the same time, the other James was
active in the affairs of the Larne and Kilwaughter congregation, although he
does not appear in its surviving early roster of ruling elders.

Combining the men would require the same James to represent Taylor's
congregation at Synod while being established in the affairs of another
congregation whose own minister attended with a different elder. That is
possible in theory, but no evidence supports it. The records favour separate
identities. Separation of the two men does not itself rule out kinship; it
only prevents their records from being combined.
Research Notes
Identity assessment
The strongest reconstruction of James's recorded appearances is:

:1698 — James Glasgow, ruling elder paired with William Taylor.
:1703 — James Glasgow, ruling elder again paired with William Taylor.
:1705 — James Glasgow, ruling elder paired with James Scott of Duneane.
:1705 — William Taylor separately paired with Robert King.

The 1698 and 1703 entries are near-certainly the same man. The 1705 Duneane
occurrence is probably the same man, but no surviving entry explicitly states
continuity of identity. 
Why the Randalstown and Duneane occurrences are combined
The published Synod records pair each ruling elder with a minister. The place
is derived from the known charge of that minister:

* William Taylor — Randalstown or Drummaul.
* James Scott — Duneane.

The source evidence is therefore not literally "James Glasgow of
Randalstown" in 1698 and 1703 and "James Glasgow of Duneane" in 1705. More
precisely, it is:

:William Taylor — James Glasgow, 1698.
:William Taylor — James Glasgow, 1703.
:James Scott — James Glasgow, 1705.

This distinction explains why the three occurrences are combined under one
probable identity without turning the ministerial associations into exact
residences. Later indexes can obscure that distinction by presenting the
minister's congregation as though it had been written beside James's name.
Alternative explanation and possible residence
A second James Glasgow could theoretically have served Duneane in 1705. Under
that reconstruction, one James represented Taylor's congregation in 1698 and
1703 and another represented Scott's congregation in 1705. There is no
independent evidence for the second elder, so a single identity remains the
stronger hypothesis.

The Synod records do not reveal where James lived. He may have resided within
Drummaul parish, in or near Randalstown, within the district served by the
Duneane congregation, or in a locality between the congregational areas. A
move between 1703 and 1705 remains possible, but no tax, lease, estate or
other land record has been found to demonstrate it.
Possible descendants
No child of James has been identified from a contemporary record. The later
Bannside and Clough family of John Glasgow and
Jane McClure includes Rev. James McClure
Glasgow and several documented siblings. It is a substantial later Glasgow
family in the wider western or mid-Antrim area, but no record connects John to
This elder.

Rev. A. R. Crawford compiled two histories of the Glasgow family, and later
typescript copies and additions survive in the Crawford and Glasgow family
papers at PRONI, reference D2003/MIC128. The publicly available introduction
begins the later household with John Glasgow of Bannside and Jane or Jean
McClure rather than identifying John's parents. PRONI,
D2003/MIC128, Crawford and Glasgow family papers;
public introduction (https://www.sommemidulster.org/dwd/pdfs/02002.pdf).

The
distinction shows that a Glass population was already established in
Drummaul before the first known Synod occurrence of this James.

The 1740 Protestant Householders' Return continues that pattern with Adam
Glass, John Glass and two Glass widows in Drummaul. W. MacAfee,
1740 County Antrim Protestant Householders' Return (https://www.billmacafee.com/1740returns/1740protestantreturnsantrim.pdf), Drummaul and Duneane
entries.

The unusual form and locality make him the most
interesting unresolved spelling candidate for a son or younger relative of
James, but the return supplies no relationship evidence and does not establish
that his surname was Glasgow.

Useful search variants include:

* Glasgow.
* Glasgo.
* Glascho.
* Glaskow.
* Glask.
* Glass.
* Glads.

A variant should be assigned to this family only when chronology, locality,
associates or another record support the identification.
Relationship to the Kilwaughter family
No relationship has been proved between this western elder and the Glasgow
family established around Larne and Kilwaughter. They could belong to a wider
Scottish or Ulster family, and County Antrim Presbyterian migration patterns
make a connection plausible in general terms. No baptism, will, deed,
congregational minute or family record presently identifies a common ancestor.

The uncertain attachment to James of Kilwaughter therefore
records a working theory, not a proved parent-child relationship. Evidence
belonging to the two men should remain separated unless a direct bridge is
found.
Record coverage and archive leads
Ordinary local church registers do not reach James's likely child-bearing
period. Old Randalstown Presbyterian baptisms begin in 1853; Randalstown First
marriages in 1845; Randalstown Second baptisms and session minutes in 1850;
and Duneane Presbyterian baptisms in 1864 and marriages in 1845. Broad searches
of those surviving registers cannot identify children born about 1695–1720.

The most important church source is the Presbyterian Historical Society
material catalogued by the Irish Manuscripts Commission as "Antrim
Presbytery: Parcel of minutes, 1697–1713". The collection also includes an
earlier volume for 1671–1691 and Connor Presbytery minutes covering
1693–1735. Irish Manuscripts Commission,
Presbyterian Historical Society collection description (https://irishmanuscripts.ie/womenshistorysources/index.php?whp_function=1&whp_identifier=6204).

Presbyterian
Historical Society of Ireland,
"Timeline for Presbyterianism in Ireland" (https://presbyterianhistoryireland.com/history/timeline-for-presbyterianism-in-ireland/).

National
Archives of Ireland, CSO/RP/1833/6068, original reference 1833/6354 (https://csorp.nationalarchives.ie/search/index.php?browse=true&browseresults=true&category=27&offset=6060&subcategory=204), 11 items and 27 pages.

Registry of Deeds Index Project,
County
Antrim townland-index update (https://blog.irishdeedsindex.net/index.php/major-townland-index-update), townland-index film guide (https://irishdeedsindex.net/guides/townland_films.htm), and project
database (https://www.irishdeedsindex.net/).

Presbyterian Church in Ireland. Records of the General Synod of Ulster, from 1691 to 1820, vol. 1. Belfast, 1890. Synod records for 1698, 1703 and 1705. Internet Archive scan (https://archive.org/details/recordsofgeneral01pres).

Presbyterian Church in Ireland. Records of the General Synod of Ulster, from 1691 to 1820, vol. 1. Searchable Internet Archive text (https://archive.org/stream/recordsofgeneral01pres/recordsofgeneral01pres_djvu.txt).

Bolton, Charles Knowles. Scotch Irish Pioneers in Ulster and America. Boston: Bacon and Brown, 1910. Later index to ruling elders; useful as a finding aid, while the published Synod records above remain the principal source. Internet Archive (https://archive.org/details/scotchirish00boltrich).

MacAfee, W. 1669 County Antrim Hearth Money Roll transcription (https://www.billmacafee.com/1660shearthmoneyrolls/1669hearthmoneyrollsantrim.pdf), used to distinguish the Drummaul Glass households and the separate Kilwaughter Glasgow family.
MacAfee, W. 1740 County Antrim Protestant Householders' Return (https://www.billmacafee.com/1740returns/1740protestantreturnsantrim.pdf), Drummaul and Duneane entries.

Porter, Classon. "Congregational Memoirs: Larne and Kilwaughter." The Christian Unitarian, vol. 3 (1864), used for comparison with the separate James Glasgow of Kilwaughter. Internet Archive (https://archive.org/details/christianunitari0003unse).

James Glasgow and Nancy McCord, marriage registration, 29 November 1851, Cookstown registration district (https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/details-civil/178e293212496) at Irish Civil Registration - Marriages.

Research NotesParentage
James's 1851 marriage record confirms that his father was named William Glasgow and was a farmer. 

The 1799 baptism candidate names the child's parents as William and Mary Glasgow. If this baptism belongs to James, his mother was Mary, surname unknown.

The available records do not establish that James's father was specifically William Glasgow (abt.1760-), whose profile reportedly claims a Scottish origin based only on an online family tree. A documentary link between that William and this James has not been found.

The former attachment of Margaret Mitchell as James's mother is unsupported by an original record and conflicts with the strong baptism candidate naming his mother as Mary. Margaret Mitchell should therefore not be treated as James's mother without further evidence.

The other children attributed to the same tree-derived parents are likewise unproved as James's siblings. Each requires independent evidence before a shared nuclear family can be established.
Nancy McCord's children
Nancy's 1911 census return states that she had five children, of whom three were still living. Two of the surviving children are believed to have been Margaret Jane and Thomas, leaving one surviving child of Nancy not yet identified. Marriage records for people surnamed Glasgow who named their father as James may help identify that child.

There is a possible candidate, Mary Ann Glasgow (https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/details-civil/6567713134957), who married David Bell in 1867 and named her father as James Glasgow. Her residence was recorded as Killycurragh, however, so this is not sufficient evidence to identify her as a daughter of this James.
Explanation of children
The following people recorded Ballynasollus as their residence on marriage and named their father as James Glasgow:

* James Glasgow (abt.1828-1907)
* Margaret Jane Glasgow (abt.1851-)
* William Glasgow (abt.1823-)

Thomas Glasgow (abt.1860-aft.1935) is identified as a son of Nancy through census evidence. Thomas was also the informant at the deaths of both this James and James's son James. He was still living in 1935, when he attended the funeral of Martha Glasgow. No other Thomas Glasgow found in the census or civil death registrations appears to fit this evidence.

John Glasgow (abt.1824-1906) and Margaret Jane are identified as siblings because the funeral of John's daughter Jane was attended by Cunningham Glasgow.

John's daughter Ellen was the informant at Nancy Glasgow's death and was described as Nancy's granddaughter. Thomas Glasgow later appeared at Ellen's funeral. Taken together, this supports John being a son of James, although the precise relationship evidence should remain documented rather than assumed solely from patronymics.

The following person has not been attached as a child because his marriage record gives Killycurragh as his residence. Griffith's Valuation shows that other men named James Glasgow were associated with Killycurragh, so further evidence is required:

* David Glasgow (abt.1836-1883)
Corrected assessmentParentage
James's marriage confirms only that his father was named William Glasgow and was a farmer. The 1799 baptism candidate names the child's parents as William and Mary Glasgow. If it is this James, Mary, surname unknown, is his mother.

The available records do not establish that his father was specifically William Glasgow (abt.1760-). The current attachment of Margaret Mitchell is unsupported by an original record and conflicts with the strong baptism candidate naming Mary. Retain both current parent links as uncertain pending a supported structural resolution; do not infer the other attached children as James's siblings.
Children and open identifications
Nancy's 1911 census return states that she had five children, three then living. A possible daughter, Mary Ann Glasgow (https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/details-civil/6567713134957), married David Bell in 1867 and named her father James, but her Killycurragh residence is insufficient to identify her.

People who recorded Ballynasollus on marriage and named their father James include James Glasgow (abt.1828-1907), Margaret Jane Glasgow (abt.1851-), and William Glasgow (abt.1823-). Thomas Glasgow (abt.1860-aft.1935) is supported as Nancy's son by census evidence and as the informant at James's death. Evidence also supports John Glasgow (abt.1824-1906) as James's son, but its precise relationship evidence should remain documented rather than inferred from patronymics alone. David Glasgow (abt.1836-1883) remains unattached: his marriage gives Killycurragh, where other men named James Glasgow lived.

The death of James Glasgow was registered on 15 March 1882 in Cookstown, aged 83. GRONI civil death index (https://geni.nidirect.gov.uk/search/death), James Glasgow, 15 March 1882, aged 83, Cookstown registration district, D/1882/100/1009/7/125.

sources.citation: Margaret H. B. Sanderson, “The People of Sixteenth Century Ayrshire,” (https://aanhs.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/people-of-ayrshire.pdf#page=36) Ayrshire Collections 14, no. 8 (1987), appendix, “The Cunninghame Teind Lists of 1559–60,” printed p. 331, citing Register of Acts and Decreets, vol. 22, fols. 102v–167v.

National Records of Scotland, Charter Chest of the Earls of Glencairn, GD39/5/59 (https://catalogue.nrscotland.gov.uk/nrsonlinecatalogue/details.aspx?reference=GD39%2F5%2F59), letters of reversion concerning annual rent from the 40-shilling land of Corsinkell, barony of Stevenston, sheriffdom of Ayr, dated 9 February 1571.

His date and place of death have not been identified. The supported death statement is therefore after 9 February 1571, place unknown.

A death date in or after November 1580 appears to derive from conflation with a different Glasgow family and should not be applied to this profile without additional evidence.
Research NotesBirth estimate
The former estimate of about 1540 is too late.

James Glasgow younger was separately listed alongside James elder at Corsinkell in the 1559–1560 teind material. The 1571 record then directly identifies the younger James as the elder James's son. 

If the younger James was at least about eighteen to twenty-one in 1559, he was born by approximately 1538–1541. Normal generational spacing would place his father's birth around 1510–1520.

About 1515 is used as an uncertain working estimate. A more conservative statement would be that James elder was born before about 1525.
Parentage
William Glasgow is attached as James's father.

The relationship is chronologically possible, but no inspected record connects William's Glasgow burgh family with James at Corsinkell. The attachment should remain uncertain and should not be described as proved.

Isobel Brade is attached as James's mother. No record cited on this profile establishes that relationship. It should likewise remain uncertain.

The earlier attachment to John Glasgow was unsupported and chronologically problematic.
Wife or Campbell associates
Katherine Campbell was listed at Corsinkell with James elder and James younger in the 1559–1560 teind material. 

Christian Campbell was named among the occupiers in the 1571 archival catalogue description. 

Neither source states that either woman was James's wife, daughter or other relative. Katherine and Christian should not be assumed to be the same person, and neither should be attached as James's spouse without further evidence.
Son James
The younger James named at Corsinkell is represented by James Glasgow.

The repeated holding, the elder/younger distinction and the 1571 statement of relationship make this identification well supported.

Earlier links to James Glasgow should not be restored unless separate evidence shows that profile represents the Corsinkell son.
Son John
The 1571 record directly proves that James elder had a son named John. John Glasgow now represents that record-defined son and is attached confidently.

The Kilwinning John remains an uncertain identity candidate. A record connecting Burrowland or Dalgarven with Corsinkell is still required before the two profiles can be merged. The former link to John Glasgow should not be used.
Landholding context
Corsinkell formed part of lands held under branches of the Cunninghame family.

A charter made at Kerelaw on 4 February 1527 and confirmed on 25 May 1536 granted David Cunningham of Bertaneholme the five-merk lands of Corsinkell and Middlepart with other Stevenston lands. Parentage
The apprenticeship record directly identifies James's father as Robert Glasgow, servant to William Crichtoun in Wester Duddingston. 

Robert Glasgow is a plausible existing-profile match for this father because of the Wester Duddingston association and chronology. The record does not, however, contain enough information to prove that the named father and the existing profile represent the same man. That relationship should therefore remain uncertain.

The record does not name James's mother.

Deborah Ivey is not identified as his mother in any inspected record. Any attachment should remain uncertain and be treated as a working hypothesis rather than an established relationship.
Distinct from the Inveresk James
This James was not James Glasgow, who was baptised at Inveresk and Musselburgh on 19 March 1626 as a son of Alexander Glasgow and Jannet Clerk. “Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564–1950,” database, FamilySearch, James Glasgow, baptised 19 March 1626, Inveresk and Musselburgh, son of Alexander Glasgow, record VQ4V-GQW (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQ4V-GQW) (accessed 2025).

James Montgomery's elder brother was Sir Henry-Conyngham Montgomery, an East India Company cavalry officer, Member of Parliament and the first Montgomery Baronet of the Hall. He was created a baronet on 3 October 1808. 

The marriage therefore placed Jemima Glasgow within the immediate family of a newly created baronetcy and linked the Glasgows to a landed Montgomery family with military, parliamentary and East India Company connections.
Children
James and Jemima Montgomery had at least two known children:

* Jemima Montgomery, born at Sea-View, County Donegal, on 23 October 1807. 
* Conyngham Montgomery, born on 2 January 1809. 
Granddaughter: Baroness von Tautphoeus
James Glasgow's granddaughter, Jemima Montgomery, became significant as both a member of the Bavarian nobility and a published novelist.

On 29 January 1838, she married Cajetan Joseph Friedrich, Baron von Tautphoeus, of Marquartstein in Bavaria. He was a Bavarian government official and chamberlain to the King of Bavaria. The detailed family package can be traced to Brøderbund World Family Tree, volume 2, tree 6075 (1995), later imported into WeRelate. This documents pedigree provenance, not the events.

Joseph Glasgow, Wythe County, Virginia, will dated 2 April 1831 and proved 11 April 1831, transcription at Southwest Virginians (https://swvirginians.wordpress.com/2014/12/12/joseph-glasgow-pulaski-co-va-will-of-1831/); Library of Virginia catalogue (https://www.lva.virginia.gov/collections/ccmf/VA/VA305).
Family letter dated 6 November 1806, transcribed in Faris, Glasgow Family, pp. 14–19.

Cumberland County, Pennsylvania, Will Book C, p. 161, will of John Glasgow, dated 14 March and proved 3 September 1779; published will-book index (https://www.sampubco.com/wills/pa/pacumberland01.htm).
1775 petition of Protestant dissenters associated with Cookstown congregation, PRONI T/808/15307; transcription (https://cotyroneireland.com/misc/cookstown3.html).

Ellen Glasgow's 1954 account instead says that Arthur, then about sixteen and described as a ward, emigrated in 1766 with his mother and elder brothers; it associates the family with Counties Down and Antrim. These accounts differ on date, party, and locality. Neither supports the claim that James and Mary themselves immigrated together in 1770.

Pennsylvania naturalization index
In 1804 a man indexed as “James Glassgo” appeared in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania naturalization indexes. 

The index establishes a same-name naturalization record. It does not by itself identify the applicant as Robert's father, Mary Harkness's husband, the person in Turk's 1770 reference, or “James Glasgow of Moneymore.” If born about 1722, the applicant would have been about eighty-two, making the underlying card and petition especially important. The earlier statement that this record confirmed this James's Irish birth and long United States residence therefore remains an interpretation to be tested, not an established conclusion.
Identity and Relationship Questions
There is continuing ambiguity surrounding James's identity:

Private family details withheld.

Its reported earliest-ancestor label “James Glasgow” is consistent with Faris's later statement that Robert's father was James of Moneymore, but it remains a copied pedigree label. It cannot resolve whether that man is the conflicted WikiTree profile Glasgow-1024.

FamilySearch full-text deed search
A focused FamilySearch full-text search covered James Glasgow, James Glasgo, James Glascow, Mary Harkness and Mary Glasgow in eighteenth-century Moneymore, Derryloran, Cookstown and Kilrea. No matching record naming Mary Harkness or Mary Glasgow was found.

The James results were inspected rather than assigned by name alone. They concern already-separated men in Larne and the Aghadonvane/Leitrim-Donegal network, including a 1766 Larne ropemaker deed (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJW-J9XP-J), a 1776 Aghadonvane mortgage (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJW-N9YN-4), a 1780 Aghadonvane transaction (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJW-P9LW-G), and a 1778 Larne farmer affidavit (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSH3-9WVP-C). None names Moneymore, Derryloran, Cookstown, Kilrea, Mary Harkness or the emigrant sibling group. No result can presently be assigned to this James.

sources.citation: James McClure Glasgow missionary journal, 1857–1862 (https://revjamesmcclureglasgow.blogspot.com/), first-person journal in which James repeatedly identifies Adam Dickie Glasgow and Robert Glasgow of Victoria as his brothers (accessed 17 July 2026).

The entry does not state her name. The date matches the known chronology of the attached Jane McClure, but an independent identity source should be found before adding 21 May 1858 to her profile as a proved death date.
Academic career
After returning to Belfast in 1864, James was appointed Professor of Living Oriental Languages at both Magee College, Londonderry, and Assembly’s College, Belfast.

His towering intellect and profound scholarship were combined with an almost child-like simplicity and straightforwardness of character.

He also served as a government examiner in Gujarati for the Indian Civil Service.

In 1869 James was elected a member of the Belfast Literary Society. In 1872 he was elected its president.
Publications and translations
James’s publications included:

* The Psalms of David, Translated into Gujarati Verse, for the Use of Native Churches and Families (Surat Mission Press, 1856);
* The Apocalypse—Translated & Expounded (Edinburgh: T. & T. Clark, 1873).

He also translated Dr. Robert Stewart’s Family Worship and the Bible into Gujarati, together with many other writings in both English and Gujarati.
Children
James and Mary had five daughters, three of whom survived into adulthood:

* Margaret Jane Glasgow, born in Bombay on 16 March 1841; died at Rajkot on 11 June 1841 and was buried in the Anglican cemetery there;
* Jane Henrie Glasgow, who died on 14 April 1845 aged three months and was buried in the Anglican cemetery at Rajkot;
* Mary Elizabeth Glasgow, known as “Minnie”, born in 1845; she never married and died in 1874;
* Annie Coulson Glasgow, born in 1848; she married William Crawford;
* Harriet Glasgow, born in Ulster in 1851; she married John Acheson.

Annie’s husband, William Crawford, was the ninth child of the Rev. Alexander Crawford of Randalstown. He later became managing director of the York Street Flax Spinning Company and chairman of the Board of Governors of the Royal Victoria Hospital, Belfast. He was subsequently knighted.

Harriet’s husband, John Acheson, was also a linen manufacturer and was proprietor of the Bannview Weaving Factory at Portadown.
Later life
In Belfast, James and Mary lived at number 82 University Street, now numbered 86.

In 1878 they moved to Portadown to be near their daughter Harriet and son-in-law John Acheson.

Mary died on 19 February 1885.

James retired from his professorial posts in 1889.
Death and burial
James died on 30 June 1890 at Dunavon, Portadown.

His civil death registration described him as an 85-year-old widower, Presbyterian minister and Doctor of Divinity. His son-in-law John Acheson was present at the death. sources.citation: In 1841, Robert Glasgow, age 65, of independent means, born in Scotland, was living at Holly Walk, Leamington Priors, with Ann Glasgow age 40, Mary Glasgow age 19, Ann Robertson age 18, Jane Robertson age 20, Charlotte Robertson age 10 and Wilhelmina Robertson age 1, one male servant and four female servants. All the children were listed as being born in Scotland. Wilhelmina was the daughter of Robert Glasgow's eldest son, also Robert. The baptism of Charlotte in Edinburgh on 20/07/1828 gives her birth as Rome, 22/11/1827. Anne Glasgow the elder has not been traced and had presumably died by 1841. Anne Glasgow or Robertson the younger was born in Edinburgh 05/10/1805 and baptised 26/03/1805 in Ayton, Berwickshire. It is this younger Anne, the daughter, not the wife of Robert, who appears in the 1841 census.

This profile formerly contained structured dates and a Scottish birthplace belonging to Jane Allan Glasgow, daughter of John Glasgow and Christina Forsyth. sources.citation: Public Record Office of Northern Ireland, 1669 County Antrim Hearth Money Roll, T/307/A; W. Macafee, transcription (https://www.billmacafee.com/1660shearthmoneyrolls/1669hearthmoneyrollsantrim.pdf), records 5347–5348, PDF p. 36.

The abbreviation Jo. most probably represents John. The exact co-location and uncommon surname make a close relationship between John and James Glasgow probable, although the tax roll gives no ages, household members or relationship.
John Glasgow senior, c. 1699–1700
Classon Porter later published substantial extracts from an early record of the Larne and Kilwaughter congregation. Porter stated that he had been unable to locate the original in his day and was working from a transcript made or procured for Rev. D. Davison, portions of which had already been published in 1826. Porter arranged his quotations by subject rather than strict chronology. Classon Porter, "Congregational Memoirs—Larne and Kilwaughter," The Christian Unitarian, vol. 2 (1863–1864), pp. 410–415; Internet Archive (https://archive.org/details/christianunitari0002unse). Porter describes the provenance of the transcript on p. 410.

Porter immediately reproduced the Presbytery's minute for the same deputation. It names the same four men — Samuel Smealley, William Hare, John Glasgow and James Callwell — but calls him simply John Glasgow. 

This is useful identity evidence. Senior was a contextual qualifier; the same man could be recorded without it in another record of the same transaction.

On 17 May, John again appears as:

 "John Glasgow, sen., for Kilwochter" 

He and Patrick Agnew bound for Kilwaughter's £8 share of the minister's stipend, together with obligations for firing, ploughing and harrowing. 

John was also among the heads of families entrusted with considering the rebuilding of the meeting house. These entries establish that he was a substantial member of the Kilwaughter congregation and a representative of its householders. They do not establish that he held the office of elder.

The following year's material again records plain John Glasgow acting for Kilwaughter. On 27 February 1700 in the record's dating, John Glasgow and Robert White were chosen for Kilwaughter to inspect the minister's land. In the same meeting, Patrick Agnew and John Glasgow were selected for Kilwaughter to consider repairs to the minister's house. Classon Porter, "Congregational Memoirs—Larne and Kilwaughter," The Christian Unitarian, vol. 3 (1864), pp. 15–18; Internet Archive (https://archive.org/details/christianunitari0003unse).

The identification remains inferential because no surviving entry explicitly says that the 1669 and c.1700 men were identical.
Family
James Glasgow was recorded immediately beside John at Kilwaughter in 1669. About 1700 a James Glasgow was appointed overseer for Kilwaughter during work on the minister's house. 

The repeated John-and-James presence in the same small district strengthens the case that they belonged to one close family cluster. Their exact relationship remains unknown.

John is currently placed as an uncertain son of Robert Glasgow, the Robert Glaskow associated with Larne during the period of the 1641 rebellion. Trinity College Dublin, MS 838, fol. 153r, examination of Con O'Sheale, 21 April 1653, identifier 838153r210; Robert is described as "one Robert Glaskow liuing in Larne"; 1641 Depositions Project transcription (https://1641dep.abdn.ac.uk/items/show/42821.html).

No located published extract explicitly names a John Glasgow junior, however, and senior does not itself prove a father-son relationship. The younger namesake could have been:

* John's son;
* a nephew;
* a cousin;
* another younger member of the same Glasgow cluster.

A son is a plausible hypothesis, but not yet a relationship suitable for attachment without further evidence.

The important distinction is therefore:

:Probable: Jo Glascho of Kilwaughter in 1669 = John Glasgow senior of Kilwaughter c.1700.
:Possible: the younger John implied by senior was his son.
:Unknown: the younger John's identity and later history.

No reliable WikiTree profile has yet been identified for this younger namesake.
Could the c.1700 senior have been a son of the 1669 John?
It is chronologically possible but presently less likely.

A male householder in 1669 could readily still have been active about 1700. Even if John had been only about twenty-one in 1669, he would have been about fifty-two by 1700 — entirely compatible with being the established senior John, a head of family and congregational bondsman.

Making the c.1700 senior a son instead requires an additional same-name generation for which no record has yet been found. It would also require some other younger John to explain why that second-generation John was himself called senior.

The simpler reconstruction fits all presently located evidence without adding an undocumented generation.

Current assessment: same person probable; father-son replacement possible but unsupported.
Parentage and Scottish hypothesis
The current uncertain father hypothesis should distinguish two separate questions.

Robert Glasgow is the Robert Glaskow associated with Larne in the 1653 examination. He is a plausible earlier member of the Larne–Kilwaughter Glasgow family and is currently attached as John's uncertain father.

A separate Robert Glasgow was recorded in Glasgow, Scotland, in 1618. That Scottish Robert has been proposed as identical with the Larne Robert, but no documentary migration or identity bridge has been found.

The two hypotheses should not be collapsed:

* Robert of Larne → John of Kilwaughter: possible; unproved.
* Scottish Robert → Robert of Larne: possible identity; unproved.

John's mother remains unknown.
Record survival
Porter's nineteenth-century publication is derivative: he stated that the original early congregational record could not then be found and that he was using a transcript. 

There is now a more concrete archival route. Modern scholarship identifies surviving Larne and Kilwaughter session material for 1699–1701 and 1720–1769 and cites PRONI MIC1B/6A/1B. Robert Whan, The Presbyterians of Ulster, 1680–1730 (Boydell Press, 2013), introduction and bibliography, identifying Larne and Kilwaughter session records for 1699–1701 and 1720–1769 and citing PRONI MIC1B/6A/1B; Cambridge bibliography (https://resolve.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/C038A358FF15C0285190286F12E951A4/9781782041894bib_p202-230_CBO.pdf/bibliography.pdf).

John married three times. His first wife was Elizabeth "Betsey" Eddy, widow of a Mr. Hoagland. Only one child of that marriage survived to adulthood: Mary J. Glasgow, later wife of James Gould of Wheeling, Missouri.

sources.citation: John Glasgow family register and descendant page (https://hiltner.com/mckeown/getperson.php?personID=I368&tree=tree1) (accessed 20 July 2026).

John Glasgow to Jane Glasgow Gray, 20 March 1847 (https://www.hiltner.com/mckeown/documents/John%20Glasgow%20letter%20to%20Jane%20Glasgow%20Gray%203-20-1847.pdf), scan and transcript (accessed 20 July 2026).

The family lived at Inishrush, County Londonderry. In 1847, John recalled that they had kept more bees there than they ever kept at one time after leaving Ireland. 

The first secure evidence of John in Ohio is his 1833 purchase of land in Guernsey County. Guernsey County deeds, volume H, page 457 (http://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QS7-89WY-TFPB).

“United States Census, 1840,” database with images, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XHRF-1B6 : 8 September 2017), John Glascow, Guernsey, Ohio, United States; citing p. 355, NARA microfilm publication M704, roll 396; FHL microfilm 20,165.

They were living in Arthur's household in Londonderry Township in 1850. “United States Census, 1850,” database with images, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:MX3M-HP3 : 12 April 2016), John Glasgow in household of Arthur Glasgow, Londonderry, Guernsey, Ohio, United States; citing family 1538, NARA microfilm publication M432.

John's surviving letter reflects this outlook through repeated references to prayer, salvation and holding to Christ “for righteousness and life.” 

John died on 23 December 1851 and was buried in the Scotch Covenanter Cemetery in Guernsey County. “Find A Grave Index,” database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QVKX-FB2D : 13 December 2015), John Glasgow, died 1851; burial in Scotch Covenanter Cemetery, Guernsey County, Ohio; citing .

* Rose or “Rosanna”, born 4 March 1799; married Alexander McKeown in Ireland and settled in Harrison County, Ohio.
* Maria , born 22 September 1800.
* Jane, born 5 October 1802; married John Gray in Ireland and settled in Kentucky. John's 1847 letter was apparently addressed to her. 
* Adam, born 7 July 1804.
* Lavinia, born 21 June 1806.
* James, born 9 November 1808; died 20 April 1823.
* Margaret, born 17 October 1810; married John H. Walkinshaw.
* John, born 4 March 1813; died 17 August 1836 in Ohio.
* Arthur, born 1 July 1815; married Jane Neil.
Research Notes
* John Glasgow (bef.1813-) represents the John Glasco who headed house 2 at Inishrush in the 1831 census. His household contained four males and four females, all Presbyterian. “Tamlaght O'Crilly Census – 1831” (https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/Tamlaght/1831census_3.html), entry 1019, John Glasco, Innisrush house 2; transcription by Richard John Torrens (accessed 20 July 2026).

* The John Glasgow recorded in Richland Township, Belmont County, in 1830 was aged forty to forty-nine and was almost certainly a different man. John, born in 1767, would have been about sixty-three. The citation is retained to document the rejected identification, but should not be used as evidence that he was in Ohio by 1830. 1830 United States census, Richland Township, Ohio (https://archive.org/details/populationsc18300127unit/page/n484/mode/1up), original census image (accessed 20 July 2026).
Family of John Glasgow and Mary Arthur (https://www.hiltner.com/mckeown/familychart.php?personID=I368&tree=tree1), Hiltner.com.
Glasgow Surname Project at FamilyTreeDNA (https://www.familytreedna.com/groups/glasgow/about).

sources.citation: "Tamlaght O'Crilly Census - 1831" (https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/Tamlaght/1831census_3.html), entry 1019, John Glasco, Innisrush house 2; transcription by Richard John Torrens (accessed 20 July 2026).

Adam was born about 1758. Their shared surname, small townland and Presbyterian religion make them probable close relatives, but the census states no relationship.

If John was the man born in 1767 who is represented by Glasgow-822, Adam was only about nine years older and cannot have been his father. Brother is the best working placement, with cousin the principal alternative. John is therefore attached uncertainly to Adam's unidentified-father placeholder, Glasgow-3905, so that the probable sibling reconstruction can be represented. No record yet names their shared father or mother.
Possible church identity
A John Glasgow attended a Reformed Presbyterian session at Drumlamph in 1809 and was an elder present at Drimbolg on 19 July 1827. "Drimbolg Reformed Presbyterian Church" (https://www.oneirishrover.com/drimbolg-reformed-presbyterian-church/), congregation history and session extracts (accessed 20 July 2026).
John Glasgow family register and descendant page (https://hiltner.com/mckeown/getperson.php?personID=I368&tree=tree1) (accessed 20 July 2026).

John Glasgow to Jane Glasgow Gray, 20 March 1847 (https://www.hiltner.com/mckeown/documents/John%20Glasgow%20letter%20to%20Jane%20Glasgow%20Gray%203-20-1847.pdf), scan and transcript (accessed 20 July 2026).
Scotland's People, "Forenames: traditional naming patterns" (https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/help-and-support/guides/forenames) (accessed 20 July 2026).

A separate McKeown family-Bible transcription records that John Glasgow McKeown, son of Rosanna Glasgow, was born at Inishrush on 17 April 1821 and baptised by the Rev. Joseph Orr. John Glasgow McKeown (https://www.hiltner.com/mckeown/getperson.php?personID=I1&tree=tree1), family-Bible transcription and descendant page, Hiltner genealogy; the underlying Bible image has not been inspected for this account.

This independently connects the proposed Glasgow-822 family to the townland and congregation. It strengthens the identity case but does not name Adam as a brother or establish shared parents; the proposed merge remains subject to review.
Evidence previously used to exclude the proposed identity
The original 1830 Richland Township, Ohio, census recorded its household head as aged forty to forty-nine. 1830 United States census, Richland Township, Ohio (https://archive.org/details/populationsc18300127unit/page/n484/mode/1up), original census image (accessed 20 July 2026).

James Glasgow, proved by gravestone to be Adam's son, remained a farmer at Inishrush. "Tamlaght Graveyard" (https://www.oneirishrover.com/tamlaght-graveyard/), Glasgow gravestone transcriptions and photographs (accessed 20 July 2026).

* Children — Mary Jane (1854), Sarah Anne (1862), and Elizabeth (1868) are securely linked as his children via marriage records that explicitly name their father as John Glasgow. Additional Glasgow marriages in the area (e.g., a Samuel Glasgow indexed 23 Mar 1870) may indicate further children; evidence not yet evaluated.
* Name & Place Variants — Surname appears as Glasgow and occasionally Glasson in indexes; bridegroom Lennon is indexed as Lennon/Leemon. Townland appears as Drumgreenagh/Drumgreeney within the civil parish of Derrynoose (sometimes written Killyreavy).
* To Do — Seek Church of Ireland or Presbyterian registers for Derrynoose/Keady area for baptisms and burial; consult PRONI Freeholders books, Tithe Applotment (1820s–1830s), and Valuation Revision Books for chain of occupancy; locate primary source for the stated death date (30 Apr 1849).
Earlier Drumgreenagh namesake
A deed made on 13 February 1786 identifies an older John Glasgow as a farmer at Drumgreenagh and husband of Jane Murphy. He cannot be this profile, who was born about 1794. The shared residence makes an older-family relationship plausible, but the deed names no child and does not prove that the older John was this John's father. sources.citation: W. Macafee, 1796 Flaxgrowers' List for Co. Londonderry [T3419], sorted by surname, barony and parish, dated 21 February 2011, printed p. 49, record 2070: John Glasgow, Coleraine barony, Desertoghill [Desartoghill], two wheels. Published transcription (https://www.billmacafee.com/1796flaxgrowerslist/1796flaxgrowersderry.pdf#page=49). The compiler cites archival reference T3419; this citation is to the transcription rather than an independently inspected original list.

Research NotesPossible move from Londonderry to Antrim
The 1851 census of Lisnagaver records John Glasgow, aged 50, as born in County Antrim, while his brother Samuel Glasgow, aged 60, was born in County Londonderry. Their recorded ages suggest births about 1801 and 1791 respectively. W. Scott and W. Macafee, 1851 Census for some Parishes and Townlands in the Barony of Kilconway, Co. Antrim, dated 7 May 2014, printed p. 141, Lisnagavor household 34, references 16848–16851. John Glasgow: head, 50, farmer, born Antrim; Samuel Glasgow: brother, 60, linen weaver, born Londonderry. Published census transcription (https://www.billmacafee.com/census/1851censuskilconway.pdf#page=141).

This remains a migration hypothesis dependent on the proposed family identification. The dates are approximate, and a child's birthplace does not necessarily establish the parents' usual residence.
Identity
This profile documents the John Glasgow named in the 1796 Desertoghill entry. Whether he was the same man as another John Glasgow already represented on WikiTree remains unresolved.
Possible identification with John Glasgow of Inishrush
The Glasgow surname research catalogue identifies the flax-list entry as a possible earlier record of John Glasgow, born in 1767, husband of Mary Arthur and associated with Inishrush before emigrating to Ohio. However, the catalogue explicitly leaves this identification unproved: the parish differs, and the flax list supplies no family details connecting the two records. Glasgow Surname Project, research dossier for John Glasgow, Glasgow-822 (https://glasgow.phenotype.dev/people/glasgow-822.html), source assessment of the 1796 County Londonderry flax-premium list and discussion of the 1831 Inishrush household. Research synthesis, not an independent record of the proposed identification.

Possible identification with the father of John Glasgow of Lisnagaver
Another possibility is that this man was the John Glasgow, farmer named as the father of John Glasgow of Lisnagaver when the younger John married Margaret Garvin on 16 November 1846 at Second Garvagh Presbyterian Church. General Register Office of Ireland, civil marriage register, Coleraine registration district, Second Garvagh Presbyterian Church, Errigal parish, County Londonderry, entry 13: John Glasgow and Margaret Garvin, 16 November 1846. Register image, IrishGenealogy.ie (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1846/09306/5369439.pdf).

Grant, ed., Commissariot Record of Glasgow: Register of Testaments, 1547-1800 (Edinburgh: Scottish Record Society, 1901), p. 426 (https://archive.org/details/scottishrecordso07scotuoft/page/n435/mode/1up), Robertson, Bessie, 17 August 1610; cross-reference under Glasgow, John, p. 196 (https://archive.org/details/scottishrecordso07scotuoft/page/196/mode/1up).
National Records of Scotland, Lanark Commissary Court, CC14/5/5, images 65–66, testament dative and inventory of John Glasgow in Quodquen; confirmed 27 May 1650.

Francis J. Grant, ed., The Commissariot Record of Lanark: Register of Testaments, 1595–1800 (Edinburgh: Scottish Record Society, 1903), printed p. 38, “Glasgow, John, in Quodquen,” 27 May 1650, digital copy (https://www.tradeshouselibrary.org/uploads/4/7/7/2/47723681/the_commissariot_record_of_lanark__register_of_testaments__1595-1800_~_1903.pdf#page=50).

It names no parent, wife, son or daughter. Thomas Glasgow, deceased, and a William Glasgow appear in the financial account, but their relationships to John are not stated.
Residence and death
John Glasgow lived at Quodquen, in Lanarkshire, Scotland. National Records of Scotland, Lanark Commissary Court, Wills and Testaments, reference CC14/5/5, testament dative and inventory of John Glasgow in Quodquen, images 65–66.

Bessie Glasgow was appointed executrix dative. The testament expressly describes her as John’s:

“laufull sister”

The confirmation later describes John as:

“hir brother”

The relationship is therefore directly stated twice in the original record.

On 27 May 1650 Bessie appeared before Master John Carmichael, commissary of Lanark, presented the inventory and was confirmed as executrix after providing the required caution. 
Estate
John’s physical possessions included: 

* three kine, valued together at £8 Scots;
* his clothing or bodily apparel, valued at £20 Scots.

The physical inventory totalled £28 Scots.

The testament also listed debts and sums owing to John’s estate. The clerk recorded:

“Na debtis awin be ye deid”

No debts owed by John himself were entered.

The clerk also recorded:

“Na divisioun”

No formal division of the estate was entered.
FamilySister
* Bessie Glasgow — John’s lawful sister and executrix dative. 

No parent, wife, son or daughter is identified in John’s 1650 testament.

The absence of a wife or child from the record does not prove that John had never married or had no children. It means only that none is named in this testament.
Possible wife: Bessie Robertson
The published index to the Glasgow Commissariot Register contains the entry:

“Robertson, Bessie, spouse to John Glasgow, in Montfoid — 17 Aug. 1610”

The corresponding entry under Glasgow reads:

“Glasgow, John, in Montfoid. See Robertson, Bessie.”

This establishes that Bessie Robertson was the wife of a John Glasgow in Montfoid. The date is the testament date, not a marriage date. Francis J. Grant, ed., The Commissariot Record of Glasgow: Register of Testaments, 1547–1800, Scottish Record Society, vol. 7 (Edinburgh, 1901), p. 426, entry for Robertson, Bessie, dated 17 August 1610, digital copy (https://archive.org/details/scottishrecordso07scotuoft/page/426/mode/2up).

sources.citation: “Scotland Births and Baptisms, 1564–1950,” FamilySearch, John Glasgow and Agnes Martine, baptism of son John, 8 October 1693, Irvine 595/ M.

Irvine Burgh catalogue, 1725 ship-share entry. The catalogue PDF link formerly supplied by Ayrshire Archives returned HTTP 410 Gone when checked 26 August 2026; the source title and entry detail are retained pending recovery of a stable archive catalogue URL.

The shared name and Irvine setting make the 1725 skipper and 1740 bailie possible matches, but the cited records do not supply an occupation, family relationship or other bridge proving they were the same man.
Comparison with Glasgow-1434
John Glasgow, baptised in 1679 at Kilwinning and later associated with Stevenston, remains an open candidate for part of this reconstruction. He would have been only about fourteen when the son John was baptised in 1693, which weighs against—but does not by itself disprove—the father proposition. The alleged duplicate-son conflict is not decisive because the skipper, bailie and family identifications on this profile are themselves reconstructed. The profiles should not be merged or detached without burgh or parish evidence linking the Kilwinning/Stevenston man to Irvine.

John's death remains unknown. If the 1740 bailie was the same person represented here, he was alive in that year; that equation is not proved.
Research Notes
* The 1693 father, 1725 skipper and 1740 bailie are three separate propositions.
* The attached spouse Agnes Martine and son John are retained as uncertain links, not proved members of the skipper/bailie household.
* “Elder” proves only that a younger namesake existed, not that the younger man was his son.
* The possible relationship to Michael Glasgow remains unproved.
* Compare witnesses, occupations and residences in Irvine burgh and shipping records before considering a merge with Glasgow-1434.

* A 1721 Irvine prize bond lists “John Glasgow for one” among subscribers pledging a half crown toward an annual shooting prize. The name and town make this a possible earlier occurrence of the 1725 skipper, but the bond gives no occupation, kin or identifying description. Muniments of the Royal Burgh of Irvine, vol. Research Notes
No inspected record names John's wife.

Absolom Glasgow, born about 1799, is attached as John's son. The 1820 household is compatible with John, a wife and Absolom, but it does not name the younger people and therefore does not itself prove the relationship. No additional son of John has been identified.

Hiram Glasgow should not be added as another son. The will of Mary, widow of Wilson Glasgow, directly calls Hiram her son. sources.citation: "Tamlaght O'Crilly Census - 1831" (https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/Tamlaght/1831census_3.html), entry 1019, John Glasco, Innisrush house 2; transcription by Richard John Torrens (accessed 20 July 2026).

Adam was born about 1758. Their shared surname, small townland and Presbyterian religion make them probable close relatives, but the census states no relationship.

If John was the man born in 1767 who is represented by Glasgow-822, Adam was only about nine years older and cannot have been his father. Brother is the best working placement, with cousin the principal alternative. John is therefore attached uncertainly to Adam's unidentified-father placeholder, Glasgow-3905, so that the probable sibling reconstruction can be represented. No record yet names their shared father or mother.
Possible church identity
A John Glasgow attended a Reformed Presbyterian session at Drumlamph in 1809 and was an elder present at Drimbolg on 19 July 1827. "Drimbolg Reformed Presbyterian Church" (https://www.oneirishrover.com/drimbolg-reformed-presbyterian-church/), congregation history and session extracts (accessed 20 July 2026).
John Glasgow family register and descendant page (https://hiltner.com/mckeown/getperson.php?personID=I368&tree=tree1) (accessed 20 July 2026).

John Glasgow to Jane Glasgow Gray, 20 March 1847 (https://www.hiltner.com/mckeown/documents/John%20Glasgow%20letter%20to%20Jane%20Glasgow%20Gray%203-20-1847.pdf), scan and transcript (accessed 20 July 2026).
Scotland's People, "Forenames: traditional naming patterns" (https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/help-and-support/guides/forenames) (accessed 20 July 2026).

A separate McKeown family-Bible transcription records that John Glasgow McKeown, son of Rosanna Glasgow, was born at Inishrush on 17 April 1821 and baptised by the Rev. Joseph Orr. John Glasgow McKeown (https://www.hiltner.com/mckeown/getperson.php?personID=I1&tree=tree1), family-Bible transcription and descendant page, Hiltner genealogy; the underlying Bible image has not been inspected for this account.

This independently connects the proposed Glasgow-822 family to the townland and congregation. It strengthens the identity case but does not name Adam as a brother or establish shared parents; the proposed merge remains subject to review.
Evidence previously used to exclude the proposed identity
The original 1830 Richland Township, Ohio, census recorded its household head as aged forty to forty-nine. 1830 United States census, Richland Township, Ohio (https://archive.org/details/populationsc18300127unit/page/n484/mode/1up), original census image (accessed 20 July 2026).

James Glasgow, proved by gravestone to be Adam's son, remained a farmer at Inishrush. "Tamlaght Graveyard" (https://www.oneirishrover.com/tamlaght-graveyard/), Glasgow gravestone transcriptions and photographs (accessed 20 July 2026).
1831 County Londonderry census name index (https://www.billmacafee.com/1831census/1831derrycensusnames.pdf), Henry Barkley, Tyanee (accessed 20 July 2026).

Kilrea First Presbyterian Church marriages, 1828 (https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/KilreaP1/Marriages/1828.html), marriage of Jane Barklie, daughter of Henry Barklie (accessed 20 July 2026).
marriage notice, 14 January 1842 (https://cotyrone.com/~inthenews/marriages-notices-1840-42/), Nancy, sixth daughter of Adam Glasgow of Inishrush (accessed 20 July 2026).

Earlier Tamlaght O'Crilly network
A declaration dated 6 April 1772 listed Hugh Glasgow, Thomas Mulhollan and James Berkley among people described as inhabitants of Tamlaght O'Crilly who surrendered arms to Henry Ellis of Inishrush. Belfast News-Letter, 14 April 1772 (https://arborealis.ca/records/newspapers/kilrea-news/1770-1779/), declaration dated 6 April 1772 concerning inhabitants of Tamlaght O'Crilly (accessed 20 July 2026).

Underlying record source: john glasgow 1 (https://www.billmacafee.com/1796flaxgrowerslist/1796flaxgrowersderry.pdf); Underlying record source: john glasgow 2 (https://apps.proni.gov.uk/freeholders/default.aspx).

John Jr.'s sketch instead dates their arrival at Jonesville to 1848. Both accounts establish that the couple migrated from County Tyrone to Hillsdale County during the 1840s. John's death date has not been established.
Research NotesBirth and migration conflicts
John's birth year of about 1778 comes from the 1888 sketch of John Jr. His birth location remains uncertain because the same volume gives conflicting accounts: Scotland in one sketch and County Tyrone in another. The family's residence near Cookstown is better supported than John's exact birthplace.

The 1844 and 1848 immigration dates should remain as competing published accounts until passenger, census, land or naturalisation records settle the sequence.
Other Cookstown-area Johns
This John may be confused with John Glasgow, whose profile groups a different set of children, or John Glasgow of Killycurragh, associated with Benjamin and Henry Glasgow. A John Glasgow recorded at Drummeen in the 1827 Lissan tithe applotment book is geographically and chronologically compatible with this man before migration, but the entry gives no relatives and cannot presently identify him.

No compatible WikiTree profiles have yet been established for children Robert, Mary A., Bessie, James or Margaret. They should not be attached to same-name profiles without Michigan or New York records linking them to John and Jane.
Drummeen and Cookstown candidate
John Glasgow appears at Drummeen in the 1827 tithe material and a John Glasgow of Cookstown appears in the 1851 probate index. These records fit the district and broad generation of this John, but they are not proved to concern one man or this profile. sources.citation: 1851 Census of Ireland (https://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/pages/1851/Antrim/Kilconway/Rasharkin/Lisnagaver/34/), Lisnagaver house 34, Rasharkin, County Antrim; original census image (http://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/reels/c19/007246523/007246523_00173.pdf).

Pauline O'Keeffe and Helen Evans, Rasharkin Second Presbyterian Church headstones (https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/RasharkinP/graveyard.html), transcription made August 2004, Glasgo memorial erected by James Garvin Glasgo.

IrishGenealogy.ie (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/view/?record_id=cima-3156063), civil marriage registration of John Glasgow and Margaret Garvin, 16 November 1846, Ballymena registration district, group registration ID 3156063; original register image (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1846/09306/5369439.pdf).

The 1851 household contained John, Margaret, their three-year-old daughter
Ann, and John's brother Samuel Glasgow. John
Patterson, a fifteen-year-old linen weaver, was their servant. The return records
1846 as the marriage year and explicitly describes Samuel as John's brother. 

Ann married Francis Bellingham on 18 February 1875. Her
marriage names her father as John Glasgow, farmer. General Register Office of Ireland, civil marriage register (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1875/11190/8100682.pdf), Francis Bellingham and Annie Glasgow, 18 February 1875, Finvoy parish church, entry 40.

General Register Office of Ireland, civil marriage register (https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/images/marriage_returns/marriages_1886/10840/5957283.pdf), James Garvin Glasgow and Eliza Ann Aiken, 1 July 1886, Clough, entry 62.

The gravestone records that Margaret died on 10 January 1892 aged seventy-four
and John died on 20 June 1895 aged seventy-eight. Their son James erected the
memorial at Rasharkin Second Presbyterian Church. 
Marriage
John married Margaret Garvin on 16 November 1846 at Second Garvagh Presbyterian Church, in Errigal parish, County Londonderry. The marriage was by licence and was registered in Coleraine, not Ballymena. 

The contemporary return describes John as a full-age bachelor and farmer of Lisnagaver, parish of Rasharkin, son of John Glasgow, farmer. Margaret was a full-age spinster of Rockfield, parish of Desertoghill, daughter of James Garvin, farmer. 

The witnesses were James Garvin and a man whose name was read as Wm Keely, not the previously reported Ann Kelly. The second surname remains a handwriting reading rather than an established identification. Neither witness's relationship to the couple is stated; the witness James Garvin should not automatically be identified as Margaret's father. The minister's signature was read as James B. Rentoul. 
Lisnagaver household, 1851
The surviving census places the family at house 34, Lisnagaver. It records 1846 as John and Margaret's marriage year, agreeing with their marriage return.

The return directly establishes that Samuel was John's brother. It contains five household members, not five children: Ann is the only child of John listed in this household. 
Children
The following children are supported by the household and family records. This is not necessarily a complete child group.

* Ann Glasgow, aged three in 1851 and born in County Londonderry. The working identification is Annie Glasgow, who married Francis Bellingham on 18 February 1875 at Finvoy parish church. Annie was a full-age spinster of the parish of Rasharkin, daughter of John Glasgow, farmer. Francis was a full-age bachelor and farmer of Culmore, parish of Rasharkin, son of Thomas Bellingham, farmer. The witnesses were Thomas Bellingham and Mary Ann M'Caughern, as read. The marriage does not name Annie's mother or supply a townland for her, so it is consistent with, but does not alone complete, the identification with the census daughter. General Register Office of Ireland, contemporary civil marriage return, Ballymoney registration district, page 191, entry 40: Francis Bellingham and Annie Glasgow, 18 February 1875, Finvoy parish church, County Antrim. Register image (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1875/11190/8100682.pdf).

General Register Office of Ireland, civil marriage return, entry 62: James Garvin Glasgow and Eliza Ann Aiken, 1 July 1886, Clough. Register image (https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/images/marriage_returns/marriages_1886/10840/5957283.pdf).

James's original death return independently records his full name as James Garvin Glasgow. He died at Lisnagaver on 14 February 1918, a married farmer aged 64, from acute pneumonia of six days' duration, certified. The informant was Eliza Ann Glasgow, widow, present at death, Lisnagaver; registration followed on 8 March 1918. General Register Office of Ireland, contemporary civil death return, Ballymoney superintendent registrar's district, Dirraw registrar's district, County Antrim, entry 165: James Garvin Glasgow, Lisnagaver, 14 February 1918; registered 8 March 1918. Register image (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/deaths_returns/deaths_1918/05197/4435754.pdf).

Death and family memorial
The GLASGO memorial at Rasharkin Second Presbyterian Church was erected by James Garvin Glasgo and names his father John and mother Margaret Garvin. The available source is a modern transcription made by Pauline O'Keeffe and Helen Evans in August 2004; a photograph of this particular stone has not yet been inspected.

The 1885 return gives the cause of death as cancer in lip, three years, with no medical attendant. It directly documents a John Glasgow and son James at Lisnagaver. It does not name John's wife, give James a middle name, or state James's age. 

The deceased has a separate profile, John Glasgow. An earlier version of this biography excluded him solely because the memorial transcription gives 1895. That exclusion was not justified. The same age, the Lisnagaver connection and the son James make identity with this John a substantial possibility.

A transcription error is a plausible explanation, not an established correction. Both the day and year differ: 24 June 1885 against 20 June 1895. A photograph could show whether the published transcription misreads the stone; if the stone itself says 1895, the conflict would still need investigation. Different men, an error on the memorial, or another record error remain possible. The agreement in age does not by itself settle identity. 

The memorial transcription also records:
* Margaret Garvin, James's mother, died 10 January 1892, aged 74.
* John Garvin, an infant son of James.
* James Garvin, died 14 February 1918, aged 67.
* Elizabeth Ann, died 16 June 1933, aged 84. 

Margaret's original January 1892 death registration has not yet been obtained. Her married or widowed status, address and informant could help distinguish the competing death scenarios, once the record is securely identified as hers. A matching 1895 civil death has likewise not been verified.
Research Notes
Current evidence assessmentParentage
John's marriage proves that his father was another John Glasgow, farmer.
The father is currently represented by John Glasgow as an
uncertain working identification. No record yet gives the older man's residence,
wife or age. If the gravestone age is correct, the older John would have been
about sixty-five when this John was born; possible, but not enough to identify
him uniquely.

The conflict between the 1851 age of fifty and the gravestone age of seventy-
eight at death remains unresolved. The marriage, residence, wife and 1846
marriage year securely identify the 1851 household, while the gravestone was
erected by the couple's son and names both parents. The birth year should
therefore remain estimated.
Alexander Glasgow of Glenleslie
Alexander Glasgow was previously attached as John's son.
However, Alexander was already a full-age bachelor when he married in April
1847, only five months after John and Margaret's marriage. Alexander's original
marriage also names his father as John Glasgow, labourer. He was detached
from this household because he belongs to an older, separate father-John branch. General Register Office of Ireland, civil marriage register (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1847/09322/5375567.pdf), Alexander Glasgow and Mary Anne Martin, 6 April 1847, Clogh, entry 31; derivative FamilySearch index entry (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QGVD-P9CS).

Earlier descriptions of John as born before 1798 depended on the former attachment of Alexander Glasgow as his son. That attachment is not a sound basis for dating John's birth.
Father and earlier parentage theories
The marriage return establishes a father named John Glasgow, farmer. It does not identify him uniquely as John Glasgow of Glenleslie, nor give his residence, wife or age. 

John of Glenleslie remains a possible father and may be retained as an uncertain working placement. Shared name and occupation do not prove the connection. The earlier identification of John and Samuel as sons of that John and Rose Alexander has no demonstrated contemporary link to the Lisnagaver household.

An alternative reconstruction made the brothers sons of Adam Glasgow and Rose, based on ages, Samuel's County Londonderry birthplace, the Inishrush family's proximity and the wider local Glasgow cluster. That theory conflicts with John's recorded father. A proposed father Robert Glasgow likewise conflicts with the marriage return. There is no current evidence that the father's name in the return is wrong. 

Samuel's stated brotherhood supports investigating the two men together, but does not identify their parents. A half-brother relationship is possible in principle, not something established by the census. 

The Glenleslie John and the Lisnagaver John should also not be treated as the same man: their reported 1851 ages imply substantially different generations. The suggested connection is father and son, not a same-person identification.
Possible connection to Nancy Glasgow of Plattsburgh
A probate citation for Nancy Glasgow of Plattsburgh, New York, dated 14 January 1892 and published in The Plattsburgh Sentinel on 26 February 1892, names:

: "James G. Glasgow, Ann [blank] and Lizzie [blank], the children of John Glasgow, late of Baladonly, county Antrime, Ireland". The Plattsburgh Sentinel, 26 February 1892, page 6, legal notice concerning Nancy Glasgow, deceased; citation dated 14 January 1892, returnable 9 May 1892. Contemporary newspaper clipping inspected in the research; newspaper issue locator (https://www.nyshistoricnewspapers.org/?a=d&d=plts18920226-01.1.6). Square-bracketed blanks in the quotation represent printed dashes where surnames were not supplied.

* Ann is a candidate for Ann/Annie Glasgow, later Bellingham. The 1875 marriage provides a father John, but does not identify Nancy or supply the missing sibling group. 
* Lizzie remains unidentified. No recovered record yet establishes her as a daughter of John and Margaret.

Baladonly remains unresolved; Baladony is retained as a search variant. It should not be silently replaced with Lisnagaver or another townland. The notice leaves the daughters' surnames blank and describes the cited Glasgow children's residences as unknown, so it does not establish that they lived in New York or remained in their fathers' Irish localities. 

The phrase "late of" is not treated as independent proof of John's death. A death in 1885 would precede the citation; a death in 1895 would not. The wording alone cannot choose between those dates.

The same notice names Mary Jane and Ann, children of Robert Glasgow, and a separate child group under Alexander Glasgow. It does not explicitly state that John, Robert and Alexander were Nancy's brothers. A sibling reconstruction, or an older-Alexander/cousin reconstruction, remains a hypothesis rather than a relationship stated in the notice. 

The citation's Robert remains unidentified. Existing candidates Robert of Glenleslie, Robert of Coltrim, Robert who died in Ballymoney district in 1868, Robert, son of Alexander of Lisnagaver, and Robert of the Doonbought/Illinois branch have not supplied the required documented Mary Jane and Ann daughter pair in the research reviewed. Neither the shared surname nor the 1834 Lisnagaver tithe Robert establishes a relationship to this John.
Unresolved Elizabeth witness lead
A modern transcription of marriages involving Cullybackey people records Elizabeth Glasgow as a witness, with John Taylor, to the marriage of Moore Paul of Carnlea and Lizzie Rock of Dunminning at Killymorris Presbyterian Church on 3 May 1878. The stated fathers are David Paul and John Rock respectively. Cullybackey and District Historical Society, Cullybackey People Married in Other Churches, 1870-1921 (https://cullybackeyhistory.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/CULLYBACKEY-PEOPLE-MARRIED-IN-OTHER-CHURCH-1870-1921.pdf), PDF page 4, Moore Paul and Lizzie Rock, 3 May 1878. Modern transcription table inspected; underlying marriage return not inspected for this lead.

General Register Office of Ireland, civil marriage return, entry 31: Alexander Glasgow and Mary Anne Martin, 6 April 1847, Clogh. Register image (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1847/09322/5375567.pdf); derivative FamilySearch index (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QGVD-P9CS), retained as a finding aid.

FamilySearch record (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:KDXL-YJ1), John Glasgow, reported birth during a voyage to New York, 25 August 1849; FamilySearch record (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:M6HW-FPR), John Glasgow in Illinois, 1870. Retained derivative identity checks, not evidence for this John's life.
FamilySearch record (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:M47Q-56D), John and Jane Glasgow, Ontario. Retained derivative identity check.

The concentration of Glasgow households is useful geographical context, not proof that their heads were brothers or father and son. In particular, no direct evidence currently makes Robert of Danbought John's father or brother. The separate question of Alexander's father must be tested against Alexander's own records rather than answered from neighbouring households.

Earlier naming arguments concerned a Matilda reportedly associated with John's family who died aged 23, a later Matilda said to have been named 22 years afterwards in Robert Glasgow's branch, and another Matilda born in 1901 in the family associated with Glasgow-943. Those notes described the two Roberts as 1840-1902 and 1880-1931; these date ranges and the claimed connections have not been established by the records examined for this update. The earlier notes also mentioned repeated use of Archibald. These are retained as unverified leads, not evidence of parentage or a reason to restore detached children.
Further research
# Obtain a photograph or independent reading of the GLASGO memorial. The target is the stone erected by James Garvin, naming John, Margaret Garvin and Elizabeth Ann. Check both the day and year of John's death. The Find a Grave cemetery entry (https://www.findagrave.com/cemetery/2561344/rasharkin-presbyterian-church-graveyard) was located, but the individual memorial photographs could not be fully inspected. No photograph of this particular stone was located in the searches completed by 15 September 2026.
