“United States Census, 1840,” database with images, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XHRF-1B6 : 8 September 2017), John Glascow, Guernsey, Ohio, United States; citing p. 355, NARA microfilm publication M704, roll 396; FHL microfilm 20,165.

They were living in Arthur's household in Londonderry Township in 1850. “United States Census, 1850,” database with images, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:MX3M-HP3 : 12 April 2016), John Glasgow in household of Arthur Glasgow, Londonderry, Guernsey, Ohio, United States; citing family 1538, NARA microfilm publication M432.

John's surviving letter reflects this outlook through repeated references to prayer, salvation and holding to Christ “for righteousness and life.” 

John died on 23 December 1851 and was buried in the Scotch Covenanter Cemetery in Guernsey County. “Find A Grave Index,” database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QVKX-FB2D : 13 December 2015), John Glasgow, died 1851; burial in Scotch Covenanter Cemetery, Guernsey County, Ohio; citing .

* Rose or “Rosanna”, born 4 March 1799; married Alexander McKeown in Ireland and settled in Harrison County, Ohio.
* Maria , born 22 September 1800.
* Jane, born 5 October 1802; married John Gray in Ireland and settled in Kentucky. John's 1847 letter was apparently addressed to her. 
* Adam, born 7 July 1804.
* Lavinia, born 21 June 1806.
* James, born 9 November 1808; died 20 April 1823.
* Margaret, born 17 October 1810; married John H. Walkinshaw.
* John, born 4 March 1813; died 17 August 1836 in Ohio.
* Arthur, born 1 July 1815; married Jane Neil.
Research Notes
* John Glasgow (bef.1813-) represents the John Glasco who headed house 2 at Inishrush in the 1831 census. His household contained four males and four females, all Presbyterian. “Tamlaght O'Crilly Census – 1831” (https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/Tamlaght/1831census_3.html), entry 1019, John Glasco, Innisrush house 2; transcription by Richard John Torrens (accessed 20 July 2026).

* The John Glasgow recorded in Richland Township, Belmont County, in 1830 was aged forty to forty-nine and was almost certainly a different man. John, born in 1767, would have been about sixty-three. The citation is retained to document the rejected identification, but should not be used as evidence that he was in Ohio by 1830. 1830 United States census, Richland Township, Ohio (https://archive.org/details/populationsc18300127unit/page/n484/mode/1up), original census image (accessed 20 July 2026).

sources.citation: Scotland's People, Church of Scotland Old Parish Registers, births and baptisms, Glasgow parish 644/1, reference 40/56, James Glasgow, male, 25 November 1645, parents indexed as “Rot. Glasgow/Jonet Cunnyngham”. Original register image inspected 31 August 2026; it names James Cunynghame and Johne Muir as godfathers. See also FamilySearch record VQHK-VMK (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQHK-VMK), a derivative index to the same event.

He has been proposed as identical with James Glasgow of Kilwaughter, County Antrim, first securely recorded there in 1669. No inspected record supplies migration, residence, occupation or family evidence joining them. They remain separate profiles; Jonet should not be attached to Glasgow-1081 on the present evidence.
Proposed husband
Robert Glasgow, baptised on 17 November 1618, remains a possible father of the 1645 child. The register gives the father only as Robert Glasgow and supplies no age, occupation, residence, birthplace or parentage, so it cannot identify him as the 1618 child. The relationship should remain uncertain.

An exact-surname Scotland-wide search of the indexed Church of Scotland marriage registers for Robert Glasgow from 1630 through 1650 returned no result. Scotland's People, Old Parish Register marriages search (https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/search-records/church-registers/church-banns-marriages/opr-marriages), exact surname Glasgow and forename beginning Robert, 1630–1650, searched 31 August 2026.

Research Notes
{| class="wikitable" style="background:#e8f5e9; border:1px solid #2e7d32;"
! Claim !! Assessment !! Reason
|-
| Born before 6 August 1765 || Strong || Joseph was almost certainly the man aged 45 or over in his named 1810 household.
|-
| Born about 1755 in County Londonderry || Probable estimate || Compatible with the census and Robert's sworn origin, but not directly recorded for Joseph.
|-
| Brothers Arthur and Robert || Proved || Independent family-letter and testamentary wording.
|-
| Father James of Moneymore || Plausible, unproved || Derived from Faris's statement about Robert.
|-
| Mother Mary Harkness || Unsupported || No independent source links her to Joseph or his proved brothers.
|-
| John of Peters Township as brother || Credible hypothesis || Local association and Joseph's will witnessing are suggestive but not kinship proof.
|-
| Betty as wife, probably Elizabeth || Strong but indirect || Joint 1806 letter; no marriage or maiden-name record located.
|-
| William as biological son || Unproved || Joseph said William was “raised by me,” not “my son.”
|-
| Brooke County inquest member, 1802 || Possible same-name candidate || The record gives no identifier connecting him to Joseph of Wythe County.
|-
| Death on 11 April 1831 || Unsupported as an exact day || This was the probate date; Joseph was last known alive on 2 April.
|}
Published family tradition
Morton states that “Arthur Glasgow was a descendant of Earl Glasgow, of Scotland,” gives information about Arthur's family through Alexander McNutt Glasgow, and says Glasgow Township was named for the family. These statements are retained as part of the published family tradition. They do not establish Joseph's parents or a genealogical connection to an Earl of Glasgow.
Priority records
# Pulaski County Register of Deaths, 1853–1870, for William Glasgow's reported 1865 death.
# Joseph's original will, 11 April 1831 probate order, appraisal, sale and final settlement in the Wythe County volumes.
# Wythe grantor and grantee deeds for Joseph, Betty or Elizabeth, and William.
# Brooke County court material surrounding the March 1802 inquest, to identify the same-name Joseph Glasgow and determine whether he appears in other local records.
# Cumberland Will Book C, p. 161, plus John Glasgow's original probate, guardianship and estate files.
# Faris, pp. 14–19, with the provenance of the 1806 letter and source for “James Glasgow of Moneymore.”
# Irish congregational, presbytery and estate material; surviving Moneymore Presbyterian baptism registers begin too late for this family.
Reassessment of the unidentified brother
Faris's catalogue summary says Robert migrated with three brothers and one sister. David Faris, The Glasgow Family of Adams County, Ohio (1990), WorldCat catalogue summary (https://search.worldcat.org/title/22731567).

----
 
Diamond Wedding; Mr & Mrs James Glasgow, of Short Street, Papakura, celebrated their Diamond Wedding on Saturday, having been married 60 years ago in the Presbyterian Church, Orritor, County Tyrone, Ireland. 
They came out a few weeks after to New Zealand, landing in Auckland, in the sailing ship 'British Empire' which carried 275 passengers. They first joined Mr Glasgow's brother at Epsom, afterwards going to Onehunga. Five years after Mr Glasgow took up a milk service, retailing milk in Onehunga & district for 40 years. For 45years Mr & Mrs Glasgow were members of the Onehunga Presbyterian Church. Mr Glasgow was a member of the Mangere Road Board and school committee for a number of years. For a time he farmed a property in Wairoa Road, Papakura, leaving there five years ago for Short Street, his present address. There are 10 Children, most of whom were able to attend the celebrations. Mr Glasgow is 91 years of age, and is still able to milk his cow night and morning. Mrs Glasgow is well and still able to enjoy life.

Kildress Old Churchyard, Cookstown, Tyrone

Margaret Rutherford
Some ancestry.com trees give her maiden name as "Rutherford". In light of the above evidence, this is clearly a a mistake, conflating this couple with James Glasgow (abt.1700-abt.1759) and Margaret Rutherford (1700-). 

That couple are described in a letter T1959/3 held by PRONI, see here for transcription (https://www.genealogy.com/forum/surnames/topics/rutherford/5445/). It can be seen that the description of the children of James Glasgow and Margaret Rutherford does not match this profile, but does match the 18th century couple. 

The tree has a lot more information about the earlier James Glasgow and Margaret Rutherford.
Death informant
The death informant's identity is unclear. There is Elizabeth Jane Glasgow (abt.1863-1935) -- the wife of her grandson -- however they did not marry until about a month after the death was informed.

The death of Margaret Glasgow was registered on 21 March 1892 in Cookstown, aged 81. GRONI civil death index (https://geni.nidirect.gov.uk/search/death), Margaret Glasgow, 21 March 1892, aged 81, Cookstown registration district, D/1892/99/1009/14/123.

sources.citation: Scotland, Census, 1881. George Kerr household, Bothwell, Lanarkshire. Margaret Kerr, wife, age 27, birthplace Lanarkshire. FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:KM2J-BDX).
Scotland, Census, 1891. George Kerr household, Bothwell, Lanarkshire. Maggie Kerr, wife, age 37, birthplace Lanarkshire. FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:KS63-5F5).

Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564–1950. George Kerr, born 29 Nov 1851, Blackford, Perthshire, Scotland. Parents George Kerr and Jane Scobie. FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:X1F6-SZ3).

In 1891 they were again in Bothwell, where Margaret was recorded as Maggie Kerr, wife, age 37, born in Lanarkshire. 
Children
Children identified from census and vital records include:

* George Kerr, born about 1877 in Lanarkshire. 
* Margaret Kerr, born 28 December 1880 in Tradeston, Lanarkshire. Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564–1950. Entry for Margaret Kerr, born 28 Dec 1880, Tradeston, Lanarkshire. FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XTXD-F8S).

* Jane "Jean" (Kerr) Gilmour, born 31 May 1884 in Bothwell, Lanarkshire, and died 10 December 1945 in Dearborn, Wayne County, Michigan. Her Scottish statutory birth index records her as Jane Kerr and gives her mother's maiden surname as McDougall; her Michigan death certificate records her as Jean Gilmour and names George Kerr and Margaret McDougall as her parents. National Records of Scotland, statutory register of births, Jane Kerr, 1884, Bothwell, mother's maiden surname McDougall, 625/1/252; Scotland's People index (https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/search-records/statutory-records/stat_births).

Michigan, Death Certificates, 1921–1952. Jean Gilmour, died 10 Dec 1945, Dearborn, Wayne, Michigan; parents George Kerr and Margaret McDougall. FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:KFQH-RHR).

Later Life and Death
Margaret was living with George Kerr and their children in Bothwell in 1891. Her death record has not yet been confirmed. A death in 1931 appears in some online trees, but no corresponding Scottish death registration has yet been attached to this profile. George Kerr died in 1918.
Research NotesParentage
Margaret's parentage is not confirmed. Two possible sets of parents appear in Scottish parish records:

* William McDougall and Elizabeth Clark had a daughter Margaret McDougall baptized 31 March 1851 in Glasgow, Lanarkshire. Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564–1950. Margaret McDougall, baptized 31 Mar 1851, Glasgow, Lanarkshire. Parents William McDougall and Elizabeth Clark. FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQ6Q-QH2).

Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564–1950. Margaret McDougall, born or baptized 25 May 1850, Gorbals, Glasgow, Lanarkshire. Parents William McDougall and Mary McMillan. FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQ64-58N).

Church of Scotland: Old Parish Registers - Banns and Marriages. Mary McMillan and William McDougall, marriage on or after 2 Mar 1850, Paisley Middle, Renfrewshire, Scotland. National Records of Scotland, parish 573/2, ref. 40/271, frame 827; cited in Mary (McMillan) McDougall profile, WikiTree.

* John McDougall, born or baptized 10 April 1852 in Gorbals, Glasgow, Lanarkshire. Church of Scotland: Old Parish Registers - Births and Baptisms. John McDougall, born or baptized 10 Apr 1852, Gorbals, Lanarkshire. Parents William McDougall and Mary McMillan. National Records of Scotland, parish 644/2, ref. 50/289, frame 1035; cited in Mary (McMillan) McDougall profile, WikiTree.

Church of Scotland: Old Parish Registers - Births and Baptisms. Ann McDougall, born or baptized 16 Apr 1854, Gorbals, Lanarkshire. Parents William McDougall and Mary McMillan. National Records of Scotland, parish 644/2, ref. 50/334, frame 1058; cited in Mary (McMillan) McDougall profile, WikiTree.
WikiTree, Mary (McMillan) McDougall profile, McMillan-4259, biography and sources listing children of William McDougall and Mary McMillan. WikiTree (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/McMillan-4259).

* Agnes Stewart McDougall, born 28 September 1860 in Glasgow, Lanarkshire. 
* Robert McDougall, born 24 February 1861 in Anderston, Glasgow, Lanarkshire. 
* William McDougall, born 29 September 1862 in Bridgeton, Glasgow, Lanarkshire. 
* Jane McDougall, born about 1868 in Bridgeton, Glasgow, Lanarkshire. 

Mary McMillan's parents were John McMillan and Margaret Urquhart. Mary McDougall or McDougal, maiden surname McMillan, died 21 November 1892 in Cathcart, Lanarkshire; her death registration reportedly gives her mother's maiden surname as Urquhart. Statutory Register of Deaths. Mary McDougal, death registered 1892, Cathcart, Lanarkshire, age 64, mother's maiden surname Urquhart. National Records of Scotland, ref. 560/265; cited in Mary (McMillan) McDougall profile, WikiTree.

* The 1850 Gorbals baptism is close to Margaret's census-implied birth year of about 1853. A two- or three-year discrepancy is plausible in census ages.
* The first known daughter of George Kerr and Margaret McDougall was named Margaret. If Margaret McDougall was the daughter of Mary McMillan, this is consistent with possible naming for the maternal line, since Mary McMillan's mother was Margaret Urquhart. 
* The McDougall-McMillan family can be followed more clearly through indexed parish and census material than the McDougall-Clark family.

Points against or still unresolved:

* Margaret Kerr's census ages imply birth about 1853, not 1850. 
* The second son in a strict Scottish naming pattern might be expected to carry the name of the mother's father, William or possibly John, but the Kerrs' known second son was Hugh. Naming patterns are suggestive only and not proof.
Candidate 2: William McDougall and Elizabeth Clark
The second candidate is Margaret McDougall, baptized 31 March 1851 in Glasgow, daughter of William McDougall and Elizabeth Clark. This baptism is slightly closer to Margaret Kerr's census-implied birth year than the 1850 Gorbals baptism.

A possible additional child of this couple was Thomas Paterson McDougall, reportedly born 4 December 1848 in Glasgow to William McDougall and Elizabeth Clark. Ancestry.com, indexed family tree/search result for Thomas Paterson MacDougall, born 4 Dec 1848, Glasgow, Lanarkshire, parents William McDougall and Elizabeth Clark. This is a secondary clue only and should be confirmed in original records.

Scottish Asylum Patients - General Register of Lunatics index MC7. Thomas McDougall, also known as Thomas Paterson McDougall, death 23 Jan 1927, Gartloch; Glasgow Royal Asylum 1902-1904. Old Scottish. Old Scottish (https://www.oldscottish.com/asylum-patients-mcdougall-mcgill.html).

* The family appears to have been in Glasgow around the same period as Margaret's birth.

Points against or still unresolved:

* No census entry has yet been found that clearly follows the William McDougall and Elizabeth Clark family forward with a daughter Margaret.
* No record has yet been found linking this Margaret McDougall to Bothwell, to George Kerr, or to the later Kerr children.
* If Margaret followed the common Scottish naming pattern, her first daughter might be expected to be named Elizabeth after Elizabeth Clark. Instead, the first known daughter was Margaret. This does not eliminate the candidate but weakens it.
* The family is less well documented in accessible sources than the McDougall-McMillan family.
Daughter Jane or Jean Kerr
Margaret's daughter was registered at birth as Jane Kerr. After marrying William Gilmour at Bothwell in 1902, she used Jean Gilmour. National Records of Scotland, statutory register of marriages, William Gilmour and Jeanie Kerr, 1902, Bothwell, 625/1/100; Scotland's People index (https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/search-records/statutory-records/stat_marriages).

Research NotesIdentity
Named as a lawful daughter in Andrew's 1598 testament. No later record has been securely connected to her; the same-name Glasgow women of the period have no Corsoun, Stevenson, sibling or succession bridge to this household, so none is attached here.

A separate Marion Glasgow is identified as Ninian Glasgow's sister in his 1613 testament and as the mother of James Fultoun in a 1610 Glasgow baptism. Neither record names Andrew, Elizat or Corsoun. This is a same-name identity comparison, not a proved match; keep the profiles separate pending a connecting record. The published Rasharkin baptism transcription contains no baptism entries for 1840 or 1841. Robert's missing baptism is therefore more likely to reflect incomplete record coverage or transcription than evidence that he belonged to another family. 
1851 Census
In the surviving 1851 census, Mary was living at Lisnagaver with her husband Alexander and their children Robert, James and Ann.

Alexander was aged 40 and Mary was also aged 40. Both were born in County Antrim, and the detailed census transcription records 1836 as their first-marriage year. National Archives of Ireland, Census of Ireland, 1851, Lisnagaver, Rasharkin, County Antrim, household 35, Alexander Glasgow household; household images (http://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/pages/1851/Antrim/Kilconway/Rasharkin/Lisnagaver/35/) (accessed 16 July 2026).

Mary's age therefore supports a birth about 1810 or 1811. Earlier estimates placing her birth around 1817 or 1818 are inconsistent with this contemporary census evidence.
Residences
The surviving records place Alexander and Mary within a small area of Rasharkin parish over a period of years:

Lisnagaver, Gortereagh and Moneyleck are separate adjoining townlands in Rasharkin civil parish, barony of Kilconway, County Antrim. Lisnagaver Townland, County Antrim (https://www.townlands.ie/antrim/kilconway/rasharkin/killoquin/lisnagaver/), administrative divisions and adjoining-townland map (accessed 2026).

Enumeration order does not prove that the houses stood immediately beside one another. It does establish that John, Samuel, Alexander and Thomas belonged to the same small Lisnagaver residential cluster.

The census explicitly identifies John and Samuel as brothers. It does not identify Alexander or Thomas as their brothers.

Later valuation evidence provides a separate land-based connection. John, Alexander and Thomas occupied consecutive principal holdings at Lisnagaver under the same immediate lessor, Robert Harvey.

The consecutive lot numbers strongly suggest that the holdings were physically close. The valuation map should still be consulted before stating that every plot directly adjoined or shared a boundary.

The combined census, church and land evidence supports a close Glasgow family-and-neighbour network at Lisnagaver while leaving the precise relationships unresolved.
Alexander and Thomas Glasgow
There is substantial circumstantial evidence that Thomas Glasgow was a close relative, and possibly a brother, of Mary's husband Alexander Glasgow.

Alexander and Thomas were:

* born in County Antrim about five years apart;
* farmers;
* able to read and write;
* associated with the same Presbyterian congregation;
* recorded within the same Lisnagaver–Gortereagh–Moneyleck micro-area;
* heads of closely grouped Lisnagaver households in 1851;
* and later occupiers of consecutive valuation lots under the same lessor.

The contemporary Rasharkin Presbyterian baptism register provides a particularly strong FAN connection.

Alexander and Mary or Molly used the congregation while associated with Gortereagh and Lisnagaver. Thomas and Mary Ann McCracken used the same congregation while associated with Moneyleck and Lisnagaver. 

Most notably:

* Alexander and Mary's son James was born at Lisnagaver on 9 October 1843;
* Thomas and Mary Ann's daughter Eliza was born there on 17 October 1843.

The children were born only eight days apart in the same small townland and appear in the same Presbyterian register. 

This is substantial FAN evidence for a close relationship.

No surviving record presently calls Alexander and Thomas brothers. Thomas should therefore be treated as Alexander's probable close relative and possible brother, not as a proved sibling.
Thomas and Daniel Glasgow
A reported will record for Daniel Glasgow of Kilrea identifies Thomas Glasgow as his "late brother" and Daniel Neely Glasgow as a nephew. Will of Daniel Glasgow of Kilrea, proved 1871, reported in accumulated family research as identifying Thomas Glasgow as his "late brother". The original probate copy and complete archival citation are still required.

Possible John McCaughen Connection
A John McCaughen of Mount Pleasant Township, Washington County, Pennsylvania, made a will dated 22 February 1815 in which he referred to:

:my onley daughter which I left in Ireland when I came to America.

The daughter was named Mary McCaughen, and John reportedly left half of his estate to her. sources.citation: In 1841, Robert Glasgow, age 65, of independent means, born in Scotland, was living at Holly Walk, Leamington Priors, with Ann Glasgow age 40, Mary Glasgow age 19, Ann Robertson age 18, Jane Robertson age 20, Charlotte Robertson age 10 and Wilhelmina Robertson age 1, one male servant and four female servants. All the children were listed as being born in Scotland. Wilhelmina was the daughter of Robert Glasgow's eldest son, also Robert. The baptism of Charlotte in Edinburgh on 20/07/1828 gives her birth as Rome, 22/11/1827. Anne Glasgow the elder has not been traced and had presumably died by 1841. Anne Glasgow or Robertson the younger was born in Edinburgh 05/10/1805 and baptised 26/03/1805 in Ayton, Berwickshire. It is this younger Anne, the daughter, not the wife of Robert, who appears in the 1841 census.

sources.citation:
Francis J. Grant, ed.,
The Commissariot Record of Glasgow: Register of Testaments, 1547–1800 (https://archive.org/details/scottishrecordso07scotuoft/page/196/mode/2up?q=Glasgow%2C)
(Edinburgh: Scottish Record Society, 1901), p. 196: “Mary, spouse to James
Montgomerie, sailor in Saltcoats, par. of Ardrossan,” 24 October 1677.

Research Notes
Birth and parentage
Mary's existing birth year of about 1613 is an estimate for which no supporting
record has yet been identified. Saltcoats is relevant because the 1677 index
describes her husband there, but it does not expressly state that Mary was born
there. The populated date and location should be retained as uncertain while
better evidence is sought.

Edward Glasgow and Catherine Hamilton are
attached as Mary's parents. The 1677 index does not name either parent, and no
inspected source presently proves those relationships. The links should remain
uncertain unless a record establishes specific replacement parents; they
should not simply be removed and left blank.
Distinct 1637 household
The testament dative and inventory of John Glasgow, sailor in Saltcoats, is a
different record. It names Isobell Gray as John's widow and Katherine and
Agnes Glasgow as his lawful children. It does not name Mary or Marie and gives
no basis for attaching this profile to that household. National Records of
Scotland, Glasgow Commissary Court, testament dative and inventory of John
Glasgow, sailor in Saltcoats, NRS CC9/7/27, register pp. 478–480; death in
December 1636 and court proceedings in April 1637; original register re-read
September 2026; locate by reference through the
Scotland's People wills search (https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/search-records/legal-records/wills).

sources.citation: Registry of Deeds, Ireland, memorial of marriage settlement, John McGavock and Mary Glasgow, dated 10 February 1843, affidavit 14 February, registered 18 February 1843; FamilySearch, opening image 499 (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJW-FQ3Q) and continuation image 500 (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJW-F3BZ), original images inspected 21 September 2026. The complete book and memorial reference remains to be verified.

Probable census identification
The 1851 census for house 1, Cross Street, Larne, records John McGavock, 50, widower, merchant and innkeeper, with marriage years 1824, 1827 and 1843. Its deceased-household table lists Mary McGavock, wife, aged 37, who died of jaundice in autumn 1843. National Archives of Ireland, 1851 census, County Antrim, Larne, Cross Street, house 1, John McGavock household; household and marriage table, image 007246521_00320 (https://nationalarchives.ie/collections/search-the-census/view-pdf/?doc=007246521_00320&c19=true) and absent and deceased household members, image 007246521_00321 (https://nationalarchives.ie/collections/search-the-census/view-pdf/?doc=007246521_00321&c19=true), original return inspected 21 September 2026.

Research Notes
Uncertain father
Hugh Glasgow, the deceased testator, is attached as Mary's uncertain father. A father's provision for a daughter's marriage is a coherent working explanation for the estate payment, but no father-daughter wording appears in the inspected deed. He could have been another relative or benefactor. His own proposed attachment to James Glasgow is a separate low-confidence hypothesis, not evidence establishing Mary's parentage. 
Possible duplicate: Mary Glasgow-3989
Mary Glasgow, daughter of William Glasgow, remains a possible identity for the bride. The Larne monument names her father and records her death on 18 October 1844 aged 37, conflicting with the probable census wife's death in autumn 1843 aged 37. "Armorial Sculptured Stones of the County Antrim," Ulster Journal of Archaeology, second series, volume 6 (1900), p. 47 (https://archive.org/details/ulsterjournalofa06ulstiala/page/47/mode/1up), William Glasgow family monument transcription.

records.association: Witness to sasine for Janet Cunningham and Alexander Earl of Glencairn
records.note: The official catalogue names Michael Glasgow among the witnesses but supplies no occupation, patronymic or residence; identity with the 1559-60 Stevenston tenant is probable rather than explicit.
records.location_basis: The sasine concerned the lands and barony of Stevenston; the catalogue does not identify Michael's dwelling.
records.source_title: NRS GD39/1/59: sasine for Janet Cunningham and Alexander Earl of Glencairn, witnessed by Michael Glasgow
records.source_status: Official National Records of Scotland catalogue entry inspected; no manuscript image is available online.

sources.citation: National Records of Scotland, Charter Chest of the Earls of Glencairn, GD39/1/59 (https://catalogue.nrscotland.gov.uk/nrsonlinecatalogue/details.aspx?reference=GD39%2F1%2F59), instrument of sasine in favour of Janet Cunningham and Alexander, Earl of Glencairn, 28 January 1549. The official catalogue entry was inspected; no manuscript image is available online.

Margaret H. B. Sanderson, The People of Sixteenth Century Ayrshire, Ayrshire Collections, vol. 14, no. 8 (Ayrshire Archaeological and Natural History Society, 1987), appendix "The Cunninghame Teind Lists of 1559–60," p. 331 (https://aanhs.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/people-of-ayrshire.pdf#page=36), Brakpleuch Over and Nether entry. Sanderson identifies the underlying record as Scottish Record Office, Register of Acts and Decreets, vol. 22, fols. 102v–167v.

In Glasgow, David Mathy and Robert Glasgow were fellow burgesses witnessing the same sasines in 1554. Robert Renwick, ed., Abstracts of Protocols of the Town Clerks of Glasgow, vol. 1, protocols 183–184, 10 May 1554, printed p. 63 (https://archive.org/details/abstractsprotoc07robegoog/page/n90/mode/2up).

Inquisitionum ad Capellam Domini Regis Retornatarum ... Abbreviatio, vol. 2, tutory retours 100–101, 20 January 1607, digitised volume (https://books.google.com/books?id=PiVDAAAAcAAJ); underlying register, National Records of Scotland, C22/3 (https://catalogue.nrscotland.gov.uk/nrsonlinecatalogue/browsetreeview.aspx?reference=C22).

Sanderson warns that one tenant could hold more than one property. The Brakpleuch and Dubbs entries may therefore describe one Michael Glasgow or two contemporaries.

No reviewed source identifies Michael's parents, spouse, children, precise birthplace, or death. James Glasgow, Matthew Glasgow, and the other Glasgow surname bearers in the 1559 Stevenston rental form a local record cluster, but co-tenancy and locality do not prove kinship. No parent has therefore been attached.

This Michael is not Michael Glasgow, whose estimated birth was more than a century later.
Possible family placement
Michael is best placed as a probable brother or cousin, rather than a son, of James Glasgow elder of Corsankell. Michael was already an adult legal witness in the Glencairn estate network on 28 January 1549, National Records of Scotland, Charter Chest of the Earls of Glencairn, GD39/1/59 (https://catalogue.nrscotland.gov.uk/nrsonlinecatalogue/details.aspx?reference=GD39%2F1%2F59), 28 January 1549.

Margaret H. B. Sanderson, The People of Sixteenth Century Ayrshire, appendix “The Cunninghame Teind Lists of 1559-60,” p. 331 (https://aanhs.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/people-of-ayrshire.pdf#page=36).

sources.citation:
The John Glasgow, farmer named as father in the 1846 marriage of John Glasgow of Lisnagaver is a candidate for Nancy's father only if the proposed siblings shared that parent. Full and half-sibling relationships remain unresolved. The proposed father represented by John Glasgow is not thereby identified with the 1796 Desertoghill flax-premium recipient. Nancy was earlier attached to Alexander Glasgow and Rosanna Unknown; that parentage remains unproved, but omission of Thomas's or Daniel's family from the citation does not disprove it. Neither their absence nor the probable sibling network establishes a replacement father. No mother has been identified. 
Plattsburgh and Will
On 15 January 1889 Nancy made her Last Will and Testament at Plattsburgh. She described herself as unmarried and about 68 years old, suggesting a birth about 1820–1821. Clinton County, New York, Surrogate's Court, Records of wills, 1807–1902, vol. Q, pp. 255–259, Nancy Glasgow of Plattsburgh; will dated 15 January 1889, admitted to probate 9 May 1892. FamilySearch catalogue, Records of wills, 1807–1902 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/catalog/319520).

The Plattsburgh Sentinel (Plattsburgh, New York), 26 February 1892, p. 6, "Legal Notices", probate citation in the estate of Nancy Glasgow, dated 14 January 1892; digital newspaper page (https://www.nyshistoricnewspapers.org/?a=d&d=plts18920226-01.1.6).

Nathaniel continued in the ministry there until his death in April 1743. Contemporary records of the General Synod of Ulster report his death during that month. Records of the General Synod of Ulster, vol. 2, pp. 284, 314 and 339. https://archive.org/details/recordsofgeneral02pres
Irish probate index transcription supplied July 2026, entry for Nathaniel Glasgow, Diocese of Clogher, 1746, residence Cavan, Donaghcavey.

These entries establish that Nathaniel left:

* an unnamed widow; and
* at least two unnamed children.

The plural wording “children” supports a minimum of two children, but the surviving Synod minutes do not give their names, ages, sexes or places of residence.

The 1746 probate record may be particularly important. A surviving copy, abstract, administration bond or related diocesan record could identify:

* Nathaniel’s widow;
* his children;
* executors or administrators;
* guardians acting for minor children;
* relatives or sureties; or
* property belonging to the estate.

No spouse or child should be created or attached without a record naming that person.
Family and Relationship Research
No inspected record conclusively identifies Nathaniel’s parents or siblings.

A descent from Thomas Glasgow of Ballindrait, Shannon or Lifford remains chronologically and geographically possible, but no record examined to date names Nathaniel as Thomas’s son.

There is likewise no proven relationship between Nathaniel and:

* Archibald Glasgow M.A. (1614–bef.1677);
* Jacob or James Glasgow M.A. (1700–);
* Thomas Glasgow of Ballindrait, Shannon or Lifford; or
* any other identified Glasgow family in seventeenth-century Donegal.

The proposed descent:

Archibald Glasgow
|

Thomas Glasgow of Ballindrait, Shannon or Lifford
|

|

|
at least two unnamed children

is a research hypothesis only. Each question mark represents an unproved relationship.

Nathaniel’s description as Scoto-Hibernus supports an association with both Scotland and Ireland. It does not prove:

* birth in Glasgow;
* descent from the Glasgow family of that city;
* descent from Archibald Glasgow of Ramelton;
* descent from Thomas Glasgow of Lifford; or
* any specific Scottish birthplace.

Geography, chronology, education and surname similarity are useful research leads but are insufficient to attach parents or siblings.
Research Notes
A publication issued in 1725 under the name “Nathaniel Glasgow” should not be attributed to this Nathaniel. The catalogue identifies the author as “Nathaniel Glasgow (pseud.)”, showing that the name was a pen name. sources.citation:
James R. Anderson, ed.,
Burgesses & Guild Brethren of Glasgow, 1573–1750 (1925),
p.
24 (https://archive.org/details/scottishrecordso43scotuoft/page/24/mode/2up), 23 October 1596.

George Crawfurd, A Sketch of the Rise and Progress
of the Trades' House of Glasgow (1858), pp. 49, 56–57.

National Records of Scotland, Glasgow Commissary Court,
CC9/7/5, images 82–83, testament of Jonet Meik.

National Records of Scotland,
Glasgow Commissary Court, CC9/7/9, images 142–145, testament testamentar and
inventory of Ninian Glasgow, made 10 January 1613 and confirmed 8 May 1613.
Working transcription of the original images supplied 6 September 2026.

Identity, trade and civic status
Niniane Glasgw was a fyscher and burges of Glasgw — a fisher and burgess of Glasgow. 

The occupation was formerly misread as flescher, meaning butcher. That reading should be withdrawn. The manuscript word is fyscher. An independent burgess list also places Niniane Glasgow under the heading Marinellis and Fischeris, meaning mariners and fishers. George Crawfurd, A Sketch of the Rise and Progress of the Trades' House of Glasgow: Its Constitution, Funds, and Bye-laws (Glasgow: Bell & Bain, 1858), pp. 49 and 56–57, reproducing the burgess roll associated with the reorganisation of 14 February 1605; Niniane Glasgow appears under “Marinellis and Fischeris”.

* By 1607 — he was the husband of Jonet Meik and the father of Robert Glasgow. Jonet's testament was indexed or recorded on 27 August 1607. National Records of Scotland, Glasgow Commissary Court, CC9/7/5, Images 82–83, testament testamentar and inventory of Jonet Meik, spouse to Niniane Glasgw.

Francis J. Grant, ed., The Commissariot Record of Glasgow: Register of Testaments, 1547–1800, Scottish Record Society, old series vol. 7 (Edinburgh, 1901), entries under Glasgow, Ninian, and Meik, Jonet.

* January 1613 — he died during that month; the exact day is not stated. 
* 8 May 1613 — his testament was indexed or recorded under that date. 

The 8 May date is not his date of death.
Earlier known wife: Jonet Meik
The earlier wife was Jonet Meik. Her surname is written Meik in the manuscript and in the printed testament index. The database form Melk is a later transcription or OCR error and should not be used as her surname. 

Jonet's testament describes her as:

:Jonet meik spous to Niniane glasgw burges of glasgw

The executor or giving-up clause names:

:Niniane glasgw hir spous and Robert glasgw hir sone

A later legacy or residue clause again calls Robert:

:Robert glasgw hir sone

Robert is therefore directly identified as Jonet's son in two places. Niniane's 1613 testament independently calls Robert his son. This establishes Robert as the son of both Niniane Glasgow and Jonet Meik, rather than merely a probable relative.

Jonet also left a legacy to:

:Johne meik hir brother

A Marion Glasgow is named as a legatee in Jonet's testament, apparently receiving an article of clothing, but the clerk does not call Marion her daughter. Other Glasgow recipients may occur in the legacy list, but their forenames or relationships are not sufficiently clear to establish additional children.

Jonet was dead before her testament was recorded on 27 August 1607. Her death clause appears to refer to February, but the precise year numeral is not treated as settled here.
Later wife: Jonet Hutchesoun
Niniane had remarried by 10 January 1613. His later wife was another woman named Jonet. Her surname appears twice in his testament: once in the nomination of executors and again in the confirmation clause.

The best palaeographic reading is Hutchesoun, possibly Huchesoun. The middle of the word contains a crossed t followed by a ch-type group. The earlier working reading Herbessoun was closer than Smythesoun, but does not fit the repeated letter pattern as well. Smythesoun should be withdrawn.

In a cautious semi-diplomatic transcription the name should be shown as:

:Jonet ⟦Hutchesoun?⟧

Jonet Hutchesoun and Robert Glasgow were appointed executors and intromitters with Niniane's movable estate. 

No surviving clause states that Jonet Hutchesoun was the mother of Robert or William. Robert's mother is independently proved to have been Jonet Meik. William's mother is not established by either testament.

The 1605 fisher list also contains a man printed as Niniane Hutchisonne immediately beside Niniane Glasgow. This makes Hutchesoun a locally and occupationally plausible surname, but it does not prove that the listed man was related to Niniane's later wife.

His assumed brother, John Glasgow (abt.1540-1576) married a Margaret (Hutcheson) Glasgow (1550-), and his presumed Uncle William Glasgow (abt.1525-bef.1586), married Margaret (Herbison) Glasgow (abt.1540-). Margaret’s father, Sir William Herbesoun, was a Roman priest with close ties to the Hutcheson family through his sister Helen Herbertson, who married Thomas Hutcheson of Lambhill. This connection made Margaret Herbison likely a cousin of George Hutcheson and Thomas Hutcheson Jr..
Evidence that the records concern the same Niniane Glasgow
The 1607 and 1613 testamentary records should be treated as referring to the same man.

The identification rests on a combined evidence set:

# Both records name Niniane Glasgow in Glasgow.
# The 1607 record calls him a burgess of Glasgow.
# The 1605 roll lists a Niniane Glasgow among Glasgow's mariners and fishers.
# The 1613 record calls him a fisher and burgess of Glasgow.
# The 1607 testament calls Robert Glasgow the son of Jonet Meik.
# The 1613 testament calls Robert Glasgow the son of Niniane Glasgow.
# The records fall only six years apart and form a coherent sequence: Jonet Meik died, Niniane remarried, and Niniane later made his own testament.

The shared son Robert is the strongest point. The identification does not depend only on the rarity of the surname, although the rarity of the name combination provides further support. A second contemporary Ninian Glasgow, burgess or fisher of Glasgow, with a son Robert would be required to displace this identification.
Children and other stated family
The records establish the following relationships:

* Robert Glasgw — son of Niniane Glasgow and Jonet Meik.
** Jonet's 1607 testament calls him hir sone.
** Niniane's 1613 testament calls him his sone.
** He appears in the administration of both estates.
* William Glasgw — son of Niniane Glasgow.
** He received a separate provision in Niniane's 1613 testament.
** His mother is not identified in the surviving wording.
* Johne Glasgw — brother of Niniane Glasgow.
** Niniane left him ane new gowne.
* Johne Meik — brother of Jonet Meik.
** Jonet left him a legacy in her testament.
* Marion Glasgow — named as a legatee by Jonet Meik.
** No relationship is stated, so she should not presently be attached as a daughter solely from this entry.

Neither testament names Niniane's father or mother. No birthplace is stated.
Inventory and estate
Niniane's inventory concerns his household goods, furnishings, vessels, money and debts.

Substantially readable items include:

* twa kistis and ane pres — two chests and a press or cupboard;
* ane mekill and littill buird — a large and a small board or table;
* all vther tymmer wark — the remaining wooden furniture;
* pewter vessels, described by weight;
* brewing vessels and other household vessels;
* the abuilzement of his bodie — his clothing or personal apparel.

The clerk lists debts owed to Niniane, debts payable from his estate, the free gear remaining after deduction, and division of the net movable estate. The exact totals and several debtor or creditor names remain too compressed or faded to quote safely from the present images.

The presence of brewing vessels is ordinary household evidence and does not make Niniane a brewer. His stated occupation remains fisher.
Testamentary provisions
Niniane's personal testament begins at Glasgow on 10 January 1613. He was described as sick in body but of sound or perfect memory. He committed his soul to God and directed that his body be buried, although the precise burial wording is indistinct.

He appointed:

* his later wife, Jonet Hutchesoun; and
* his son, Robert Glasgw

as his executors and intromitters.

Among the readable legacies:

* Johne Glasgw his brother was to receive ane new gowne;
* William Glasgw his sone received a separate provision, the exact object or amount being partly indistinct;
* further directions concern debts, expenses, legacies and the administration of the remaining estate.
Confirmation and archival extent
Niniane's testament begins partway down Image 142, continues through Images 143 and 144, and concludes in the upper portion of Image 145. The large new testament heading in the lower portion of Image 145 belongs to another deceased person.

The lower part of Image 144 and upper part of Image 145 contain the formal Commissary Court confirmation. Jonet Hutchesoun and Robert Glasgow are again named in the executor wording. A cautioner or surety was provided, though the name and parts of the formula remain difficult to read.
Key semi-diplomatic extracts
Jonet Meik's testament, 1607

:Jonet meik spous to Niniane glasgw burges of glasgw
:...
:be Niniane glasgw hir spous and Robert glasgw hir sone
:...
:to Johne meik hir brother
:...
:Robert glasgw hir sone

Niniane Glasgow's testament, 1613

:The testament testamentar and Inventar
:of the guidis geir debitis and sowmes of money q[uhi]lkis
:pertening to vmq[uhi]le Niniane glasgw fyscher burges
:of glasgw ...

:At glasgw the tent day of Januar 1613 zeiris
:...
:constitutis Jonet ⟦Hutchesoun?⟧ his spous & Robert
:glasgw his sone his executouris & intromettouris
:...
:Item to Johne glasgw his brother ane new gowne
:...
:Item to William glasgw his sone ⟦legacy partly indistinct⟧
Modern English rendering
Ninian Glasgow was a fisher and burgess of Glasgow. A burgess roll from 1605 places him among the city's mariners and fishers.

His earlier known wife was Janet Meik. Her testament identifies Ninian as her husband and Robert Glasgow as her son. It again describes Robert as her son in the legacy or residue section. Ninian's own testament later describes Robert as his son, directly establishing Robert as the child of both spouses.

Janet Meik died before her testament was recorded in August 1607. Ninian subsequently remarried. By January 1613 his wife was another Janet, whose surname is best read as Hutchesoun. She and Robert were appointed to administer Ninian's estate.

Ninian made his will at Glasgow on 10 January 1613 and died during that month. He left a new gown to his brother John Glasgow and made a separate provision for his son William. His testament was recorded or confirmed on 8 May 1613.
Research Notes
Current evidence assessment
The manuscript calls Ninian a fyscher, not a flesher or butcher. The word
sister does not establish whether Marion was his full or half-sister, so
their common father should not be treated as certain solely from this clause.

A William Glasgow occurs in debt material and near the damaged foot of the
will's opening, but the previously asserted words his sone cannot be read
securely. William Glasgow, mealmaker in Leith, remains only a
possible son and possible identity match. The debtor and damaged will
occurrence may not be the same man. William's son Archibald was apprenticed at Edinburgh in 1639, Francis J. Grant, ed., Register of Apprentices of the City of Edinburgh, 1583–1666 (1906), p. 71 (https://archive.org/details/scottishrecordso28scotuoft/page/71/mode/2up), 23 October 1639.

Henry Paton, ed., The Register of Marriages for the Parish of Edinburgh, 1595–1700, printed p. 267 (https://www.tradeshouselibrary.org/uploads/4/7/7/2/47723681/register_of_marriages_for_the_parish_of_edinburgh_1595-1700_~_1898.pdf#page=277).

The printed testament index remains useful as a finding aid. Francis J.
Grant, ed., The Commissariot Record of Glasgow: Register of Testaments,
1547–1800 (Edinburgh, 1901), entries for Ninian Glasgow and Jonet Meik.

Public Record Office of Northern Ireland, Valuation Revision Book for Killoquin Lower electoral division, Rasharkin parish, PRONI VAL/12/B/4/16A, folios 52–53, Lisnagaver lots 24–26; see also Griffith's Valuation transcript for Rasharkin (https://www.failteromhat.com/griffiths/antrim/rasharkin.htm),
 accessed 5 August 2026.

Isaac Slater, Slater's National Commercial Directory of Ireland (https://www.failteromhat.com/slater/0192.pdf) (1846), Kilrea, p. 473, under “Watch & Clock Makers”, listing Daniel Glasco and James Shaw (accessed 16 July 2026).

"Trying to find Glasgow" (https://www.genesreunited.co.uk/boards/board/general_topics/thread/465937), Genes Reunited, post by Peter dated 25 January 2007, with later replies, naming Alexander and Rosanna as the parents of Thomas Glasgow of Lisnagaver, reporting Rosanna's death about 23 October 1822, and mentioning two possible clockmaker uncles at Kilrea (accessed 16 July 2026). This is descendant testimony rather than a contemporary parent record.

Public Record Office of Northern Ireland, Will Calendars (https://apps.proni.gov.uk/willscalendar_ie/willssearch.aspx), original registered will of Daniel Glasgow of Kilrea, proved 1871 (accessed 17 July 2026).

IrishGenealogy.ie (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/en/), civil marriage registration of Daniel Neely Glasgow and Mary Jane Boyd, 28 June 1888, Boveedy First Presbyterian Church; groom described as a farmer of Lisnagaver and his father recorded as Thomas Glasgow, farmer (accessed 17 July 2026).

W. Scott and William Macafee, 1851 Census for some Parishes and Townlands in the Barony of Kilconway, Co. Antrim (https://www.billmacafee.com/census/1851censuskilconway.pdf), Rasharkin parish, Lisnagavor, families 34, 35 and 37, recording the households of John, Alexander and Thomas Glasgow (accessed 19 July 2026).

An 1831 County Londonderry census transcription records “Danl.” in Kilrea town, house 37, under the standardised surname Glasgow. The surname as read from the census return is shown as “Glosger [?]”. The house was shared by two families and contained eight males and two females; nine occupants were Presbyterian and one belonged to the Established Church. William Macafee, Names of Householders listed in the 1831 Census Returns for the County of Londonderry (https://www.billmacafee.com/1831census/1831derrycensusplace.pdf) (transcription from PRONI MIC/5A/5–9B), Kilrea town, house 37, recording “Danl.” under the standardised surname Glasgow, with the surname in the return read as “Glosger [?]”; and Tamlaght O'Crilly parish, Inishrush, houses 2 and 91, recording John and Adam “Glasco” (accessed 19 July 2026).

"Tamlaght O'Crilly Lower Graveyard" (https://www.oneirishrover.com/tamlaght-graveyard/), transcription of the Glasgow gravestone recording Rose, wife of Adam Glasgow; Adam Glasgow; their daughter Eliza; their son James; and grandson William. The same page transcribes the 1842 marriage notice of Nancy, sixth daughter of Adam Glasgow of Inishrush (accessed 16 July 2026).

John W. Kernohan, The Parishes of Kilrea and Tamlaght O'Crilly (https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/books/Kilrea/Kilrea07.html), Appendix E, “Protestant householders in Tamlaght O'Crilly Parish in 1740,” containing two entries for Hugh Glasgow (online transcription by Richard John Torrens; accessed 19 July 2026).

“1770–1779: News transcripts for Kilrea & environs” (https://arborealis.ca/records/newspapers/kilrea-news/1770-1779/), Arborealis, transcript of the Belfast News-Letter, 14 April 1772, declaration dated Innisrush, 6 April 1772, listing Hugh Glasgow among inhabitants of Tamlaght O'Crilly parish (accessed 19 July 2026).

The return supplies no ages, occupations or relationships within either household. Alexander could theoretically have been an unnamed male in one of them, but there is no evidence that he was. John and Adam were probably part of the same local surname cluster, though their precise relationship is unknown.

The 1833 Tithe Applotment transcription records Adam Glasgow at Innisrush. “Tithe Applotment Books 1823–1838: Tamlaght O Crilly Parish, county Derry” (https://www.irishgenealogyhub.com/derry/tithe-applotments/tamlaght-o-crilly-parish.php), transcription entry for Adam Glasgow, Innisrush, 1833 (accessed 19 July 2026).

William Macafee, Data from the Tithe Applotment Books covering North Antrim (https://www.billmacafee.com/182030stithe/tithenorthantrim.pdf), records 7501–7502, Alexander and Robert Glasgow at Lisnagaver, Rasharkin parish, 1834 (accessed 16 July 2026).

"Rasharkin Presbyterian Church Baptisms" (https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/RasharkinP/Baptisms_1834.html), entries for the households of Alexander Glasgow and Molly McAughern and Thomas Glasgow and Mary Ann McCracken (accessed 19 July 2026).

Samuel was born about 1790 or 1791, placing him in roughly the same generation as Daniel Glasgow of Kilrea. His presence gives a concrete County Londonderry connection within the Glasgow household immediately beside the younger Alexander.

The census explicitly proves only that Samuel and John were brothers. It does not prove that either man was related to the younger Alexander, Thomas or Daniel. Household proximity is evidence for investigation, not a stated relationship.
Death
Alexander's date and place of death have not been identified.

He was alive before the births of his proposed children, but no secure burial, gravestone, probate or land record has been found that establishes a later date.

No Alexander Glasgow probate-calendar entry has been identified in the surviving PRONI calendars. This does not prove that Alexander left no will, since he may have died before the calendars begin or his estate may not have required probate.

"High Court of Justiciary Trial Papers," index, Scottish Indexes (https://www.scottishindexes.com/jcdetail.aspx?jcid=1797040&pid=179704079 : accessed 28 July 2026), Peter Glasgow of Whitebank, accused of rioting, tried 9 October 1797; citing National Records of Scotland, JC26/1797/40.

This Peter may have been the husband of Elizabeth Dick, but the identification is not proved.

Reasons the identification is plausible:

* Peter would have been about 35 in 1797.
* His last currently known child was baptised in 1795.
* No later baptism or death record has yet been securely identified for him.
* A sentence of transportation could explain his disappearance from later Scottish records.

Reasons for caution:

* The trial index gives no age, birthplace, occupation, spouse or relatives.
* The designation Whitebank has not yet been connected to Peter's Bathgate family.
* The other accused were associated with Haddington, Bankhead, Crooklaw and Dunse, whereas Peter's documented family was centred on West Calder and Bathgate.
* A sentence of transportation does not itself prove that the sentence was carried out.
* Another man of the same name could have been involved.

The 1797 prosecution should remain recorded as a possible event until the original trial papers, precognition and court minutes provide enough identifying information.
Possible identity of Peter's father
The John Glasgow who married or partnered with Margaret Mill is represented by the FamilySearch profile:

* John Glasgow, FamilySearch ID 9Q1F-9BL (https://www.familysearch.org/en/tree/person/9Q1F-9BL)

A leading working hypothesis identifies him with John Glasgow baptised on 28 March 1740 at Irvine, Ayrshire, son of George Glasgow and Margaret Martin.

That identification is supported by:

* John's suitable age to father Peter in 1762;
* the recurrence of Andrew, Margaret and Agnes in following generations;
* the wider family's movement through Ayrshire, Edinburgh, West Calder and Bathgate;
* the absence of another known wife or family for the Irvine-born John;
* an existing association between the wider Glasgow family and women surnamed Mill.

It remains unproved. No record has yet been found explicitly identifying the Irvine-born John as Margaret Mill's husband.

Son John and the Canongate family
Peter and Elizabeth's eldest known son, John Glasgow, was reportedly born on 7 June 1783 and baptised at Bathgate on 6 July 1783. 

He is probably the John Glasgow who later lived with Jean Bryce at Hume's Close, Canongate, Edinburgh, and worked as a shop porter.

Evidence supporting that identification includes:

* the age is within one year of the age recorded in 1841;
* Bathgate was outside Midlothian, matching the census response;
* Peter, John, Margaret, Elizabeth and William recur in both families;
* the family followed a plausible West Calder–Bathgate–Canongate migration route;
* John's probable sister Elizabeth is reported to have married at Canongate in 1809.

The identification remains circumstantial because no adult record explicitly states that the Bathgate-born John became the Canongate porter.
Unresolved 1800 marriage entry
A marriage index dated 1800 associates a woman surnamed Glasgow with Alexander Hunter. "Scotland, Marriages, 1561–1910," database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XYSW-FB4 : accessed 28 July 2026), Glasgow in entry for Alexander Hunter, 1800.

sources.citation:
Richard John Torrens,
"Kilrea First Presbyterian Church Records: Baptisms in 1827" (https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/KilreaP1/Baptisms/1827.html), entry
146, transcribed by Barbara Braswell: Robert, son of Daniel Glasgow and
Margaret Irwin of Kilrea, born 1 September and baptised 30 September
1827 (accessed 16 July 2026). The web page is a transcription of the
church register rather than an image of the original entry.

The transcription says that Daniel and Margaret were of Kilrea.
Kilrea should therefore be used as Robert's birthplace unless examination
of the original register shows that the residence statement applied only
to his parents and that he was born elsewhere.

Because the entry provides an exact birth date, Robert's birth should not
be entered merely as “about 1827”.
Parents
The baptismal entry explicitly names both parents. The relationships to
Daniel Glasgow and Margaret Irwin may therefore be marked certain.

|-

The baptism establishes parenthood but does not expressly describe
Margaret as Daniel's wife. No marriage entry for Daniel and Margaret has
yet been located.
Family background
Robert's father Daniel was later documented as a watch and clock maker at
Kilrea.

Slater's 1846 directory lists:

Slater's National
Commercial Directory of Ireland (https://www.failteromhat.com/slater/0192.pdf) (1846), Kilrea, p. 473, "Watch &
Clock Makers", listing Daniel Glasco and James Shaw (accessed 16 July
2026).

Fáilte
Romhat,
"Griffith's
Valuation of Ireland — Kilrea, County Derry" (https://www.failteromhat.com/griffiths/derry/kilrea.php), entries for Daniel
Glasgow at Church Street, Kilrea, and Claragh (accessed 16 July 2026).
This is a derivative index; the original valuation pages should be
examined.

Len Swindley,
"Glasgow
Genealogy Notes, Counties Tyrone & Londonderry, Northern Ireland
1840–69" (https://www.cotyroneireland.com/surnames/glasgow.html), transcription of a notice published in the Londonderry
Sentinel, 18 February 1853: James Glasgow, artist, died at Brooklyn,
New York, on 21 January 1853 and was described as the third son of
Daniel Glasgow of Kilrea (accessed 16 July 2026). The original newspaper
image has not yet been examined.

|-
| James Glasgow
| About 1828
| Unknown
| Certain son of Daniel; mother not identified in the death notice 
|}

The birth order of Robert and the unidentified son is not yet known.
Robert may have been Daniel's eldest or second son.
Later life
No record after Robert's baptism has been securely connected to him.

The following details remain unknown:

* whether he survived childhood;
* whether he remained at Kilrea;
* whether he followed Daniel into clockmaking;
* whether he married;
* whether he had children;
* whether he emigrated;
* his death date and place.

Robert's WikiTree death fields should therefore be entered conservatively:

{| class="wikitable" style="padding:5px; width:100%;"
|+ Recommended death fields
|-
! style="background-color:#E1F0B4;" | Field
! style="background-color:#E1F0B4;" | Entry
! style="background-color:#E1F0B4;" | Reason
|-
| Death date
| After 30 September 1827
| He was alive when baptised
|-
| Death place
| Unknown
| No later identifying record has been found
|}

Entering “after 1827” is technically supportable but adds little useful
information. Leaving the death date and place blank may be preferable
until another record is found.
Research NotesIdentity caution
Robert had a common forename combined with a surname found in several
unrelated or unproved Irish and Scottish families.

He should not be merged with another Robert Glasgow merely because that
person:

* was born in Ireland in approximately 1827;
* lived in County Londonderry or County Antrim;
* was a watchmaker or other craftsman;
* emigrated to the United States, Canada, Scotland, England or Australia;
* had relatives named Daniel, James or Margaret.

A later record should contain at least two or more identifying features,
such as:

* an exact or closely matching birth date;
* Kilrea as birthplace or residence;
* Daniel Glasgow named as father;
* Margaret Irwin named as mother;
* clockmaking or watchmaking within the family;
* a relationship to James Glasgow, the artist who died at Brooklyn;
* a relationship to Daniel's executor or proven Kilrea associates.
Not the Lisnagaver Robert Glasgow
A separate Robert Glasgow was living with Alexander and Mary Glasgow at
Lisnagaver, County Antrim, in the surviving 1851 census. That Robert was
aged ten and was therefore born about 1840 or 1841. "1851 Irish Census Returns: comma-delimited transcription" (https://durrushistory.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/10/1851irishcensusreturnscommadelimitedtextfilejul24_071.pdf), Lisnagaver,
Rasharkin, County Antrim, household 35, Alexander Glasgow household,
printed p. 183 (accessed 16 July 2026).

Montgreenan Mansion
In 1817, Robert Glasgow commissioned the construction of a Georgian mansion on his estate, which included architectural features designed by Alexander 'Greek' Thompson. This building, known as Montgreenan Mansion, was the home of the Viscounts Weir until 1982, when it was sold and converted into a hotel. The building is Category A listed by Historic Scotland. The modern house of Mountgreenan is located about three miles from Kilwinning. The original seat was located on a small knoll in a pleasant valley by the side of the Lugton, about half a mile north from the current mansion. Today, the building is used as a school or academy for boys, under the charge of Mr. Wilson from Glasgow. The school can accommodate forty boys within the house, and it is reportedly in a thriving state and highly regarded. 
Last Will and Testament of Dr. Robert Glasgow
Robert Glasgow passed away at Montgreenan House on 19 April 1827. By an earlier trust settlement, he had left sums of money to both his son (who was now deceased, without legitimate issue) and elder daughter, and also his brother James's natural sons, Robert and James. However, it is believed the bequests to his nephews was later successfully challenged in court. 
Biography of Robert Robertson Glasgow
Robert Robertson Glasgow, the beneficiary under the will of his father-in-law Dr. Robert Glasgow, changed his name to Glasgow as per the will's provision. The eldest son of Alexander Robertson of Gunsgreen House, Eyemouth, Robert Robertson succeeded his father in 1804. He married Anne Glasgow, the natural daughter and heir of Robert Glasgow, inheriting the sugar plantations of Mt Greenan and Sans Souci in St Vincent in 1828. He submitted claims for compensation for these plantations. Robert graduated in Medicine from the University of Edinburgh in 1797 and became a Fellow of the Royal College of Surgeons in 1802. He and Anne had four surviving children: Robert, Philadelphia Jane, Anne, and Charlotte Marie Cecilia. In 1841, Robert Glasgow, then aged 65 and of independent means, was living at Holly Walk, Leamington Priors, with his family and several servants. His eldest son, also Robert, was the father of Wilhelmina, who was one year old at the time. sources.citation: 1851 Census of Ireland, County Antrim, barony of Kilconway, parish of Dunaghy, Glenleslie, household 23. National Archives of Ireland, legacy household locator (http://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/pages/1851/Antrim/Kilconway/Dunaghy/Glenleslie/23/). Detailed transcription: 1851 Irish Census Returns: comma-delimited transcription (https://durrushistory.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/10/1851irishcensusreturnscommadelimitedtextfilejul24_071.pdf), printed p. 103, Glenleslie household 23. The transcription, including its absent-member and death entries, was examined; the full original return was not re-examined for this revision.

Household and family in 1851
Robert and Catherine occupied household 23 at Glenleslie. The seven people recorded as present were: 

{| class="wikitable sortable" style="padding: 5px; width:100%;"
|+ Glenleslie household 23: residents in 1851
|-

! style="background-color:#E1F0B4;" | Occupation or status
|-
| Robert Glasgow || Head || 72 || Farmer; could read; married in 1803
|-
| Catherine Glasgow || Wife || 68 || Spinning flax; could read; married in 1803
|-
| Margaret Glasgow || Daughter || 50 || Unmarried; no occupation recorded
|-
| Mary Glasgow || Niece || 34 || Unmarried; linen weaver
|-
| Mary Young || Granddaughter || 15 || Winding yarn
|-
| James Young || Grandson || 15 || Labourer; could read and write
|-
| Margaret McKillop || Servant || 18 || House servant
|}

All seven were recorded as born in County Antrim. Two further family members were entered as absent in America: John Glasgow, Robert's son, aged forty and a labourer; and Samuel Glasgow, his son, aged thirty and a linen weaver. They should not be counted among the residents physically present at Glenleslie. 

The death section records Catherine Hume, Robert's granddaughter, who died of scarlatina in spring 1850, aged three months. Her parents are not identified in the entry. 

The census therefore identifies Margaret, John and Samuel as Robert's children. His will independently identifies Margaret as his daughter and James and Mary Young as Margaret's children. It does not follow that these were his only children. Robert Glasgow of Glenleslie, will dated 3 February 1851, proved 13 February 1854; National Archives of Ireland copy, FamilySearch, image 229 (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJ8-MQQJ?view=fullText). Will details are retained from the earlier research transcription supplied for this profile; the image was not independently re-examined during this revision.

The probate notation states that he died in or about 1852. The will was proved on 13 February 1854. These details support an approximate death in 1852, not an exact death date or a separately verified place of death. 

The earlier research also identified a PRONI index entry for Robert Glasgow of Glenleslie among the Connor Diocesan Wills, 1854. The date of the will, the approximate death year and the probate year are distinct events. Public Record Office of Northern Ireland, Name Search, Pre-1858 Wills and Admons, Connor Diocesan Wills: Robert Glasgow, Glenleslie, 1854. PRONI Name Search (https://apps.proni.gov.uk/ProniNames_IE/SearchPage.aspx). Entry details retained from the earlier profile's recorded search of 5 August 2026.

1851 Census of Ireland, County Antrim, Dunaghy, Donbought, household 16. Detailed comma-delimited transcription (https://durrushistory.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/10/1851irishcensusreturnscommadelimitedtextfilejul24_071.pdf), printed p. 100. Compare W. Scott and W. Macafee, 1851 Census for some Parishes and Townlands in the Barony of Kilconway, Co. Antrim (https://www.billmacafee.com/census/1851censuskilconway.pdf), printed pp. 77-78, references 7883-7890. These are transcriptions of the same census, not independent family records.

W. Macafee, Data from the Tithe Applotment Books covering the Baronies of Cary, Dunluce and Kilconway in North Antrim plus the Barony of N. E. Liberties, Co. Londonderry (https://www.billmacafee.com/182030stithe/tithenorthantrimrevisionnamespdf.pdf), surname order, dated 17 October 2016, printed p. 41, index 5804: Robert Glasco, Doonbought [Dunbught No. 2], Dunaghy, 1825. Transcription, not an inspected original tithe-book image.

The will is not a complete list of children. John and Samuel are named as sons in the census but are not among the beneficiaries in the supplied will summary. The absence of the younger Robert from that summary therefore does not disprove the proposed relationship. Equally, an incomplete beneficiary list cannot be used to prove an additional child. 

The father-son link could be strengthened by a documented land succession, a church entry, or an independently established relationship between the younger Robert and one of this man's proved children. A direct statement is not the only possible route to a conclusion, but the present indirect evidence does not yet distinguish a son from another relative or namesake.
Margaret and the Glenleslie holding
The Dunaghy index to Griffith's Valuation lists Margaret Glasgow at Glenleslie and, separately, Robert Glasgow at Doonbought. Fáilte Romhat, Griffith's Valuation index, Dunaghy parish, County Antrim (https://www.failteromhat.com/griffiths/antrim/dunaghy.php), entries for Margaret Glasgow, Glenleslie, and Robert Glasgow, Doonbought. Name-and-townland index; original valuation pages, plot references and revision entries have not been inspected.

Identification of the emigrant sons
The census establishes that Robert had sons John and Samuel in America in 1851; it does not establish their later residences, wives or children. The earlier attachment of John Glasgow to the Elizabeth Fee and County Armagh family remains unproved. Robert's absent son John must also be distinguished from the forty-year-old nephew in John Glasgow's nearby household 21: that nephew was present at Glenleslie, was a linen weaver and had married in 1839. 

Margaret (Glasgow) Winters, associated with a Canadian family, has not been identified with Robert's unmarried daughter at Glenleslie. Their profiles should not be merged on the strength of their common name.
Mary Glasgow, niece, and the Hugh Glasgow lead
The thirty-four-year-old niece may be Mary (Glasgow) Montgomery. The earlier civil-register research records that Mary's marriage to Thomas Montgomery on 13 September 1862 named her father as Hugh Glasgow, weaver. Her death on 22 March 1898 gives an age consistent with birth about 1818, close to the census niece's estimated birth about 1816 or 1817. General Register Office of Ireland, civil marriage register, Thomas Montgomery and Mary Glasgow, 13 September 1862: register image (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1862/09623/5489617.pdf). Record details retained from the earlier profile's research.

General Register Office of Ireland, civil death register, Mary Montgomery, 22 March 1898: register image (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/deaths_returns/deaths_1898/05842/4654852.pdf). Record details retained from the earlier profile's research.

General Register Office of Ireland, civil marriage register, Hugh Glasgow and Ann Wilson, 24 December 1852: register image (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1852/09422/5413278.pdf). Earlier research comparison.

General Register Office of Ireland, civil marriage register, William Montgomery and Eliza Glasgow, 21 August 1854: register image (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1854/09463/5428881.pdf). Earlier research comparison.

Adam Glasgow and Rose of Inishrush were previously suggested as his parents, but the attachment is not retained. Adam's reported birth about 1758 makes the paternal chronology possible, while Rose's reported birth about 1767 would make her about twelve at Robert's birth. That is a serious chronological difficulty, not evidence of maternity. Their documented County Londonderry association also supplies no link to Robert's County Antrim family.

The proposal drew on the incomplete family named on Adam and Rose's gravestone and a notice describing Nancy Glasgow as Adam's sixth daughter. Those sources show that some of Adam's children are not named on the stone; neither identifies Robert as one of them. Tamlaght O'Crilly Lower Graveyard (https://www.oneirishrover.com/tamlaght-graveyard/), Glasgow gravestone transcription and photograph naming Rose, wife of Adam Glasgow; Adam; daughter Eliza; son James; and grandson William. Source retained from the earlier research.

Marriage Notices 1840-42 (https://cotyrone.com/~inthenews/marriages-notices-1840-42/), notice published 29 January 1842: John Kyle of Tyanee married Nancy, sixth daughter of Adam Glasgow of Inishrush, on 14 January 1842. Source retained from the earlier research.

General Register Office of Ireland, civil marriage register, Robert Glasgow and Jane Graham, 1866: register image (https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/churchrecords/images/marriage_returns/marriages_1866/11531/8240963.pdf). Identification comparison retained from earlier research.
Blair Extracts from the Belfast Newsletter, 1770-1779 (https://www.kinsleuth.com/belnews/1770-1779.htm), 7 April 1772, p. 3. Source retained from the earlier profile.

records.note: Profile Glasgow-3941 represents the Coltrim occupier documented from 1820 to 1831. Coltrim is immediately beside Moneymore, but no record proves his descent from James-1025 or identifies him with the Glenleslie or Lisnagaver namesakes.

sources.citation: "Flax Growers of Ireland, 1796 — County Tyrone" (https://www.failteromhat.com/flax/tyrone.htm), entry for Robert Glasgow, Lissan parish (accessed 16 July 2026).

The flax list does not state his townland, age or family relationships. However, his later documented residence at Coltrim within the same parish makes it reasonable to identify the 1796 flax grower with the Robert Glasgow subsequently recorded at Coltrim between 1820 and 1831.

The identification is based on continuity of name, occupation and parish rather than on a record explicitly linking the two entries.
Coltrim Lease, 1820
By November 1820 Robert was an established land occupier at Coltrim in the civil parish of Lissan. The Drapers' Company granted him a lease of a holding there. Public Record Office of Northern Ireland, PRONI D3632/B/17/5, Lease of a holding in Coltrim from the Drapers' Company to Robert Glasgow, November 1820. The original is closed; PRONI directs researchers to microfilm MIC617/11. Catalogue entry accessed 5 August 2026 through the PRONI eCatalogue (https://apps.proni.gov.uk/eCatNI_IE/SearchPage.aspx).

Public Record Office of Northern Ireland, Tithe applotment book for Lissan parish, 1827, PRONI FIN/5/A/203, Coltrim, entry 275, Robert Glasgow; original digital image accessed 5 August 2026 through the PRONI eCatalogue.

Public Record Office of Northern Ireland, Tithe applotment book for Lissan parish, 1827, PRONI FIN/5/A/203, Dunnabraggy, entry for Robert Glasgow; original digital image accessed 5 August 2026 through the PRONI eCatalogue.

"Index to the Lissan Tithe Applotment Book, Lissan Parish, Counties Tyrone and Londonderry, 1827" (https://www.cotyroneireland.com/tithe/lissan.html), entries for John and Robert Glasgow (accessed 16 July 2026).

1831 Census of Ireland (http://www.census.nationalarchives.ie/pages/1831/Londonderry/Loughinshollin/Lissane/Coltrim/2/), Coltrim, Lissan parish, house 2, Robert Glasgow household (accessed 16 July 2026).

William Macafee, "Names of Householders Listed in the 1831 Census Returns for the County of Londonderry" (https://www.billmacafee.com/1831census/1831derrycensusnames.pdf), record 22320, Robert Glasgow, Coltrim, Lissan: six males, five females, total eleven (accessed 16 July 2026).

The Coltrim occupier may have held land in both townlands, but the evidence does not establish this. The Dunnabraggy occupier may instead have been another man of the same name.

The two holdings should not be combined without estate, lease or family evidence linking them.
Separation from Robert Glasgow of Glenleslie
This Robert should not be identified automatically with Robert Glasgow of Glenleslie, who was recorded with his wife Catherine and family in County Antrim in 1851.

No inspected document directly connects the Coltrim household with the Glenleslie household.

A connection would require evidence such as a lease assignment, estate rental, church record, will, valuation record or another document naming the same relatives in both locations.

The two profiles should remain separate, or be maintained as an unmerged match, unless such evidence is found.
Robert Glasgow of Lisnagaver
The 1834 Rasharkin Tithe Applotment transcription records Alexander Glasgow at Lisnagaver, followed immediately by a Robert Glasgow holding land there. William Macafee, "Data from the Tithe Applotment Books covering North Antrim" (https://www.billmacafee.com/182030stithe/tithenorthantrim.pdf), Rasharkin parish, records 7501–7502, Alexander and Robert Glasgow at Lisnagaver (accessed 16 July 2026).

Separation from the younger Robert Glasgow
This Robert should not be conflated with Robert Glasgow, who was born about 1710, married in 1729 and was still living in 1772.

The man serving as a congregational bondsman and representative in 1699 must have belonged to an earlier generation. Evidence concerning the Robert living in 1772 should therefore remain attached to Glasgow-1143 and should not be used to extend the lifespan of this profile.
Later session and discipline records
A published continuation of the Larne and Kilwaughter congregational records contains a session list naming a Robert Glasgow and marking him as “turned out.” An entry dated 17 May 1747 explains that a former session member named Robert Glasgow had refused to make public satisfaction following an accusation of fornication. Classon Porter, “Congregational Memoirs: Larne and Kilwaughter,” The Christian Unitarian, vol. 3 (1864); Internet Archive (https://archive.org/details/christianunitari0003unse).

Original deed checks, 1738–1743
The original continuation of memorial 74015, a lease dated 13 February 1738, names Robert Glasgow, Jas Glasgow junior and Rachel Glasgow otherwise Wilson, explicitly described as Robert's wife. The association of James with the linked profile draws on the combined church and later deed evidence, including the explicit 1764 son clause; this 1738 instrument alone does not establish that parentage. The holding comprised 63 acres of Lower Ballykeel and 15 acres of Upper Ballykeel. Patrick Taylor proved execution at Carrickfergus on 12 April 1742. This confirms the wife clause previously known through an abstract; "junior" is not an explicit son clause, and the renewal wording abbreviates "person and persons", not sons.
