In 1840 Robert was enumerated in Lauderdale County, Alabama, with two younger males and three females. In 1850 he was back in Giles County, Tennessee, working as a laborer. Priscilla Glascoe, aged 28 and born in Tennessee, was living in his household. Robert's death date has not been established; 1850 is his last presently documented occurrence.
Research Notes
Wife and children
Robert is attached to Nancy as an uncertain wife. No contemporary record inspected in this research names his wife. A female aged 50–59 in Robert's 1840 household is compatible with the reported Nancy, but the census gives neither her name nor her relationship. 

The Delaware marriage of Robert Glasgow and Nancy Black on 19 January 1814 belongs to another couple. Delaware Vital Records, 1650–1974 (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QPQN-BH57), Robert Glasgow and Nancy Black, 19 January 1814; FamilySearch.

Delaware Public Archives, Military Records, vol. 5 (https://archivesfiles.delaware.gov/ebooks/Military_Records_Vol_5.pdf), return naming Robert Glasgow in the 7th Company, 5th Regiment, Delaware Militia.

FamilySearch, Robert Glasgow (about 1825–1911) (https://ancestors.familysearch.org/en/L7KB-QB9/robert-glasgow-1825-1911), parents shown as Robert Glasgow and Nancy Black; a derivative family reconstruction with linked record sources.

Nancy Black was therefore not added as his wife.

The family presently attached to Robert is assessed as follows:

{| class="wikitable" style="background:#e6ffe6;"
! Person !! Evidence and status
|-
| Priscilla Glasgow, born about 1822 || Probable daughter. A female aged 15–19 in Robert's 1840 household fits Priscilla's estimated birth exactly. In 1850 Priscilla Glascoe, 28, born Tennessee, was named in Robert Glaseoe's household. The 1850 census did not state relationships, so daughter is a strong inference rather than literal census wording. 
|-
| James J Glasgow, born about 1810 || Uncertain son. Robert's 1820 household had one boy aged 10–15 and two boys under 10, compatible with James's estimated age. An 1850 deed proves that James J Glasgow was then a Giles County landholder, but neither record names a relationship to Robert. Giles County, Tennessee, deed dated 6 April 1850, James J. Glasgow to John Tornerlin, 100 acres in district 6; transcription (https://tngenweb.org/giles/deed-james-j-glasgow-to-john-tornerlin-1850/), TNGenWeb.

|-
| Jessie M Glasgow, born 1818 || Uncertain son. Jesse Martin Glasgow's documented Giles County birth fits a male under 10 in Robert's 1820 household and the male aged 20–29 in 1840, but no inspected record names Robert as his father. “Glasco, Jesse Martin” (https://www.tshaonline.org/handbook/entries/glasco-jesse-martin), Handbook of Texas Online, Texas State Historical Association.

|-
| John Glasgow, born about 1800 || John was previously attached as Robert's son. However, Robert's census-derived birth range is 1790–1800, making him at most about ten years older than John. No record names them as father and son, so John was detached from Robert and Nancy.
|}

The 1840 household also contained an unidentified male aged 10–14. He may have been another child or a different household member.
Parentage
Robert Glasgow was previously attached as Robert's father. However, the shared Glasgow memorial in Gilders Creek Cemetery directly identifies a different Robert—Robert Glasgow, who died on 12 December 1813 aged five—as the son of Glasgow-1983 and Elizabeth. Gilders Creek Cemetery transcription and linked memorial photograph (https://genealogytrails.com/scar/newberry/gilders_creek_cem.htm), Newberry County, South Carolina; inscription for Elizabeth, spouse of Robert Glasgow, and “their son” Robert.

The profile associates this family with Robert and Margaret Glasgow of Plainfield, Illinois. That remains a working identification, rather than an independently demonstrated link between the Irish and American households. The proposed father, Robert Glasgow of Glenleslie, also remains uncertain.
Household in 1851
The return records eight living residents: Robert and Margaret, four daughters and two sons. A fifth daughter, Jane, appears in the separate death section, not among the people alive in the household. W. Scott and W. Macafee, 1851 Census for some Parishes and Townlands in the Barony of Kilconway, Co. Antrim (https://www.billmacafee.com/census/1851censuskilconway.pdf), dated 7 May 2014, printed pp. 77-78, references 7883-7890, Dunbought household 16. This transcription calls the seven-year-old son Samuel; the detailed comma-delimited transcription calls him Daniel.

| Hearsay, but it supplies Robert's only explicit association with Larne.
|-
| 1 June 1653
| James Collogh
| Jennett Woodsyde, wife of Robert Browne, had told him that Robert Glasgow shot Teige with a horseman's piece. 
| Second-hand testimony through a named informant.
|-
| 1 June 1653
| John Hill
| He had heard it generally reported that Robert Glascow killed Teige O'Sheale. 
| Unattributed local report.
|-
| 1 June 1653
| William Willson
| After returning to Islandmagee, he heard that Robert Glasgow had killed Teige but could not remember who told him. 
| Hearsay from an unidentified source.
|}

The four statements are not four independent confirmations. All are hearsay, and Con O'Sheale's version attributes the fatal shot to James Browne rather than Robert.

The genealogically useful wording is:

 one Robert Glaskow liuing in Larne 

This identifies Robert with Larne in the account. It does not name a wife, child, sibling, parent, occupation or property holding. The wording also need not mean that Robert was still alive or resident there when the examination was taken in April 1653; it may describe him at the time of the reported incident.

No examination of Robert, indictment against him or recorded judicial outcome has been located.
Date and origin
Robert's age and birthplace are unknown. The reported event occurred during the early rebellion period, when he was apparently old enough to travel in company with James Browne. A birth before about 1625 is therefore only a broad working estimate.

No evidence yet connects him with the separate Robert Glasgow baptised at Glasgow High Kirk in 1618, or with any other Scottish Glasgow family.
Research NotesBrowne–McCullogh network and the 1653 transplantation list
Robert's only documented connection to this circle comes through the 1653 examinations: Con O'Sheale associated him with James Browne, while Captain James McCullogh repeated Jennett Woodsyde's accusation. Robert Browne's own examination named sons Hugh and James, and identified Hugh as a lieutenant in McCullogh's company, but it did not call Robert Glasgow a soldier, servant, tenant or relative.

A government declaration dated 23 May 1653 survives as British Library 816.m.17[74], Wing I341. In the Islandmagee, Magheramorne and Ballynure quarter, the surviving print names Hugh Hoomes and James Lawder, together with Captain James McCullogh; it does not name James Browne or Ensign William Stephenson. Ireland, Commissioners for the Settling and Securing the Province of Ulster, By the Commissioners for the settling and securing the province of Vlster (Dublin: William Bladen, 1653), British Library 816.m.17[74], Wing I341; catalogue record describing the British Library original (https://catalog.folger.edu/record/538557).
Robert M. Young, Historical Notices of Old Belfast and its Vicinity (Belfast, 1896), pp. 80–86; Internet Archive (https://archive.org/details/historicalnotice00youn/page/80/mode/2up).

The contemporary administrative dossier survives in Trinity College Dublin MS 844, formerly F.3.18. Henry Jones's draft material of 14 June 1653 is at fol. 841, with further proposals dated 30 June; the relevant folios and enclosures have not yet been collated against the two list states. Judith Mary Carroll, “The papers of Henry Jones” (MSc thesis, Aberystwyth University), p. 82; online PDF (https://pure.aber.ac.uk/ws/portalfiles/portal/26062006/Carroll_Judith_Mary_MSc.pdf).

|-
| 1669
| Jo. Glascho
| Kilwaughter Demesne
| Liable householder in the County Antrim Hearth Money Roll. Public Record Office of Northern Ireland, T/307/A, 1669 County Antrim Hearth Money Roll; W. Macafee, surname-sorted transcription (https://www.billmacafee.com/1660shearthmoneyrolls/1669hearthmoneyrollsantrim.pdf), records 5347–5348 and 5730.

|-
| 1669
| Elizabeth Glascho
| Glenarm Town, Tickmacrevan parish
| Same-surname householder elsewhere in east County Antrim. No relationship is stated. 
|-
| 1700
| John Glasgow
| Kilwaughter
| Represented Kilwaughter in arrangements for the Larne and Kilwaughter Presbyterian congregation. Classon Porter, “Congregational Memoirs—Larne and Kilwaughter,” The Christian Unitarian, vol. 3 (1864), pp. 16–18 and subsequent extracts from the older congregational records; Internet Archive (https://archive.org/details/christianunitari0003unse).

|-
| 1700
| Robert Glasgow
| South side of Larne Water
| Represented a different part of the congregation. His relationship to John and James is not stated. 
|}

These records establish a continuing Glasgow presence within the Larne–Kilwaughter district. They do not establish that the 1653 Robert was father of James Glasgow, John Glasgow or Elizabeth Glasgow.

The present WikiTree attachment of James Glasgow as Robert's son is based on surname, chronology and neighbouring locations. No located record states that relationship. Robert could instead have been an uncle, brother, cousin, other collateral relative or an unrelated namesake.

Conclusion: possible family connection; unproved.

Jo/John and James Glascho were consecutive Kilwaughter Demesne householders in 1669, then recur in the same district's congregational business about 1700, when John represented Kilwaughter and James served as an overseer. This repeated association makes John and James probable close relatives, but no record states an exact kinship or proves either man was Robert's son.
A documented later Kilwaughter family
A later family can be established more securely.

The surviving Larne and Kilwaughter Presbyterian register records the baptism of James Glasgow, born 24 May 1731, as a son of Robert Glasgow and Rachel Wilson. Larne and Kilwaughter Non-Subscribing Presbyterian congregation, baptismal register beginning 1720, baptism of James Glasgow, son of Robert Glasgow and Rachel Wilson, born 24 May 1731; Public Record Office of Northern Ireland microfilm and congregational register series. The original register image should be cited when available.

Registry of Deeds, Ireland, memorial 74015, book 105, p. 301, deed dated 13 February 1738 and registered 12 April 1742; William Agnew of Kilwaughter to Robert Glasgow of Kilwaughter, naming Rachel Glasgow alias Wilson and James Glasgow junior as additional lives.

South Carolina equity pleadings and associated Wilson–Glasgow inheritance papers, 1817–1818, sworn answers concerning the estate of Archibald Wilson. The pleadings identify Rachel Wilson as wife of Robert Glasgow; James Glasgow as their son; and the deponent Robert Glasgow as James's eldest son and Rachel's paternal grandson. Surviving online transcriptions should be checked against the original court papers.

The Robert associated with the early-1640s incident was already old enough to accompany James Browne. Even at an implausibly young age of about fifteen in 1641, he would have been about 112 in 1738 and about 121 in 1747.

The two Roberts therefore should not be merged.

The later Robert could have been a son, grandson, great-grandson, nephew or other relative of the 1653 Robert. No record yet specifies which, if any, relationship applied.
The missing generational bridge
The evidence currently produces two separate groups:

:Early group
:* Robert Glaskow of Larne, associated with events about 1641
:* Jo. Glascho and James Glascho, householders at Kilwaughter in 1669

:Later documented family
:* Robert Glasgow and Rachel Wilson
:* their son James Glasgow, born in 1731

The missing evidence is a record identifying the parentage of the later Robert Glasgow, or naming the heirs or children of James Glasgow or John Glasgow.

A 1727 probate index entry exists for “James Glasgow, Kilwater”. The underlying pre-1858 probate file appears not to survive, so the index cannot establish his heirs. Diocese of Connor probate index, 1727, entry for James Glasgow of Kilwater. The entry establishes that probate proceedings once existed but does not preserve the will's contents or name beneficiaries.

Glasgow surname Y-DNA project results and published project grouping for tested descendants of northern Irish Glasgow lines. DNA evidence supports paternal relatedness among the tested later branches but does not identify the seventeenth-century connecting ancestor.

National Records of Scotland, Glasgow High Kirk Old Parish Register 644/1, reported reference 10/272, baptism of Robert Glasgow, 17 November 1618. The reported entry names Robert Glasgow and Jonet Conynghame as parents.

| Certain
| Named as Robert's mother in the same entry. 
|}

The baptism establishes parenthood but does not expressly describe
Margaret as Daniel's wife. No marriage entry for Daniel and Margaret has
yet been located.
Family background
Robert's father Daniel was later documented as a watch and clock maker at
Kilrea.

Slater's 1846 directory lists:

{| class="wikitable" style="padding:5px; width:100%;"
|+ Watch and clock makers at Kilrea, 1846
|-
! style="background-color:#E1F0B4;" | Name
! style="background-color:#E1F0B4;" | Directory heading
! style="background-color:#E1F0B4;" | Place
|-
| Glasco Daniel
| Watch & Clock Makers
| Kilrea
|-
| Shaw James
| Watch & Clock Makers
| Kilrea
|} Isaac Slater,
Slater's National
Commercial Directory of Ireland (https://www.failteromhat.com/slater/0192.pdf) (1846), Kilrea, p. 473, "Watch &
Clock Makers", listing Daniel Glasco and James Shaw (accessed 16 July
2026).

Fáilte
Romhat,
"Griffith's
Valuation of Ireland — Kilrea, County Derry" (https://www.failteromhat.com/griffiths/derry/kilrea.php), entries for Daniel
Glasgow at Church Street, Kilrea, and Claragh (accessed 16 July 2026).
This is a derivative index; the original valuation pages should be
examined.

Len Swindley,
"Glasgow
Genealogy Notes, Counties Tyrone & Londonderry, Northern Ireland
1840–69" (https://www.cotyroneireland.com/surnames/glasgow.html), transcription of a notice published in the Londonderry
Sentinel, 18 February 1853: James Glasgow, artist, died at Brooklyn,
New York, on 21 January 1853 and was described as the third son of
Daniel Glasgow of Kilrea (accessed 16 July 2026). The original newspaper
image has not yet been examined.

|-
| James Glasgow
| About 1828
| Unknown
| Certain son of Daniel; mother not identified in the death notice 
|}

The birth order of Robert and the unidentified son is not yet known.
Robert may have been Daniel's eldest or second son.
Later life
No record after Robert's baptism has been securely connected to him.

The following details remain unknown:

* whether he survived childhood;
* whether he remained at Kilrea;
* whether he followed Daniel into clockmaking;
* whether he married;
* whether he had children;
* whether he emigrated;
* his death date and place.

Robert's WikiTree death fields should therefore be entered conservatively:

{| class="wikitable" style="padding:5px; width:100%;"
|+ Recommended death fields
|-
! style="background-color:#E1F0B4;" | Field
! style="background-color:#E1F0B4;" | Entry
! style="background-color:#E1F0B4;" | Reason
|-
| Death date
| After 30 September 1827
| He was alive when baptised
|-
| Death place
| Unknown
| No later identifying record has been found
|}

Entering “after 1827” is technically supportable but adds little useful
information. Leaving the death date and place blank may be preferable
until another record is found.
Research NotesIdentity caution
Robert had a common forename combined with a surname found in several
unrelated or unproved Irish and Scottish families.

He should not be merged with another Robert Glasgow merely because that
person:

* was born in Ireland in approximately 1827;
* lived in County Londonderry or County Antrim;
* was a watchmaker or other craftsman;
* emigrated to the United States, Canada, Scotland, England or Australia;
* had relatives named Daniel, James or Margaret.

A later record should contain at least two or more identifying features,
such as:

* an exact or closely matching birth date;
* Kilrea as birthplace or residence;
* Daniel Glasgow named as father;
* Margaret Irwin named as mother;
* clockmaking or watchmaking within the family;
* a relationship to James Glasgow, the artist who died at Brooklyn;
* a relationship to Daniel's executor or proven Kilrea associates.
Not the Lisnagaver Robert Glasgow
A separate Robert Glasgow was living with Alexander and Mary Glasgow at
Lisnagaver, County Antrim, in the surviving 1851 census. That Robert was
aged ten and was therefore born about 1840 or 1841. "1851 Irish Census Returns: comma-delimited transcription" (https://durrushistory.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/10/1851irishcensusreturnscommadelimitedtextfilejul24_071.pdf), Lisnagaver,
Rasharkin, County Antrim, household 35, Alexander Glasgow household,
printed p. 183 (accessed 16 July 2026).

Identification with the 1613 cordiner
The 1613 burgess roll identifies a Robert Glasgow as a cordiner who was admitted burgess and guild brother as heir of a burgess. 

This is probably Ninian Glasgow’s son because:

* the name and location agree
* the entry occurs in the year of Ninian’s testament
* Robert was already an adult and executor
* admission as heir of a burgess is compatible with succession within an established Glasgow family

The roll does not explicitly name Ninian as the preceding burgess. The cordiner identification is therefore highly probable, while the testamentary parentage remains the direct proof.
The November 1645 James
The original Glasgow parish register records James Glasgow on 25 November 1645 as the son of Robert Glasgow and Jonet Cunynghame, with James Cunynghame and Johne Muir named as godfathers. Source: S90 Research of Barbara Flesher Nichols, Carthage, MO. Barbara Flesher Nichols of Carthage, Missouri, devoted many hours to researching her ancestors. Most of her work was between 1980 and 1993. Her main focus was on her FLESHER family and her husband's family, the NICHOLS. She also gathered information on ancestors, ROUX, MOORE, LOTT, NORTHWAY, and HERRMANN, among others. In the last years of her research she used a computer and entered her basic information into a database, but she never had access to the internet. Her research was all traditional; interviews, phone calls, snail mail, libraries and microfilm. She accumulated a small library of documents, photos, and letters. Her information is generally dependable for what she had to work with, however it was never documented by present genealogical standards. One discovery she was proud of was that Henry Fleischer who died in Virginia in 1831 was a direct ancestor to both her and her husband. I am her son-in-law. My goal is to preserve as much of her research as possible. I began by entering and improving her data into a RootsMagic database, which I hope the family will preserve. My plans are to eventually move as much as possible to wikitree.com. Dennis Bowers, Carthage, Missouri, 2023

* aged 60;
* the brother of household head John Glasgow;
* unmarried;

* born in County Londonderry.

Brother
The 1851 census explicitly identifies John Glasgow as Samuel’s brother. 

John’s original 1846 marriage register records him as a bachelor farmer of Lisnagaver, parish of Rasharkin, marrying Margaret Garvin. It names his father as John Glasgow, farmer. Civil marriage register of John Glasgow and Margaret Garvin (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/view/?record_id=cima-3156063), 16 November 1846; John Glasgow, bachelor, farmer, of Lisnagaver, parish of Rasharkin; father John Glasgow, farmer (accessed 17 July 2026).

Marriage status
Samuel never married.

He was recorded as unmarried in the 1851 census and as a bachelor in his civil death registration. 
Death
Samuel died at Lisnagaver on 17 August 1875, aged 85. 

His civil death registration described him as:

* a bachelor;
* a weaver;
* resident at Lisnagaver.

The combination of name, residence, occupation and marital status provides strong continuity with the Samuel recorded in the 1851 household.

Elizabeth Ross of Lisnagaver, present at Samuel’s death.
Research NotesParentage
Samuel was previously attached as a son of Adam Glasgow and Rose.

That reconstruction was based on:

* Samuel’s approximate age;
* his County Londonderry birthplace;
* the proximity of the Inishrush family to Lisnagaver;
* the wider local Glasgow family cluster.

No record explicitly names Adam or Rose as Samuel’s parents.

The available direct evidence points elsewhere:

# The 1851 census identifies Samuel as the brother of John Glasgow. 
# John’s original 1846 marriage register identifies his father as John Glasgow, farmer. 
# The spouse, date, residence, parish and occupation uniquely connect that marriage entry with the John who shared the Lisnagaver household with Samuel.
# Therefore, absent evidence that John and Samuel were paternal half-brothers, Samuel’s father was also John Glasgow.

The attachment to Adam Glasgow should therefore be removed.
Possible father
John Glasgow of Glenleslie is the best current candidate for the father indicated by the collateral evidence.

He was:

* an older man named John Glasgow;
* a farmer;
* resident in County Antrim;
* of a generation compatible with Samuel’s birth about 1789–1791.

His reported 1791 marriage is also broadly compatible with Samuel’s estimated birth, allowing for normal age errors in later records.

No record currently connects John Glasgow directly with Lisnagaver or explicitly names Samuel as his son. The relationship should therefore remain marked uncertain.

Samuel’s mother should remain blank unless a record identifies her.
Half-brother qualification
The census word “brother” does not expressly distinguish between full and half brothers.

It is therefore theoretically possible that Samuel and John shared only one parent. No evidence has been found for such a relationship.

The ordinary interpretation remains that they were full brothers and shared the father named in John’s marriage record.
Previous Glenleslie reconstruction
Samuel and John were previously attached as sons of John Glasgow and Rose Alexander of Glenleslie.

No contemporary record supports that parentage directly.

The Glenleslie census identifies a different younger John as the older John’s nephew and records other children, but does not connect Samuel or John Glasgow of Lisnagaver with that household.

The possible link to John Glasgow rests only on name, occupation, age and locality and must remain uncertain.
Distinction from other men named Samuel Glasgow
This Samuel should not be confused with Samuel John Glasgow, who married Margaret Calagher in 1866.

That groom named Andrew Glasgow as his father and was therefore a different man.

Samuel should also not be confused with the men appearing in the PRONI Will Calendars as:

* Samuel Glasgow of Camagh, County Armagh, who died in 1896;
* Samuel Glasgow of Belfast, who died in 1902.

No matching probate-calendar entry has been found for Samuel of Lisnagaver, who died in 1875.

This negative search does not prove that he left no will. It only excludes those exact-name probate entries from his identity.
Baptism records
The surviving Rasharkin Presbyterian baptism register begins in 1834, decades after Samuel’s birth.

It cannot therefore provide a baptism naming Samuel’s parents.

The collateral proof from the 1851 census and John’s 1846 marriage remains the strongest available evidence for Samuel’s father.
Birth estimate
Samuel’s records give slightly different implied birth years:

* age 60 in 1851 suggests birth about 1790 or 1791;
* age 85 in 1875 suggests birth about 1789 or 1790.

A birth estimate of about 1790 best accommodates both records.
Further research
Useful additional records may include:

* church or estate records predating the surviving Rasharkin Presbyterian register;
* leases or valuation records connecting Lisnagaver and Glenleslie;
* records naming the children of John Glasgow;
* probate, administration or land records for Samuel;
* burial records;
* any record distinguishing full and half siblings within the Lisnagaver family;
* records naming Samuel’s mother.

Samuel was born in 1790. He passed away in 1875.

The death of Samuel Glasgow was registered on 17 August 1875 in Ballymoney, aged 85. GRONI civil death index (https://geni.nidirect.gov.uk/search/death), Samuel Glasgow, 17 August 1875, aged 85, Ballymoney registration district, D/1875/31/1005/3/280.

General Register Office for Northern Ireland, “GRONI's online search results” (https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/gronis-online-search-results), explanation that “Full” means over 21 (accessed 9 August 2026).

Brother Daniel Glasgow of Kilrea
Thomas was a brother of Daniel Glasgow, the watch and clock maker of Kilrea.

Daniel's registered will refers to:

 “my late brother Thomas Glasgow” ... “my nephew Daniel Neely Glasgow” 

The will was proved in 1871. Public Record Office of Northern Ireland, Will Calendars (https://apps.proni.gov.uk/willscalendar_ie/willssearch.aspx), registered will of Daniel Glasgow of Kilrea, proved 1871; refers to his late brother Thomas and nephew Daniel Neely Glasgow (accessed 17 July 2026).

Together, the will and marriage identify Daniel of Kilrea as Thomas's brother and Daniel Neely as Thomas's son.

Daniel died at Kilrea on 16 October 1871, aged 75. The original civil return names Kate Glasgow, present at death, Kilrea as the informant. Ireland civil death return, no. 362, Daniel Glasgow, died 16 October 1871 at Kilrea, aged 75, widower and watchmaker; informant Kate Glasgow, present at death, Kilrea, original image (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/deaths_returns/deaths_1871/020759/7282767.pdf) (accessed 9 August 2026).

Griffith's Valuation transcript for Rasharkin parish, entries for Lisnagaver (https://www.irishgenealogyhub.com/antrim/griffiths-valuation/parish-of-rasharkin.php) (accessed 9 August 2026). This is a derivative transcript; the original valuation page, map and plot references remain to be checked.

His reported age is consistent with the age recorded in 1851 and gives an estimated birth in about 1814 or 1815. His burial place has not been identified.
Brother Daniel and the Prescott connection
Thomas was a brother of Daniel Glasgow, watchmaker of Kilrea. Daniel's will calls Thomas his late brother and Daniel Neely Glasgow his nephew; Daniel Neely's marriage independently identifies Thomas as his father. Public Record Office of Northern Ireland, Will Calendars (https://apps.proni.gov.uk/willscalendar_ie/willssearch.aspx), registered will of Daniel Glasgow of Kilrea, proved 1871 (accessed 17 July 2026).

Daniel's death return names Kate Glasgow as informant but gives no relationship. Ireland civil death return no. 362, Daniel Glasgow, died 16 October 1871, Kilrea, original image (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/deaths_returns/deaths_1871/020759/7282767.pdf) (accessed 9 August 2026).

Grenville County land records, DGS 8200419, image 35, registered will of Robert Glasgow of Prescott, dated 9 October 1849, original image (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSLG-LWY9-S).

Grenville County land records, DGS 8200419, image 36, Memorial 13, dated 30 October 1856 and registered 13 November 1856, original image (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSLG-LWYM-6).
Grenville County land records, DGS 8200419, image 240, Memorial 465, registered 7 October 1861, printed p. 397, original image (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSLG-LWB8-D).

1901 Ireland Census, Form B1, Coltrim townland, Moneymore DED, South Derry, County Londonderry, house 7, householder Thomas Glasgow, Form A schedule 6, National Archives of Ireland, original image (https://nationalarchives.ie/collections/search-the-census/view-pdf/?doc=nai000629314) (accessed 9 August 2026).

It does not call her his sister and does not state any relationship.

Catherine Glasgow, probable daughter of Thomas and Mary Ann, is a plausible candidate. She was aged 24 in October 1877 and reported three years' residence at Christchurch. That chronology is consistent with her still being in Ireland in 1871, but does not prove that she was the informant.

If the informant was Catherine, Daniel was her uncle, not her brother. An older sister, daughter, daughter-in-law, other niece or cousin remains possible.
Marriage, Daniel's mother and a possible second wife
No record has been found for the marriage of Thomas and Mary Ann.

No positive evidence has been found for another wife. Thomas and Mary Ann are named together in the 1842, 1843 and 1846 baptism entries and in the 1851 household. 

Daniel Neely's marriage names his father but not his mother. Mary Ann is therefore his probable mother, based on the established family and chronology, but the relationship remains unproved.

Daniel was born before June 1867 rather than about 1870. Mary Ann, born about 1821, would have been no more than about 45 or 46. The chronology does not require a second marriage.
Parents
A later family account identifies Thomas as a son of Alexander Glasgow and Rosanna and states that Rosanna died about 23 October 1822. 

No contemporary record naming Thomas's parents has been found. Both relationships should remain uncertain. Rosanna's maiden surname has sometimes been given as Shaw, but no source proving that surname has been identified.
Priority Research
* Priority 1 — identify the Coltrim Thomas: obtain Form A schedule 6 for house 7, Coltrim, Moneymore DED, 1901. Record every occupant, age, relationship, occupation and birthplace. This will determine whether the discarded circa-1823 estimate had any basis.

* Priority 1 — later baptisms: inspect PRONI MIC1P/292, Rasharkin Presbyterian baptisms, 1847–1867, for Nancy, Margaret, Catherine or Kate, Sarah, Alexander and Daniel Glasgow. Search Glasgow, Glasgo, Glascow, Glasco and Glassgow, with McCracken, McCrackin, McCraken and McCochrane variants. A Daniel entry naming Mary Ann would substantially resolve the second-marriage question; another mother would provide the first positive evidence for a second wife. Public Record Office of Northern Ireland, Guide to Church Records (https://www.proni.gov.uk/publications/proni-guide-church-records), entries for Rasharkin Presbyterian MIC1P/292, Second Portglenone MIC1P/357, Boveedy MIC1P/18, First Kilrea MIC1P/87 and Second Kilrea MIC1P/20 (accessed 9 August 2026).

* Priority 2 — Catherine: obtain Catherine Ekberg's original 1946 Victorian death certificate, registration 12550. Record both parents' full names, birthplace, duration in each colony or state and the informant. Compare these details with the 1877 New Zealand marriage notice and the 1871 Kate Glasgow informant.

* Priority 2 — Sarah: locate the marriage of Sarah Glasgow and Charles Taylor, probably before the birth of Ellen Taylor in January 1897. The marriage should state Sarah's age, residence and father.

* Priority 2 — land succession: obtain the original Griffith's Valuation page and map for Lisnagaver and follow Thomas's plot through the valuation-revision books to at least 1888. Determine whether it passed to Mary Ann, Daniel Neely or another relative, and compare the adjoining holdings of John and Alexander Glasgow.

* Priority 3 — deaths: obtain Thomas's original 1870 civil death return and the candidate 1914 death registration for Mary Ann. Record the informants, exact residences and stated relationships rather than relying only on indexes.

Robert's sister Mary is independently identified in a 15 September 1869 deed, registered 1 July 1870, as Mary Black, formerly Mary Glasgow. Her children, including John Black, Rose Ann Black, Jane Miller, Agnes Black and Thomasina Montgomery, conveyed interests under Robert's will to Mary Eno Glasgow; the deed also records their inheritance of their unmarried intestate sister Elizabeth Black's share. Grenville County land records, DGS 8200420, image 277, C298, dated 15 September 1869 and registered 1 July 1870, original image (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSLG-LQTY-K).
GRONI civil death index (https://geni.nidirect.gov.uk/search/death), Thomas Glasgow, 21 June 1870, aged 55, Ballymoney registration district, D/1870/31/1005/2/197.

A different passage on the same page associates James with William born about 1708. The complete inscription has not been recovered, and a shared memorial would not by itself distinguish a son, grandson or collateral relative. James is therefore a useful descendant lead, not a proved child of this William.

No inspected record identifies William's wife or children.

Registry of Deeds memorial 62131 names an adult William Glasgow as an adjoining Larne occupier in March 1736. That occurrence cannot be this William, who was only about six, and belongs to the older Larne identity represented by William Glasgow.

The original Larne and Kilwaughter register survives at PRONI under reference `MIC/1B/6`. Its marriage and baptism entries should be searched before 1769 for William's household.
Unidentified William Glasgow, deed witness in 1772
A lease dated 12 May 1772 from John Miller, currier of Gardenmore in Old Town of Larne, to David Drennan, weaver, names Wm Glasgow, David Dickey and James Fairies, all of Larne, as witnesses. Either William Glasgow or William Glasgow could be this witness; the deed gives no age, occupation or relative to distinguish them. The son William named in the trust clause is Drennan's son, not a Glasgow relationship. Registration on 9 November 1784 does not prove that the witness William Glasgow was still alive then. sources.citation:
This profile represents that child.

No reviewed source connects the Polwarth child with the currently attached father, the Cavers Covenanter, the attached children Isabell Glasgow and William Glasgow, or the later William Glasgow and William Glasgow profiles. These links are retained as uncertain working hypotheses. A separate early derivative prisoner list names a William Glasgow of Cavers as a Covenanter, transportee and survivor of the wreck of the Croune of London near Deerness, Orkney, on 10 December 1679; that same-name man is not proved to be the Polwarth child. The 1679 Cavers deposition, survivor list and 1684 Ormistoun record are gathered on Glasgow-4138; those records also do not identify the Polwarth child. A Cloud of Witnesses, for the Royal Prerogatives of Jesus Christ (1714), Appendix, "A List of the Banished," printed pp. 274–276. The list states that men who escaped the wreck were marked with a star and records "Will. Glasgow" under Cavers with that mark. Internet Archive scan (https://archive.org/details/cloudofwitnesses00edin). A clearer reset of the list appears in John H. Thomson's 1871 edition, p. 523. Page 523 (https://archive.org/details/cloudofwitnesses00thom/page/523/mode/1up).

A. Francis Steuart, ed., Diary of Thomas Brown, Writer in Kirkwall, 1675–1693 (Kirkwall: William Peace, 1898), p. 10. Brown's contemporary entry for 10 December 1679 records the Croun, carrying about 250 men taken at Bothwell Bridge and intended for Virginia, wrecked at or near the Mull Head of Deerness at about nine in the evening. HathiTrust image (https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=hvd.32044081269342&seq=24). Brown does not name William.

Joseph Wagner, Scottish Colonization before Darien: Opportunities and Opposition in the Union of the Crowns (PhD thesis, University of St Andrews, 2020), pp. 157–158 and note 66, citing NRS SP4/5, Charles II to the Scottish Privy Council, 29 June 1679, fols. 174–175. University of St Andrews thesis (https://doi.org/10.17630/sta/47). National Records of Scotland, SP4/5, "Warrant book of Secretary for Scotland," 16 October 1678–30 April 1680. NRS catalogue (https://catalogue.nrscotland.gov.uk/nrsonlinecatalogue/details.aspx?df=&di=y&dt=&k=&ko=a&r=SP4&reference=SP4%2F5&ro=s&st=1&tc=y&tl=n&tn=n&tp=n). The original letter was not available digitally for this review.

Robert Wodrow, The History of the Sufferings of the Church of Scotland from the Restoration to the Revolution, vol. III, pp. 130–131. Google Books (https://books.google.co.uk/books?id=eEwsAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA130).

This is the principal evidence for the Cavers man, but it does not identify him with the subject of this profile.

Thomas Brown's contemporary diary independently confirms the prisoner group, intended destination, date and approximate place and time of the wreck. Later Covenanter accounts state that many prisoners remained confined below deck as the ship broke apart and give totals of roughly two hundred dead and forty to fifty survivors. John Blackadder, Memoirs of the Rev. John Blackader (Edinburgh, 1826), pp. 230–232. The published work preserves an account said to have been obtained from a survivor of the wreck. Internet Archive (https://archive.org/details/memoirsrevjohnb00blacgoog).

Those details derive from partisan or survivor-based accounts rather than an official inquiry and should be attributed accordingly.

A post-wreck petition by William Paterson, the merchant directing the transportation, survives in the published Privy Council register. Paterson alleged that English and Scottish dissenters had influenced the captain or crew and intended to land the prisoners in England or Ireland. Paterson had an obvious financial and legal interest in assigning responsibility for the failed voyage. His petition documents the dispute following the wreck but does not prove that the loss was deliberate. P. Hume Brown, ed., The Register of the Privy Council of Scotland, Third Series, vol. VI, 1678–1680 (Edinburgh: H. M. General Register House, 1914), pp. 415–417, particularly p. 416. Google Books (https://books.google.com/books?id=00_aKojSqGIC&pg=PA416). Wagner, Scottish Colonization before Darien, pp. 158–159, discusses Paterson's petition and his interest in blaming others. Thesis (https://doi.org/10.17630/sta/47).

Mark Jardine, "Beyond Orkney's Fatal Shore: The Wreck of The Croune, 10 December 1679," Jardine's Book of Martyrs, 10 December 2016. Jardine compares the 1714 list with Privy Council material, identifies corroborated prisoners and discusses the list's unknown provenance. Article (https://drmarkjardine.wordpress.com/2016/12/10/beyond-orkneys-fatal-shore-the-wreck-of-the-croune-10-december-1679-history-scotland/).

No relationship between John Glasgow and the Cavers William is stated. Their appearance together establishes only that both were assigned to the same Cavers parish group.

The earliest source located during this review that specifically places William after the wreck is Joseph A. Waddell's 1886 first edition of Annals of Augusta County, Virginia. Waddell reproduced part of the banished-prisoner list, explained that the survivors' names were printed in italics, included John and William "Glascow" under Cavers, and then stated that all fifty survivors made their way to northern Ireland. Joseph A. Waddell, Annals of Augusta County, Virginia (Richmond: Wm. Ellis Jones, 1886), p. 5, note 1. Waddell includes John and William "Glascow" under Cavers and states that the fifty survivors reached northern Ireland. His note cites A Cloud of Witnesses for the prisoner list but does not identify a source for the destination statement. Page image and transcription (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:Annals_of_Augusta_County.djvu/21).

Joseph A. Waddell, Annals of Augusta County, Virginia, from 1726 to 1871, 2nd ed., revised and enlarged (Staunton, Virginia: C. Russell Caldwell, 1902), p. 8. The edition says that "some" escapees made their way to Ulster and names ten survivors, including James Young but neither Glasgow. Internet Archive full text (https://archive.org/stream/annalsofaugustac00wadd/annalsofaugustac00wadd_djvu.txt).

Rob Close, "Deerness Covenanter Memorial," Ayrshire Notes, no. 28 (Autumn 2004), p. 15, note 17. The note states that nine survivors were believed to have escaped to Ulster, citing J. Thomson's A Cloud of Witnesses as quoted by Robert B. Miller. PDF (https://aanhs.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/an28.pdf).

The corresponding archive catalogue entry has now been located. It describes a 1993 letter from Robert B. Miller of Richmond, Virginia, enclosing a list of survivors from the wreck of the Crown together with his sources. Orkney Library and Archive, catalogue entry, "The Wreck of 'The Crown'," 1993: letter from Robert B. Miller, Richmond, Virginia, enclosing a list of survivors from the wreck with his sources. Catalogue entry (https://yourscottisharchives.com/catalogues/598d9888-6456-3c76-8c19-128ffce82a4b?component-id=fb62ec54-9931-3921-b3ea-9b4b94ddcdb6&terms=%22Songs%22). The dossier was located but could not be inspected because no digital copy was available.

Lawrence Holden and Mark Thompson, "The Covenanters in Ulster," Part Six, "1666–1679, A Kirk Divided," pp. 6–7, Ulster-Scots Community Network. The study names ten wreck survivors said to have fled to Ulster, including James Young of Teviotdale, and describes the post-Bothwell refugee route from Irvine to Carrickfergus and government watch at Larne and Donaghadee. PDF (https://ulster-scots.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/USCN-Covenanters-in-Ulster-Tabloid.pdf). This is a modern secondary study; its evidence for each named destination requires verification.

FamilySearch, Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564–1950: Elizabeth Glasgow, baptised 17 August 1656 at Polwarth, father William Glasgow, record XYL3-24Q (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XYL3-24Q); William Glasgow, baptised 4 April 1658 at Polwarth, father William Glasgow, record XTBH-RJS (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XTBH-RJS). These are derivative entries from the same indexed collection. The original register images were not accessible for this review.

Ancestry, Scotland, Select Births and Baptisms, 1564–1950, William Glasgow, Polwarth, 4 April 1658. Record (https://www.ancestry.co.uk/discoveryui-content/view/13605720:60143?indiv=1&tid=&pid=&queryId=3716e5a39223fa4f412cbf7454bff742&usePUB=true&_phsrc=UPT9&_phstart=successSource).

National Records of Scotland, Old Parish Registers, Polwarth, parish 754, reference 10/62, frame 37, marriage of James Glasgow and Agnes Waitte, 18 June 1663; FamilySearch, Scotland Marriages, 1561–1910. FamilySearch record XTL8-X6D (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XTL8-X6D).

FamilySearch, Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564–1950: John Glasgow, 29 April 1666, XTBS-Z9H (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XTBS-Z9H); Patrick Glasgow, 4 August 1667, XTBS-98Z (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XTBS-98Z); Jean Glasgow, 16 April 1671, XYLM-Y4Z (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XYLM-Y4Z); Robert Glasgow, 1 April 1673, XYHJ-3R9 (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XYHJ-3R9); Agnes Glasgow, 29 October 1676, XYLM-Y4H (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XYLM-Y4H); and Margaret Glasgow, 24 May 1679, XYL9-Q32 (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XYL9-Q32). These are derivative indexes. The entries name a father James but, as indexed, do not establish the mother's identity or prove that every entry concerns the 1663 groom.

FamilySearch, Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564–1950, William Glasgow, baptised 24 September 1671 at Kirknewton and East Calder, father Andrew Glasgow. Record VQ4K-F2B (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQ4K-F2B).

Francis J. Grant, ed., The Commissariot Record of Lanark: Register of Testaments, 1595–1800 (Edinburgh, 1903), p. 38, citing commissary record CC14/5/9. PDF (https://www.tradeshouselibrary.org/uploads/4/7/7/2/47723681/the_commissariot_record_of_lanark__register_of_testaments__1595-1800_~_1903.pdf#page=50).

FamilySearch, Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564–1950, Margaret Glasgo, baptised 7 February 1692 at Hawick, father William Glasgo. Record X11X-46N (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:X11X-46N). This is a derivative index entry.

FamilySearch, Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564–1950, Isabell Glasgow, 12 November 1694, Cavers. Record VQH7-5PY (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQH7-5PY). The original register image was not accessible for this review.

FamilySearch, Scotland, Marriages, 1561–1910: Patrick Glasgow and Helen Fairbairn, Stitchel, 23 May 1707, XYQ1-96T (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XYQ1-96T); Eccles, 1 July 1707, XTL4-LPT (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XTL4-LPT). FamilySearch baptisms at Stitchel: John, 2 May 1708, FMMW-9QT (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:FMMW-9QT); Agnes, 31 July 1709, X111-P2H (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:X111-P2H); James, 11 May 1712, FMM7-GMJ (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:FMM7-GMJ); and Isobell, 10 August 1716, FMMM-S4Y (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:FMMM-S4Y). The marriage indexes do not name Patrick's parents.

FamilySearch, Scotland, Marriages, 1561–1910, William Glasgow and Margaret Scott, married 4 March 1709 at Cavers. Record XYQG-3XD (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:XYQG-3XD). This is a derivative index entry.

Trinity College Dublin, 1641 Depositions Project, examination of Con O Sheale, taken at Lisnegarvy on 21 April 1653, TCD MS 838, fol. 153r, identifier 838153r210. The allegation involving Robert was hearsay; the record is used here only for the statement that Robert Glaskow lived at Larne. Transcript (https://1641dep.abdn.ac.uk/items/show/42821.html).

W. Macafee, transcription of Hearth Money Rolls (1669) for the Baronies of Cary, Dunluce, Kilconway, Toome, Antrim and Glenarm in Co. Antrim (2011), p. 36, records 5730, 5348 and 5347. PDF (https://www.billmacafee.com/1660shearthmoneyrolls/1669hearthmoneyrollsantrim.pdf). This is a modern transcription of PRONI T/307/A; the original roll was not inspected.

Robert Magill Young, ed., The Town Book of the Corporation of Belfast, 1613–1816 (Belfast, 1892), p. 271. Internet Archive full text (https://archive.org/stream/townbookofcorpor92belf/townbookofcorpor92belf_djvu.txt).

Classon Porter, "Congregational Memoirs—Larne and Kilwaughter," The Christian Unitarian, vol. II (1863), pp. 410–414, and vol. III (1864), pp. 16–18. Volume II text (https://archive.org/stream/christianunitari0002unse/christianunitari0002unse_djvu.txt); Volume III text (https://archive.org/stream/christianunitari0003unse/christianunitari0003unse_djvu.txt). Porter stated that the original congregational record could not be located and that he worked from a copy.

Melanchthon Glasgow, History of the Glasgow Family, undated descendant account written after 1892, pp. 1–2 and 5. The author describes the early ancestry as obscure and relies on family tradition without identifying a contemporary record. WikiTree-hosted PDF (https://www.wikitree.com/photo/pdf/Glasgow-590).

No documentary link between Glasgow-591 and either the Polwarth child or the Cavers survivor has been found. Family tradition / research lead only.

Research Notes
* The established identity on this profile is the child baptised at Polwarth on 4 April 1658. The Cavers Covenanter and Croune survivor is a same-name hypothesis, not an established identification.
* The Cavers heading establishes a parish association. It does not establish William's birthplace, exact residence or later home.
* For the Cavers same-name man, the Ulster hypothesis is now assessed as plausible rather than merely possible.
** Waddell's 1886 statement directly includes William among survivors said to have reached northern Ireland. 
** Waddell's 1902 revision narrows the claim and omits both Glasgows, but expressly lists only "some" survivors. 
** Close preserves a nine-survivor tradition derived through Robert B. Miller. 
** A probable member of William's exact Cavers survivor group, James Young, is repeatedly named among those who fled to Ulster. 
** None of these sources is contemporary evidence of William's own arrival or settlement.
* The 1658 Polwarth baptism is the sourced identity for this profile. It remains only a candidate for the Cavers man because the chronology fits and another adult Glasgow household can be documented in the same district.
** No record connects the Polwarth child with Cavers, Bothwell Bridge, John Glasgow or the wreck.
** The father named in the index is simply William Glasgow. The index does not identify him with William Glasgow of Inveresk.
** James Glasgow of Polwarth/Gordon is a stronger local kinship lead than the unattached Inveresk theory, but no relationship has been proved.
* The current attachments of Isabell Glasgow and William Glasgow as William's children are not established by their indexed records. Those entries prove later Glasgow activity at Cavers, not parentage.
* The attached father and children are retained as uncertain relationship hypotheses pending an original record or other evidence that bridges the identities.
* John Glasgow was another Cavers survivor, but the prisoner list states no relationship between John and William.
* Cavers and Hawick were separate adjoining parishes in Roxburghshire. Polwarth and Gordon were separate parishes in Berwickshire. Scotland's People place and record pages: Cavers (https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/place-page/Cavers/GAZ00352/-); Hawick (https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/place-page/Hawick/GAZ00597/REX01605); Hawick parish description, identifying Cavers on its eastern boundary (https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/virtual-volumes/volume-images/volume_data-OS1-29-14/REX01692); and Polwarth (https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/place-page/Polwarth/GAZ00924/REX00785).

** The named survivor lists were compared with the Cavers group. James Young of Teviotdale is the strongest associate-level bridge.

* Published Scottish testament indexes
** The published Lauder commissary testament index was searched for Glasgow, Glasgo, Glascow, Glasco and Glassgow without finding a relevant entry. Francis J. Grant, ed., The Commissariot Record of Lauder: Register of Testaments, 1561–1800 (Edinburgh: Scottish Record Society). Internet Archive (https://archive.org/details/commissariotreco18laud). Absence from a published index does not prove that no testament or related paper existed.

Scottish Record Society, published Peebles commissary testament material covering 1681–1699. Internet Archive (https://archive.org/details/scottishrecords10scot). This is a limited chronological and jurisdictional search.

* Irish probate index
** Sir Arthur Vicars's index to Irish Prerogative wills was searched for William and surname variants. No William Glasgow was found.
** The index does contain an Archibald Glasgow, clerk, associated with Rathmullan or Ramelton, County Donegal, in 1677. This confirms another pre-wreck Ulster occurrence but supplies no relationship to William. Sir Arthur Vicars, Index to the Prerogative Wills of Ireland, 1536–1810 (Dublin, 1897). PDF (https://archive.org/download/indextoprerogati00vica/indextoprerogati00vica.pdf). The Prerogative index is not a complete index to local diocesan probate records.

National Records of Scotland, "Hearth Tax, 1691–1695." Research guide (https://www.nrscotland.gov.uk/learning-and-events/research-guides/taxation-records/?section=hearth-tax-1691-1695). FamilySearch catalogue, Scottish hearth-tax records. Catalogue (https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/catalog/212753).

** Determine whether Miller included the Cavers William among the nine Ulster fugitives.
** Record every source Miller supplied and establish whether Close, Holden/Thompson and Waddell depend on the same earlier account.
** This is currently the single highest-value unresolved Ulster source.

* Original Polwarth registers
** Inspect and transcribe the original baptismal entries for Elizabeth Glasgow on 17 August 1656 and William Glasgow on 4 April 1658.
** Record the full wording, residence, occupation, mother's name, witnesses, sponsors and marginal notes.
** Search immediately before and after both entries for additional children of the same father.
** Inspect the original 1663 marriage of James Glasgow and Agnes Watt and the six Gordon baptisms.
** Compare residences and witnesses to test whether James and the father William were relatives.

* Polwarth kirk session and Marchmont estate
** Search Polwarth kirk-session minutes, NRS CH2/721, which include minutes for 1652–1668, for Glasgow, Glasgo, Glascow, Glasco and Glassgow. National Records of Scotland, CH2/721, Polwarth kirk-session records. Catalogue (https://catalogue.nrscotland.gov.uk/nrsonlinecatalogue/browseTreeview.aspx?reference=CH2%2F721). Scotland's People, Polwarth kirk-session record page. Record page (https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/place-page/Polwarth/GAZ00924/REX00785/REX00785).

sources.citation:
He is also listed among the banished who survived the shipwreck at the Moul Head of Deerness, and appears again as a servant at Ormistoun in a list of October 1684. The records place him at Cavers and Ormistoun between 1679 and 1684; no birth, family or death is stated, so his birth is placed before 1679 and Cavers is inferred from the record.
Research Notes
The 1679 deposition, the shipwreck-survivor list and the 1684 servant list are compatible stages in one man's record trail rather than three independently evidenced men. This documented Cavers man is also discussed as a same-name hypothesis on Glasgow-1605, which represents a child baptised at Polwarth in 1658. No reviewed record connects that child with the Cavers man. Their identification remains unproved.

William Glasgon, who married Margaret Scott at Hummelknows in Cavers parish on 4 March 1708/09, is another possible later identity for this Cavers man. The marriage follows the 1684 servant record by about 24 years, but gives no age, occupation, parents or other link to the Covenanter. The two adult records remain separate pending a direct bridge. Research Notes
The testament does not state Katherine's age, birthplace, marriage or death.
Saltcoats is an uncertain creation-field birthplace inferred from her father's
residence, not a stated fact. The document's use of bairn proves a
parent-child relationship; it does not by itself establish that Katherine was
a young child in 1637.

Glasgow-1030 has been excluded as the present identity of her father: his
documented Glasgow-burgh household has no Saltcoats, sailor, Isobell Gray,
Katherine or Agnes bridge. Create the distinct Saltcoats John first and attach
Katherine to that new profile with certain status.
Possible Dublin identity
Katherine Glasgow, whose birth and parents are unknown, was
buried at St Audoen, Dublin, on 3 November 1713. A Saltcoats child alive in
1637 could chronologically have survived to that date, and west-coast maritime
connections make movement to Ireland possible. Name and broad chronology do
not establish identity, however. With no age, Scottish origin, relative,
marriage or migration bridge, that profile is excluded as the present match;
later positive evidence could still justify a merge. Irish
Genealogy, Church of Ireland burial register, Katherin Glasgow, St Audoen,
Dublin, buried 3 November 1713, record identifier DU-CI-BU-25141, register p.
96, record
image (https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/church/d-116-1-1-098.pdf).

John died by 1555. He left no direct heirs. His estates passed to his nephew John (Spreul) Spreull (abt.1510-), son of his brother Robert Spreul (abt.1500-1555), burgess of Glasgow. 
Legacy and Descendants
The nephew’s grandson, also named John (Spreul) Spreull (abt.1590-), became Provost of Renfrew near the beginning of the reign of Charles I. He was father to John Spreul (1616-), Town Clerk of Glasgow and later one of the Principal Clerks of Session. 

The Town Clerk’s son, John Sprewel of Blackairne, married Agnes Sprewel, daughter of Andrew Sprewel of Milton. Their son, Andrew Sprewel of Blackairne, worked as a writer in Edinburgh. 
Clan Association
The Sprewel family, in its many spellings, has recognition as a Sept of Clan Lennox by the Chief and Council of Lennox. Proclamation Recognising Spreull Family as a Sept of Clan Lennox, 2020
